DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Safety 

 Precautions When Servicing Truck Tires 

CAUTION and SAFETY FIRST are bywords when handling tires. Careful 
attention to the suggestions that follow can prevent crippling injuries or 
even death. Make it a rule to respect the terrific force contained in an 
inflated tire.

Wheels must be properly maintained. Improperly maintained wheels and 
wheel components can adversely affect the life of the tire and the wheel. When 
inflated, a tire is potentially very destructive. Accidents are caused by 
careless handling and inexperience. 

Follow the safety procedures in this section and obtain safety 
literature from your wheel distributor, wheel manufacturer, NHTSA or OSHA. In 
addition, if you have any questions, consult the distributor or manufacturer 
directly. 

The load carrying requirements of each vehicle must also be determined 
before selecting the proper tire/wheel combination. Always remember that the 
weakest weight carrying component of the vehicle (i.e., tire, wheel, axle, 
bearings, etc.) determines the overall maximum and safe load carrying capacity 
for the vehicle.

 WARNING: EACH INDIVIDUAL AXLE, WHEEL AND TIRE HAS ITS OWN MAXIMUM WEIGHT AND 
INFLATION RATING. DO NOT OVERLOAD OR OVER-INFLATE BEYOND THE CAPACITY OF THE 
LOWEST RATED COMPONENT OF THE SYSTEM. 

 WARNING: AN INFLATED TIRE CAN BE VERY DANGEROUS IF MISUSED OR WORN OUT. MANY 
ACCIDENTS, SOME FATAL, HAVE RESULTED FROM IMPROPER HANDLING AND OPERATION OF 
TRUCK RIMS AND WHEELS. IT IS OF THE UTMOST IMPORTANCE THAT THE PRECAUTIONS 
OUTLINED ON THESE PAGES BE CAREFULLY FOLLOWED BY ALL PERSONS SERVICING WHEELS 
TO AVOID PERSONAL INJURIES AND COSTLY DAMAGE. 

 WARNING: NEVER MOUNT A SMALLER DIAMETER TIRE ON A LARGER DIAMETER WHEEL. WHEN 
REPLACING TIRES, ALWAYS MATCH THE TIRE SIZE TO THE WHEEL SIZE. IMPROPER 
MATCHING CAN CAUSE THE TIRE BEAD TO BREAK DURING MOUNTING OR INFLATION. THE 
TIRE CAN EXPLODE DURING INFLATION, EXPELLING BOTH TIRE AND WHEEL INTO THE AIR 
WITH ENOUGH FORCE TO INFLICT PROPERTY DAMAGE, SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. 

When replacing tires, use the same size, load range and construction 
type as originally installed on the truck. When replacing wheels, use original 
equipment manufacturer's wheels or equivalent available from your Ford dealer 
with equivalent capacity, width, offset and mounting configuration as those 
originally installed on your vehicle. Use of improper replacement wheels and 
tires can adversely affect ride, tire and wheel life, handling, load carrying 
capacity, bearing life, tire clearance to body and chassis components, vehicle 
ground clearance, vehicle width and brake cooling and the life of the wheels 
and tires. 

Prepare for any tire repair operation in a safe and efficient way. Use 
caution not to drop tires, wheels or assemblies on the feet, hands or body, or 
heavily on the floor. Tires are heavy. Use a wheel jack such as Rotunda Wheel 
Dolly 014-00030 or equivalent to maneuver tires.

[FIGURE: E73641A.gif]

 WARNING: NEVER POSITION BODY IN FRONT OF RIM DURING DEFLATION. ALWAYS KEEP EYES 
AWAY FROM VALVE WHEN DEFLATING TIRES. 

Deflating a tire properly is very important to your safety. First, 
reduce the pressure as much as you possibly can by pressing the valve core 
plunger. Only then should you remove the valve core to completely deflate tire 
before removal from vehicle or disassembling any components. On duals, deflate 
both tires completely. Keep your eyes away from the valve. 

Demounting tires from the wheels requires special care. Follow the 
procedures given in this section. 

Use only standard tire mounting tools and equipment. The use of 
makeshift tools to force tires on or off wheels is dangerous and must be 
avoided.

Always lubricate tire beads, wheel rim flanges and bead seats to assure 
seating of tire beads on wheel rim. Use Rubber Lubricant D9AZ-19583-A or 
equivalent meeting Ford specifications ESR-M99B135-A and ESA-M1B6-A. 

Make sure all air is out before removing tires from wheels. Use special 
care when using tire irons. 

Grip tire irons firmly and keep them free of oil and grease. They can 
slip and fly with tremendous force. 

Mark all damaged parts for destruction to prevent future use. Always 
remove rust or other foreign matter to ensure proper fitting during 
reassembly. Clean and lightly repaint all rusted wheel rim areas.

 WARNING: WHEN PAINTING USED WHEELS, DO NOT USE EXCESSIVE AMOUNTS OF PAINT. THIS 
CAN CAUSE NUT LOOSENING, WHICH CAN LEAD TO PREMATURE WHEEL FAILURE OR LOOSE 
WHEELS, RESULTING IN SERIOUS, PERHAPS FATAL, INJURY. 

 WARNING: WHEN PAINTING ANY WHEEL PARTS, ALWAYS ALLOW THE PARTS TO DRY 
THOROUGHLY. IF THE PAINT IS NOT DRY WHEN THE WHEELS ARE MOUNTED, TORQUE VALUES 
WILL NOT BE MAINTAINED BECAUSE OF THE PAINT BEING "FORCED OUT". EXCESS PAINT 
THICKNESS WILL CAUSE THE DISC WHEELS TO LOOSEN. RETIGHTEN THE WHEEL NUTS AFTER 
80-160 KM (50-100 MILES) WHEN NEW PAINTED DISC WHEELS ARE REINSTALLED ON 
VEHICLE. 

 NOTE: If replacing one component of an assembly, make sure the size and type 
are a proper match. Never use parts of a different manufacturer than the 
original wheel. Do not use a different size or type.

Replace damaged or excessively corroded parts. Abuse during road 
operations or in mounting tires can cause damage that can weaken the parts. 
Parts that are excessively corroded are weakened. Always inspect for and 
replace damaged or heavily rusted parts. Never use wheel rims that are out of 
shape, bent, excessively rusted, or cracked or broken in any way. 

 WARNING: DAMAGED WHEEL AND RIM PARTS, SUCH AS BENT FLANGES, RIMS OUT OF ROUND OR 
DEEP TOOL MARKS CAN PREVENT COMPONENTS FROM SEATING PROPERLY. THIS CAN LEAD TO 
AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION, RESULTING IN SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. DESTROY ALL 
UNSERVICEABLE PARTS. 

 WARNING: ALLOYS OR METAL SURFACES WITH CRACKS ARE DANGEROUS. THESE COMPONENTS 
CAN FAIL WITHOUT WARNING DURING INFLATION OR LATER ON THE VEHICLE. DESTROY ALL 
PARTS THAT ARE CRACKED. 

Inspect for and remove light rust and other foreign matter. 
Accumulation of such material on the engagement surfaces of the wheel rim base 
can prevent the proper fit of these parts. Use of a rust preventative during 
mounting will minimize rust. 

 WARNING: ALWAYS WEAR SAFETY GOGGLES OR A FACE SHIELD WHEN PERFORMING ANY BUFFING 
OPERATION. 

Tires and rims often require a buffing operation before being mounted 
once the regular service has been completed. 

 WARNING: AVOID HAMMERING WITH A STEEL HAMMER AS YOU CAN DAMAGE THE RIM. ANY 
HAMMERING CAN DISLODGE PARTICLES. NEVER HAMMER ON AN INFLATED ASSEMBLY. 

 WARNING: ALWAYS INFLATE THE TIRE IN ROTUNDA INFLATION CHAMBER 104-00104 OR 
EQUIVALENT, OR USE AN OSHA-APPROVED PORTABLE TIRE SAFETY CAGE. THIS IS A 
SAFEGUARD AGAINST IMPROPER ASSEMBLY, INADVERTENTLY MISMATCHED PARTS, AND OTHER 
ASSEMBLY ERRORS. REMEMBER, AN INFLATED TIRE CONTAINS POTENTIALLY EXPLOSIVE 
ENERGY, AND ASSEMBLIES CAN BE PROPELLED IF THERE IS A SUDDEN RELEASE OF AIR. 
IN EMERGENCY SITUATIONS, WHERE A SAFETY CAGE OR PORTABLE SAFETY DEVICE IS NOT 
AVAILABLE, USE THE VEHICLE'S SPARE WHEEL AND TIRE. 

 WARNING: STAND CLEAR WHEN USING A SAFETY CAGE OR AN OSHA-APPROVED RESTRAINING 
DEVICE. ALWAYS USE A CLIP-ON AIR CHUCK WITH A REMOTE VALVE AND PRESSURE GAUGE. 
DO NOT REST ANY PART OF THE BODY AGAINST THE DEVICE DURING INFLATION. IF THE 
COMPONENTS ARE NOT SEATED PROPERLY AND AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION OCCURS, THE AIR 
BLAST OR MOVEMENT OF THE RESTRAINING DEVICE CAN CAUSE INJURY. 

Place tire assembly in safety cage and inflate to a maximum of ten 
pounds. Check to see that beads are properly seated. Completely deflate tire 
to prevent tube from buckling. Reinflate to recommended pressure.

Use only accurate, tested gauges to insure proper air pressure. Check 
all gauges regularly with a master gauge. 

Never attempt to short-cut the above procedures.

A jack is provided for wheel and tire maintenance only.

 WARNING: NEVER RUN THE ENGINE WHEN THE VEHICLE IS SUPPORTED BY A JACK. 

 WARNING: PROPER PRECAUTIONS SHOULD ALWAYS BE TAKEN WHEN JACKING A VEHICLE UP TO 
PREVENT PERSONAL INJURY OR DAMAGE TO THE VEHICLE: 

ALWAYS BLOCK ONE AXLE WITH WHEEL CHOCKS TO PREVENT UNEXPECTED MOVEMENT. 

ALWAYS USE PROPER HEAVY-DUTY JACK STANDS. 

MANUALLY CAGE PARKING BRAKE CHAMBERS WHEN WORKING ON THE REAR AXLE. 

APPLY PARKING BRAKE WHEN WORKING ON FRONT AXLE. 

Do not overload wheels. Make sure the combination of load and vehicle 
weight does not exceed the rated load of the wheels used. Wheels are designed 
to sustain their rated load using the maximum tire size recommended for that 
rim width by the Tire and Rim Association.

 WARNING: EACH INDIVIDUAL AXLE, WHEEL, AND TIRE HAS ITS OWN MAXIMUM WEIGHT AND 
INFLATION RATING. DO NOT OVERLOAD OR OVERINFLATE BEYOND THE CAPACITY OF THE 
LOWEST RATED COMPONENT OF THE SYSTEM. 

 WARNING: ALLOYS OR METAL SURFACES WITH CRACKS ARE DANGEROUS. THESE COMPONENTS 
CAN FAIL WITHOUT WARNING DURING INFLATION OR LATER ON THE VEHICLE. DESTROY ALL 
PARTS THAT ARE CRACKED. 

Inspect rims and wheels for damage during tire checks and at periodic 
maintenance intervals. Remove and replace worn or damaged parts. 

 WARNING: DO NOT EXCEED MAXIMUM INFLATION PRESSURES. THIS IS DETERMINED BY THE 
SIZE AND PLY RATING OF THE TIRE, BUT IS NOT TO EXCEED THE MAXIMUM COLD 
INFLATION PRESSURE LISTED FOR THE WHEEL EVEN IF THE TIRE IS APPROVED FOR A 
HIGHER LOAD OR INFLATION. IT IS ALSO IMPORTANT TO MAINTAIN UNIFORM INFLATION 
IN BOTH TIRES OF A DUAL ASSEMBLY SO THAT WEIGHT IS EQUALLY SUSTAINED. 

 WARNING: DO NOT RUN VEHICLE ON ONE TIRE OF DUAL ASSEMBLY. WHEN THERE IS LOSS OF 
AIR IN A DUAL TIRE, THE CARRYING CAPABILITY IS REDUCED AND THE LOAD MUST BE 
SUSTAINED BY THE OTHER TIRE AND WHEEL. INFLATE BOTH TIRES TO BALANCED, 
RECOMMENDED PRESSURES BEFORE FURTHER OPERATION. 

 WARNING: THUMPING OR SIMPLY LOOKING AT THE TIRE DOES NOT GIVE AN ACCURATE 
PRESSURE READING. PERIODICALLY CHECK YOUR AIR PRESSURE GAUGE FOR ACCURACY AND 
ALWAYS USE IT TO CHECK TIRE PRESSURE. 

 WARNING: NEVER ADD AIR TO A TIRE/WHEEL ASSEMBLY OPERATED IN A RUN-FLAT OR 
UNDERINFLATED CONDITION (80% OR LESS OF RECOMMENDED PRESSURE). IF AIR IS ADDED 
TO AN ASSEMBLY WITH ANY OF THE PREVIOUS CONDITIONS, AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION 
CAN OCCUR, CAUSING SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. 

After first 80-160 km (50-100 miles) of service, recheck wheel nut 
torque. Loose wheel nuts can cause excessive wear around bolt holes, dangerous 
wheel vibration, and metal fatigue failure. Excessive torque is also dangerous 
in that it can cause stud or wheel breakage.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Wheel and Tire

 WARNING: DO NOT ATTEMPT TO MOUNT DISC WHEELS WITH COUNTERSUNK MOUNTING HOLES OR 
TWO HAND HOLES (BSN TYPE) ON WHEEL MOUNTING SYSTEMS DESIGNED FOR CENTER 
PILOTING AND TWO-PIECE INTEGRAL WASHER WHEEL NUTS (ISO TYPE). DO NOT ATTEMPT 
TO MOUNT DISC WHEELS WITH TWO-PIECE INTEGRAL WASHER WHEEL NUTS DESIGNED FOR 
CENTER PILOTING (ISO TYPE) ON WHEEL MOUNTING SYSTEMS DESIGNED FOR DISC WHEELS 
WITH COUNTERSUNK MOUNTING HOLES AND TWO HAND HOLES (BSN TYPE). USE OF 
INTERMIXED WHEELS AND MOUNTING SYSTEMS CAN LEAD TO DAMAGE TO THE WHEEL 
MOUNTING SYSTEM AND RESULT IN THE WHEELS COMING LOOSE IN OPERATION. 

[FIGURE: F6693C.gif]

[FIGURE: F8412A.gif]

 Removal 

 WARNING: NEVER ADD AIR TO A TIRE/WHEEL ASSEMBLY OPERATED IN A RUN-FLAT OR 
UNDERINFLATED CONDITION (80% OR LESS OF RECOMMENDED PRESSURE). IF AIR IS ADDED 
TO AN ASSEMBLY WITH ANY OF THE PREVIOUS CONDITIONS, AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION 
CAN OCCUR, RESULTING IN SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. 

Prior to removal of tire and wheel from vehicle, deflate tire 
completely. Reduce pressure as much as possible by pressing valve core 
plunger, then removing valve core. Refer to safety precautions. If working on 
dual wheels, deflate both tires completely before loosening mounting bolts 
when there is obvious or suspected damage to the tire or wheel components.

Loosen, but do not remove, wheel nuts. 

Raise vehicle until wheel and tire clear floor. 

Remove wheel nuts, wheel and tire from hub. In the event of replacement 
of a rear inner wheel, valve extension, if present, must be transferred to new 
wheel. 

 Wheel Installation 

Check all parts for damage, including wheels and rims. Make sure studs, 
nuts, and mounting faces of hub and wheels are clean and free from grease. 
Replace any worn or damaged parts. 

 CAUTION: Be careful not to damage stud threads. 

Mount single wheel or inner and outer dual wheel over studs. Make sure 
studs and flange nut threads are dry. Do not use oil or lubricant. 

Tighten nut and washer assemblies alternately in sequence shown. 
(Ten-hole wheel is illustrated; use similar sequence for 8-hole wheel.) Do not 
tighten fully. This procedure will permit uniform seating of nuts and ensure 
even, face-to-face contact of wheels and hub. 

 IDH ISO Disc Wheel 

[FIGURE: F7947A.gif]

 CAUTION: Insufficient mounting torque can cause wheel shimmy, resulting in 
damage to parts and extreme tire tread wear. Excessive mounting torque can 
cause studs to break and discs to crack in the stud hole area. 

Tighten M20 nuts for 8-hole ISO disc wheels to 380-447 Nm
 (280-330 lb-ft) and M22 nuts for 10-hole ISO disc wheels 
to 611-677 Nm (450-500 lb-ft) in same sequence.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Tires, Tubeless

 Demounting 

 WARNING: FAILURE TO COMPLY WITH THESE PROCEDURES CAN RESULT IN FAULTY 
POSITIONING OF THE TIRE AND WHEEL RIM PARTS, AND CAUSE THE ASSEMBLY TO BURST 
WITH EXPLOSIVE FORCE, RESULTING IN SERIOUS PHYSICAL INJURY OR DEATH. NEVER 
MOUNT OR USE DAMAGED TIRES OR WHEELS. 

 WARNING: NEVER POSITION BODY IN FRONT OF WHEEL RIM DURING DEFLATION. ALWAYS TURN 
EYES AWAY FROM VALVE WHEN DEPLATING TIRES. 

 CAUTION: Demounting and mounting tires can be extremely dangerous if proper 
safety precautions are not followed. Before starting this procedure, read all 
safety precautions under Safety at the beginning of this section. 

Before demounting, deflate tire completely by removing valve core. Run 
wire through valve to assure deflation. Loosen both beads from rim by driving 
the flat end of the tire tool between the tire bead and rim flange, straighten 
tool to a vertical position and hammer downward on the neck to pry tire from 
rim. Repeat about every 203 mm (8 inches) around flanges until beads are free 
from rim. 

[FIGURE: F8392B.gif]

Place wide side of rim down. Lubricate tire bead and rim. Insert curved 
end of both tools, and step on tire opposite valve to direct first bead into 
the well. Hold one tool in position with foot and pull second tool toward 
center of rim. Progressively work first bead off rim. 

[FIGURE: F8393B.gif]

Stand assembly in vertical position with valve near top. Lubricate 
second bead and rim. Insert straight end of tool between tire bead and the 
back rim flange, hooking the tool over the second flange. Lean tire assembly 
toward tool and provide a rocking or bouncing action to pry the rim out of the 
assembly. Be sure opposite side of second bead is into well.

[FIGURE: F8394B.gif]

 Mounting 

Before starting the mounting process, check the rim manufacturer's load 
and inflation rating and the Tire and Rim Association's recommendation for 
proper wheel rim width. Check wheel rims and components carefully for damage. 
Discard bent, cracked, and out-of-round wheel rims. Inspect the valve stem to 
assure that it is in good condition, is not cracked or bent irregularly, and 
is capable of holding proper air pressure. The rim must be thoroughly cleaned 
and painted for prevention of corrosion. 

Inspect the inside of the tire to make sure it is clean and free of 
foreign material. 

Place valve stem with rubber washer through valve hole from tire side 
of wheel rim. Screw on valve nut from opposite side, making sure the rubber 
bushing and metal collar or nut are centered and fit snugly in valve hole. 
Finish tightening to 5-6.2 Nm (45-55 lb-in), except aluminum 
disc wheels, which are tightened to 9-15 Nm (6-11 lb-ft) 
torque. 

 WARNING: USING A FLAMMABLE SUBSTANCE SUCH AS GASOLINE OR ETHYL ETHER TO SEAT THE 
BEADS ON A TUBELESS TIRE IS EXTREMELY DANGEROUS. THIS CAN CAUSE AN EXPLOSION 
THAT WILL DAMAGE THE TIRE OR RIM AND RESULT IN SEVERE INJURY OR DEATH. 

Place rim on floor with wide side down. Lubricate both bead seats 
(flanges) of the rim and both tire beads, applying Rubber Lubricant 
D9AZ-19583-A or equivalent meeting Ford specifications ESR-M99B135-A and 
ESA-M1B6-A with a brush or swab.

[FIGURE: F8401B.gif]

Lay tire on the rim. If there is a light balance mark on the tire, line 
this mark up with the valve stem. Push lower bead over flange and into rim 
well. Using straight end of tool (with stop resting on rim flange), take small 
bites to work remaining section of bead into rim.

[FIGURE: F8402B.gif]

Start upper bead over rim flange into well by standing on tire. When 
necessary, push section of bead into rim well and anchor with vise-grip pliers 
by pinching pliers onto rim flange (snub side toward tire). Using spoon end of 
tire iron, with stop toward rim, work progressively around bead. Use small 
bites until bead slips over flange onto rim base. If necessary, insert second 
tire iron and lubricate last 203 mm (8 inches) of bead before completing the 
procedure. 

[FIGURE: F8403B.gif]

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Wheels 

 Steel 

Wheel stud nuts should be inspected and tightened at 160 km (100 miles) 
of operation. At the first 1600 km (1000 miles) of operation, they should 
again be inspected and tightened. Loose wheel stud nuts can cause shimmy and 
vibration. Elongated stud holes in the wheels can also result from the loose 
stud nuts. 

 NOTE: If different types of brake drums or wheels have been interchanged with 
the original, the wheel stud standout might be incorrect. Make sure that the 
wheel studs are of the proper type and length for the components used. 

Keep the wheels and hubs clean. Stones or lumps of mud wedged between 
the wheel and drum will unbalance a wheel and tire.

Check for damage that would affect the runout of the wheels. Wobble or 
shimmy caused by a damaged wheel will eventually damage the wheel bearings and 
cause uneven tire wear. Inspect the wheel rims for dents that will permit air 
to leak from the tires.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Tires 

Tires should be checked frequently to ensure the air pressures agree 
with those specified for the tires and vehicle model. Inspect the tire tread, 
and remove all stones, nails, glass or other objects that may be wedged in the 
tread. Check for holes or cuts that will permit air leakage from the tire, and 
make the necessary repairs. 

Inspect the tire side walls for cuts, bruises, and other damage. If 
internal damage is suspected, demount the tire from the wheel for further 
inspection, service or replacement. 

Check the tire valve for air leaks, and replace the valve if necessary. 
Replace any missing valve caps.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Maintenance and Protection in Corrosive Environments

Due to aluminum's natural resistance to corrosion, aluminum forged disc 
wheels do not need to be painted for most operating conditions. Washing them 
when washing the rest of the vehicle will be enough to keep wheels looking 
good for many years (but do not use highly alkaline cleaning agents). Certain 
environments, created by some operations, can lead to corrosion. Some of these 
include livestock hauling, salt, chloride compounds used for snow removal, and 
highly alkaline materials. When these conditions are encountered, the 
following practice is recommended.

Clean frequently with steam or high-pressure water from a hose. Use of 
a mild detergent will speed up the cleaning process.

When tires are removed, clean and inspect the entire wheel. There are 
various types of coatings that give maximum protection.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Rim and Wheel Maintenance

 During Tire Inspection 

 WARNING: PROPER PRECAUTIONS SHOULD ALWAYS BE TAKEN WHEN JACKING A VEHICLE TO 
PREVENT PERSONAL INJURY OR DAMAGE TO THE VEHICLE.

ALWAYS BLOCK ONE AXLE WITH WHEEL CHOCKS TO PREVENT UNEXPECTED MOVEMENT.

ALWAYS USE PROPER HEAVY-DUTY JACK STANDS.

MANUALLY CAGE PARKING BRAKE CHAMBERS WHEN WORKING ON THE REAR AXLE.

APPLY PARKING BRAKE WHEN WORKING ON FRONT AXLE. 

Check all metal surfaces thoroughly while making tire inspections, 
including areas between duals and on inboard side of wheel. Watch for: 

excessive rust or corrosion buildup 

cracks in metal 

bent flanges, resulting from road obstructions 

loose, missing or damaged flange nuts 

bent or stripped studs 

Remove damaged wheels. Excessively corroded or cracked wheels can be 
dangerous. Deflate tires prior to removal from the vehicle. 

Mark damaged or hazardous areas with chalk so part will be removed from 
service. 

 CAUTION: Make sure replacements are made with the proper sizes and types of 
wheels. 

Replace parts as required.

Inflate tires only to recommended air pressures. 

 During Tire Changes 

 WARNING: DAMAGED WHEEL AND RIM PARTS SUCH AS BENT FLANGES, RIMS OUT OF ROUND OR 
DEEP TOOL MARKS CAN PREVENT COMPONENTS FROM SEATING PROPERLY. THIS CAN LEAD TO 
AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION, RESULTING IN SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. DESTROY ALL 
UNSERVICEABLE PARTS. 

 WARNING: ALLOYS OR METAL SURFACES WITH CRACKS ARE DANGEROUS. THESE COMPONENTS 
CAN FAIL WITHOUT WARNING DURING INFLATION OR LATER ON THE VEHICLE. DESTROY ALL 
PARTS THAT ARE CRACKED. 

Check all metal surfaces. Watch particularly for the following items: 

Cracks in the wheel rim base, in the back flange and gutter areas. 
These are caused by deep tool marks, overloading and over-inflating tires or 
using larger than recommended tire sizes. 

Cracks in the wheel disc, between the stud holes or hand holes. These 
are caused by loose wheel nuts, improper installation procedures or the use of 
incorrect sizes or types of attaching parts. 

 CAUTION: Make sure replacements are made with the proper sizes and types of 
wheels. 

Replace the parts as necessary.

Thoroughly remove rust, dirt and other foreign materials from all 
surfaces. Hand or electric wire brushes, sand blasting or chemical baths can 
be used. Make sure bead seat areas of wheel rim are free of rust and rubber 
deposits. This is especially important for drop-center tubeless rims because 
the 15-degree bead seat is the air-sealing element. 

Pay particular attention to bead seat areas. Paint rim by brush or 
spray with a fast-drying metal primer. Make sure surfaces are clean and dry 
prior to painting. Make sure bare metal areas on the outside or tire side of 
rim are covered. This is especially important on drop-center tubeless rims, 
because warm and sometimes moist air is in constant contact with the metal 
surface on the tire side of the rim. 

Using Rubber Lubricant D9AZ-19583-A or equivalent meeting Ford 
specifications ESR-M99B135-A or ESA-M1B6-A, lubricate tire side of wheel rim 
base just prior to mounting tire. Avoid use of any lubricant containing water 
or solvent that can damage rubber. A combination lubricant and rust-preventive 
compound is preferable. This protective measure is of particular importance 
with drop-center tubeless rims because the air in the tire is contained by 
tire-side wheel rim surface.

Inflate tire to recommended air pressure.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Tire Inflation 

 WARNING: STAND CLEAR WHEN USING A SAFETY CAGE OR AN OSHA-APPROVED RESTRAINING 
DEVICE. ALWAYS USE A CLIP-ON AIR CHUCK WITH A REMOTE VALVE AND PRESSURE GAUGE. 
DO NOT REST OR LEAN ANY PART OF THE BODY AGAINST THE DEVICE DURING INFLATION. 
IF AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION OCCURS, THE AIR BLAST OR MOVEMENT OF RESTRAINING 
DEVICE CAN CAUSE INJURY. 

Place the tire in OSHA-approved inflation cage such as Rotunda 
Inflation Chamber 104-00104 or equivalent. 

 NOTE: Make sure air supply tank incorporates moisture trap when used with 
drop-center tubeless rims in order to reduce the moisture in contact with the 
metal rim surfaces.

Using an extension hose equipped with an air gauge and clip-on type air 
chuck, inflate tire to a maximum of 10 pounds. Check to see that beads are 
properly seated. Deflate tire completely to prevent tube from buckling.

Check for proper bead seating by referencing any circumferential design 
element on the tire and the top of the rim flange. Make sure these are equally 
spaced around the tire. 

Inflate to 20 psi and then check tire beads for proper seating. Never 
inflate beyond 40 psi to seat any tire beads. If the beads are not seated at 
40 psi, STOP! DEFLATE AND DETERMINE THE PROBLEM. 

 CAUTION: Never inflate beyond the inflation pressure specified for the tire or 
rim. 

Inflate tire to recommended pressure. The maximum capacity of a wheel 
load and air pressure is stamped on the wheel disc adjacent to the mounting 
stud holes. Tire pressures are also listed in the Tire Capacity Ratings Chart 
at the end of this section. In no case should these maximum capacities for 
load or pressure of either the tube or wheel/rim be exceeded. 

Before removing the tire/rim assembly from the restraining device, 
always inspect for proper seating of all parts.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Driveshaft, Rear 

The driveshaft or coupling shaft is composed of the universal joints 
(U-joints), connecting shafts and the attaching yokes. 

All the vehicle U-joint spiders and sliding splines are equipped with 
lubrication fittings. They must be lubricated periodically with 
High-Temperature 4x4 Front Axle and Wheel Bearing Grease E8TZ-19590-A or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C198-A.

The vehicles are equipped with center support bearings that are 
prelubricated and sealed for the life of the bearing. 

 NOTE: All driveline shafts are balanced. If a vehicle is to be undercoated, 
cover all shafts to prevent getting undercoating material on the shafts. 

The basic parts of a U-joint assembly are shown in the illustration. 
All U-joints are of the needle bearing type and, in general, are defined by 
the shape of the bearing cap (plate or bearing strap type). The U-joints are 
held in the yoke by bearing straps or bolts.

Vehicles have the following types of driveshafts: 

Driveshaft — The shaft that accommodates the change in 
length (slip) in the driveline system. The driveshaft is the shaft which is 
the input to the rear axle. 

Coupling Shaft — All shafts which connect the 
transmission to the rear axle, except the driveshaft. Coupling shafts are 
attached to a support plate via a shaft support bearing. 

Interaxle Shaft — The shaft that connects the forward 
axle of a tandem drive unit to the rear axle.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Driving Axle, Rear

The axle drive pinion receives its power from the engine through the 
transmission. The pinion gear rotates the differential case through engagement 
with the ring gear, which is bolted to the differential case. Inside the 
differential case, four differential pinion gears are mounted on the 
differential pinion spider (cross). These pinion gears are engaged with the 
side gears to which the axle shafts are splined. Therefore, as the 
differential case turns, it rotates the axle shafts and wheels. When it is 
necessary for one wheel and axle shaft to turn faster than the other, the 
faster turning side gear causes the differential pinions to roll on the slower 
turning side gear to allow differential action between the two axle shafts.

Several rear driving axles are available. A single-speed rear axle, a 
two-speed rear axle, and a tandem axle set with different load capacities are 
the types of rear axles available. For more information, refer to Section 05-02A , Section 05-02B or Section 05-02C .

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Axle and Driveshaft

 Inspection and Verification 

Certain rear axle and driveline concern symptoms are also common to the 
engine, transmission, rear wheel bearing, tires, and other parts of the 
vehicle. For this reason, be sure that the cause of the concern is in the rear 
axle before adjusting, repairing or replacing any of the parts. Refer to 
 Section 00-04 .

 U-Joint Inspection 

Perform a visual inspection of the driveshaft and U-joints. Inspect for 
any buildup of foreign material, such as mud or undercoating, on the 
driveshaft or in the U-joints. Check the shaft for damaged or bent tubing or 
missing balance weights. 

Check the U-joint phasing arrows to make sure that U-joint phasing is 
correct. Refer to Adjustments, U-Joint Phasing in this section. Lubricate the 
U-joints and road test the vehicle to see if the condition improves. Refer to 
Lubrication, U-Joints in this section for procedure. 

If the condition does not improve, perform the following steps:

Remove driveshaft. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Manipulate rear axle shaft universal joint in each direction of 
rotation. If U-joint feels stiff or has a "lumpy," "gritty" feel in any 
direction, replace rear axle shaft universal joint. Refer to Section 05-01 .

 Alignment Inspection, Rear Axle 

Refer to Tandem Drive Axle Alignment under Description and Operation in 
 Section 04-00 .

 Noise Acceptability 

A gear-driven unit, especially a truck drive axle, will produce a 
certain amount of noise. Some noise is acceptable and may be audible at 
certain speeds or under various driving conditions such as a newly paved 
blacktop road. The slight noise is not detrimental to operation of the rear 
axle and must be considered normal.

 Failure Analysis 

The following information explains failure analysis of the drive axle 
carrier — the assembly that contains the gears, bearings and 
differential, and is removable from the housing that supports the vehicle 
load. 

A successful failure analysis requires three steps: 

Identify the type of failure. 

Determine the cause of the failure. 

Take corrective action to prevent a recurrence. 

 Reasons for Axle Carrier Failures 

The basic reasons for failure of drive axle carriers fall into the 
following four general categories: 

Vehicle application or usage 

Vehicle operation 

Maintenance 

Design or manufacturing 

 Vehicle Application or Usage 

To prevent drive axle carrier failure, the operator must understand the 
vehicle's intended usage and application. Axles are available in various 
capacities to meet application requirements. If they are used in operations 
that exceed their design limitations, premature failures and reduced life can 
be expected. 

Drive axles are rated in terms of the carrying capacity of the housing —
 in other words, the weight on its back. This is called the 
Gross Axle Weight Rating (GAWR). 

The carrier gearing is rated in terms of total vehicle weight. For 
straight trucks, buses, etc., it is the Gross Vehicle Weight (GVW) —
 the weight of the vehicle itself plus its payload. For 
tractor-trailer combinations, it is the Gross Combination Weight (GCW) —
 the combined weight of the tractor, trailer and payload. The 
rating (GVW or GCW) determines the amount of work the gearing must do to move 
the vehicle. 

[FIGURE: E80201A.gif]

Road grades and surfaces also affect the carrier gear rating. 

The road surface determines the road rolling resistance. Rolling 
resistance is the force required to push or move the vehicle over that 
surface. The harder and smoother the surface, the lower the resistance. The 
softer and rougher the surface, the greater the effort required. Soft surfaces 
may increase the needed effort as much as two to ten times.

The same axle carrier would be rated at a higher GVW/GCW for operation 
on hard surface, level roads than on soft or mountainous roads.

Care in specifying the axle is the first and most important step toward 
ensuring satisfactory performance and life. 

 Vehicle Operation 

Improper vehicle operation or abuse can also cause axle carrier failure.

Improper operation may cause either an instantaneous failure or damage 
leading to a failure later when the vehicle is operating under normal 
conditions. 

To avoid failure, the vehicle operator must be trained to drive 
properly. The operator must be aware that poor driving now may not result in 
an immediate failure but in one that occurs many miles later. 

 Maintenance 

Failures can result from improper or lack of maintenance, or from poor 
rebuilding practices. 

Recommended maintenance and rebuild practices are established when 
vehicles and components are designed. It is important that maintenance 
personnel and supervisors know and follow these recommendations. 

 Design or Manufacturing 

When an axle is designed, a great deal of engineering effort is devoted 
to ensure that the carrier will provide satisfactory performance and service 
at its rated loads. This is followed by exhaustive testing to verify that the 
design objectives have been met. 

Both the operator and the manufacturer influence the useful service 
life of drive axle carriers. The operator must be sure the vehicle is 
specified, operated and maintained properly. The manufacturer is responsible 
for the design and quality of the equipment, and for clear and specific 
maintenance recommendations. 

Some of the most common axle carrier failures are discussed in the 
following pages. This information will be helpful in identifying them and 
their causes, and in initiating action to prevent their recurrence. 

The following conditions are the most common types of drive axle 
carrier failures: 

spinout 

shock 

fatigue 

lubrication 

 Spinout Failures 

Spinout is defined as excessive differential action. On a single rear 
axle, main differential spinout occurs when one wheel remains stationary while 
the other wheel is spinning. In the case of tandems, spinout occurs in the 
interaxle differential when either one wheel or one axle remains stationary 
while its mate spins. The relatively high speed difference between the mating 
parts generates heat. When the heat becomes excessive, it can cause galling of 
the journals of the cross and the mating differential pinion bores. In extreme 
cases enough heat may be generated to weld the differential pinion to the 
cross and cause a catastrophic failure. 

Spinouts can occur in these driving situations: 

Backing under a trailer 

Starting or traveling on a slippery surface 

[FIGURE: E80211A.gif]

 Backing Under a Trailer 

When a tractor is backing under a trailer, particularly one whose 
landing gear is too low, the extra effort could cause loss of traction between 
the tire and the ground. The resulting spinout is most likely to happen on wet 
and slippery pavement, or on unpaved surfaces. 

 Starting on a Slippery Surface 

Spinout can occur when the vehicle is started on a wet or slippery 
surface. It is especially likely to happen when the vehicle is stuck in mud or 
snow and the driver attempts to free it by stepping on the throttle and 
"burning out." 

 Traveling on a Slippery Surface 

Any moving vehicle encountering a wet or slippery surface can lose 
traction and spin out. This usually happens when driving up a hill because of 
the additional torque required to negotiate the grade. 

In all the situations that result in spinouts, the interaxle 
differential (sometimes called a power divider or third differential) and main 
differential assemblies are subject to damage.

The interaxle differential of a tandem axle is more susceptible to 
spinout damage than the main differential. The interaxle differential turns at 
a higher speed. It revolves at the same speed as the prop shaft, while the 
main differential rotates at prop shaft speed divided by the axle gear ratio. 

 Tandem Axle Interaxle Differential 

[FIGURE: E80222A.gif]

The amount of lubricant available to carry off the generated heat and 
lubricate the mating surfaces is a significant factor. Since the main 
differential is actually submerged in the oil reservoir, it is more tolerant 
of spinout friction and heat than the interaxle differential, which is usually 
supplied with lubricant only by gear splash. 

Spinout can be especially damaging when the rear-rear axle of a tandem 
is spinning and the forward-rear axle wheels are stationary, or nearly so. In 
this situation there is excessive differentiation of the interaxle 
differential. It receives no splash lubrication to carry away the heat, since 
the forward rear wheels are not turning. 

All tandems have optional incorporated oil pumps to provide pressurized 
lubrication to the inside of the interaxle differential. Lubrication of the 
cross and pinions and resistance to spinout damage are thereby improved.

[FIGURE: E80231A.gif]

The main differentials of single or tandem axles are also subject to 
spinout damage, but to a much lesser degree. The differential rotates more 
slowly and is partially submerged in lubricant. Even so, the heat generated by 
severe spinout can cause galling and possible seizure of the pinions to the 
cross. 

 Spinout Failures 

[FIGURE: E8024B.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

—

Interaxle Differential Action

2

—

Main Differential Action

In summary, spinout damage is due to excessive action of the main or 
interaxle differential caused by severe wheel slippage. Heat generated by 
rapid spinning of the pinions on the cross can result in galled cross legs, 
and this is the most common characteristic of spinout failures.

Typical failed parts resulting from spinout can be seen in the 
following illustration. A close look at the differential cross shows a badly 
galled leg, two legs broken off and destroyed pinions.

[FIGURE: E80251A.gif]

The differential pinions indicate the severity of the spinout —
 they have seized the cross legs and caused them to fail. 
This is an example of how excessive differentiation generates so much heat 
that the pinions actually weld themselves to the cross legs.

[FIGURE: E80261A.gif]

This is an example of one of the cross legs having been welded to the 
differential case, again due to the extreme heat generated by the spinout.

[FIGURE: E80271A.gif]

The intense heat generated transferred metal to the pinion thrust 
washers by friction welding.

[FIGURE: E80281A.gif]

One of the broken cross legs worked its way out of the differential 
case and punched a hole in the differential cover. The result was a lubricant 
loss which caused the carrier to burn up.

[FIGURE: E80291A.gif]

This cross suffered less damage than the one shown previously. However, 
note the characteristic galling on the leg caused by the heat generated by 
spinning pinion.

[FIGURE: E80301A.gif]

Here is a cross that shows wear on its legs caused by low speed 
differential action not severe enough to result in galling. It was, however, 
enough to indicate above-normal differentiation between the axles. This can be 
caused by tires with too great a difference in rolling radii. Mismatched tires 
cause the gearsets in the two axles to turn at different speeds to maintain 
the same road speed, and so result in above-normal interaxle differential 
action. There must be no more than 19.05 mm (0.75 inch) difference on the 
circumference between the tires on the forward and rear axles of a tandem. 
Another cause of this type of damage could be different gear ratios in the 
forward and rear axles. 

[FIGURE: E80311A.gif]

After identifying a spinout failure and its probable cause, corrective 
action must be taken to keep it from reoccurring in the future. Or, better 
still, take action that will keep such failures from happening at all. 

If spinout failure is due to excessive differential action caused by 
wheel slippage, then these failures can be avoided by eliminating, or at least 
minimizing, the slippage-induced differential action. 

This can be done in two ways: 

First, by using the interaxle differential lock with which tandem axles 
are equipped. The purpose of the lock is to keep the interaxle differential 
from performing its normal function. 

When conditions exist that could result in wheel slippage, locking the 
interaxle differential will keep it from differentiating and thus prevent 
spinout damage. The circumstances under which the lock should be used are 
backing under a trailer, starting on or traveling over a slippery surface. 

The second way to avoid differential problems caused by wheel slippage 
centers on the main differential. Locking the interaxle differential in tandem 
axles will not prevent the main differential f

SERVICE PROCEDURE

Axle Housing — Welding 

 WARNING: USING INCORRECT WELDING PROCEDURES OR WELDING AT LOCATIONS OTHER THAN 
THE THREE AREAS PERMITTED BY ROCKWELL WILL MAKE THE HEAT-TREATED COMPONENT 
WEAK. A WEAK COMPONENT WILL CAUSE POOR OR UNSAFE OPERATION OF THE AXLE AND 
EARLY FAILURE. THE FOLLOWING PROCEDURE MUST BE USED. 

 CAUTION: Welding can be used when the crack or damaged area is within the old 
weld material. Replace the axle housing if the crack extends into the metal 
next to the old weld. A housing that has damage in the seam weld or cover weld 
because of overload conditions can be repaired. A repaired housing must be 
used in correct applications. 

Rockwell International will permit repairing drive axle housing 
assemblies by welding only in the following areas: 

Cover welds. 

Snorkel welds. 

Housing seam welds between the suspension attaching brackets. 

Welding procedure 

Drain the lubricant from the axle assembly. 

Remove the axle shafts and differential carrier from the axle housing.

 WARNING: BE CAREFUL WHEN USING A CLEANING SOLVENT. FOLLOW THE SOLVENT 
MANUFACTURER'S INSTRUCTIONS FOR SAFE USE TO PREVENT INJURY. 
Clean the damaged area inside and outside the housing. Cleaning solvent 
can be used. 

Grind the damaged weld to the base metal. 

Warm the complete axle housing to a temperature of 21-27°
C (70-80°F) or higher. 

Heat the damaged area to be repaired to approximately 149°
C (300°F) before you start welding. 

Use a 70,000 psi tensile weld material and the correct voltage and 
amperage for the diameter weld rod used. Examples of weld rods that can be 
used are E-7018 or ER-70S-3.

 CAUTION: If the E-7018 weld rod is used, the rod must be kept dry. Electrodes 
that are not stored in the correct sealed containers must be heated at 371°
C (700°F) for one hour before welding. Wet 
electrodes must be dried at 82°C (180°F) for 
one to two hours and then heated at 371°C (700°
F) for one hour before welding. 

 CAUTION: Do not connect the ground cable at any point on the axle assembly that 
will put a bearing between the ground cable and weld area. If a bearing is 
between the ground cable and weld, the bearing will be damaged because of 
electricity arcing. A good location to connect the ground cable is the spring 
mounting pad of the housing. 

 NOTE: To weld brackets or other components to the axle housing, use the 
procedure in Rockwell Technical Service Aid, TSA-2-95. 

Fill in the weld gap as follows:

The snorkel weld must be a 9.5-mm (0.375-inch) fillet. 

The opening in cover welds must be filled level with the old weld. 

The opening in seam welds must be ground out to 70% of the wall 
thickness. The wall thickness can be measured at the carrier opening of 
housing. 

Clean the new weld area. Carefully remove all the rough weld material. 

Install the differential carrier and axle shafts. 

Fill the axle assembly with the correct amount of lubricant. For 
complete information on lubricating drive axles and carriers, refer to Lubrication 
 in this section.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Clean Ground and Polished Parts 

 WARNING: BE CAREFUL WHEN USING CLEANING SOLVENTS. FOLLOW THE SOLVENT 
MANUFACTURER'S INSTRUCTIONS FOR SAFE USE TO PREVENT INJURY. DO NOT USE GASOLINE. 

 NOTE: Do not clean ground or polished parts in a hot solution tank, water, 
steam or alkaline solutions. 

Use a cleaning solvent to clean ground or polished parts or surfaces. 
Kerosene or diesel fuel oil can be used for this purpose. 

Use a tool with a flat blade, if required, to remove gasket material 
from parts. Be careful not to damage the ground surfaces.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Clean Rough Parts 

Clean rough parts the same as cleaning ground and polished parts, 
except that rough parts can be cleaned in hot solution tanks with a weak 
alkaline solution. 

 WARNING: BE CAREFUL WHEN USING HOT SOLUTION TANKS AND ALKALINE SOLUTIONS. FOLLOW 
THE ALKALINE MANUFACTURER'S INSTRUCTIONS FOR SAFE USE TO PREVENT INJURY. 

Leave parts in hot solution tanks until completely cleaned and heated.

Parts must be washed with water until the alkaline solution is removed.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Clean Axle Assemblies 

Steam clean complete axle assembly on the outside to remove dirt. 

Close or put a cover over all openings in the axle assembly before the 
axle is steam cleaned. Examples of openings are breathers or vents in air 
chambers. 

 Dry Parts That Have Been Cleaned 

 CAUTION: Bearings can be damaged if they are dried by rotating with compressed 
air. 

 NOTE: Except for bearings, parts can be dried with compressed air.

Dry parts immediately after cleaning with soft, clean paper or cloth 
rags.

 Prevent Corrosion and Rust on Cleaned Parts 

Apply axle lubricant to cleaned and dried parts that are not damaged 
and are to be assembled. 

Apply a special material that prevents corrosion and rust to all 
surfaces to store parts. Wrap them in a special paper that prevents corrosion 
and rust.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Inspection After Disassembly of Axle

 NOTE: Inspect all parts carefully and completely before the axle or carrier 
is assembled. Check all parts for wear and replace damaged parts. Replacement 
of damaged or worn parts now will prevent failure of the assembly later. 

 Gears 

 CAUTION: Hypoid drive pinions and ring gears are machined in matched sets. When 
a drive pinion or ring gear of a hypoid set needs to be replaced, both drive 
gear and pinion must be replaced at the same time. 

Inspect hypoid pinions and gears for wear or damage. Gears that are 
worn or damaged must be replaced.

 CAUTION: Always replace thrust washers, differential side gears and pinion gears 
in sets. A higher stress on parts and early failure of the assembly will occur 
if a new part is used with parts that are old or worn. 

Inspect the main differential assembly for wear or stress. Parts that 
are damaged must be replaced. 

Inside surfaces of both case halves. 

Both surfaces of all thrust washers. 

The four trunnion ends of the spider (cross). 

Teeth and splines of both differential side gears. 

Teeth and bore of all differential pinions.

Inspect axle shafts for wear and cracks at the flange, shaft and

 Bearing Cups and Cone and Roller Assemblies 

Inspect the cup, cone, rollers and cage of all tapered roller bearings 
in the assembly. If any of the following conditions exist, the bearing must be 
replaced. 

The center of large diameter end of rollers worn level with or below 
the outer surface. 

The radius at large diameter end of rollers worn to a sharp edge.

[FIGURE: E8731A.gif]

groove can be seen at the small or large diameter end of both parts. 

Deep cracks or breaks in the cup, cone inner race or roller surfaces.

[FIGURE: E8732A.gif]

Bright wear marks on the outer surface of the roller cage.

[FIGURE: E8733A.gif]

Damage on rollers and on surfaces of the cup and cone inner race that 
touch the rollers.

[FIGURE: E8734A.gif]

Damage on the cup and cone inner race surfaces that touch the rollers.

 Differential (Axle) Housing 

 WARNING: REPAIR OF AXLE HOUSINGS BY BENDING OR STRAIGHTENING WILL CAUSE POOR OR 
UNSAFE OPERATION OF THE AXLE AND EARLY FAILURE. 

 NOTE: Do not repair rear axle housings by bending or straightening.

Replace worn or damaged parts of an axle assembly. The following are 
some examples to check for, repair or replace. 

Replace any fastener if corners of the head are worn. 

Replace washers if damaged. 

Replace gaskets, oil seals or grease seals at the time of axle or 
carrier repair. 

Clean parts and apply new silicone gasket material where required when 
axle or carrier is assembled.

[FIGURE: E78601A.gif]

Remove nicks, mars and burrs from parts having machined or ground 
surfaces. Use a fine file, india stone, emery cloth or crocus cloth for this 
purpose.

 CAUTION: Threads must be without damage and clean so that accurate adjustments 
and correct torque values can be applied to fasteners and parts. 

Clean and repair threads of fasteners and holes. Use a die or tap of 
the correct size or a fine file for this purpose.

Tighten all fasteners to the correct torque values. Refer to the torque 
specifications chart in Section 05-02A , Section 05-02B or Section 05-02C .

[FIGURE: E65941A.gif]

 Carrier Housing 

Make sure that the hubs where the bearings mount are smooth. Carefully 
examine the bearing shoulders, which may have been damaged when the bearings 
were removed. The bearings will fail if they do not seat firmly against the 
shoulders. Check the fit (free rotation) of the differential side gears in 
their counterbores.

 Wheel Bearing and Seal 

Refer to Section 04-02B .

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Use of Dri-Loc® Fasteners and Stud and Bearing Mount

 Install New Dri-Loc® Fasteners 

Clean the oil and dirt from threaded holes. There is no special 
cleaning required. 

 CAUTION: Do not apply adhesives or sealants on new Dri-Loc® 
fasteners or in the threaded holes. If other adhesives or sealants are used, 
the new Dri-Loc® adhesive will not function correctly. 

 NOTE: There is no drying time required for Dri-Loc® 
fasteners. 

Assemble parts using the new Dri-Loc® fasteners.

Tighten the Dri-Loc® fasteners to the required torque 
value for that size fastener. There is no special procedure or torque value 
required. Refer to the torque specifications chart in Section 05-02A , Section 05-02B or Section 05-02C .

 Install Old Dri-Loc® Fasteners Using Stud and 
Bearing Mount 

Clean the oil and dirt from threaded holes. There is no special 
cleaning required and it is not necessary to remove the old Dri-Loc®
 adhesive from threads. 

 CAUTION: Do not apply adhesive to the fastener threads. Air pressure in the hole 
will push the adhesive out as the fastener is installed. 

 NOTE: There is no drying time required for Stud and Bearing Mount 
EOAZ-19554-BA or equivalent meeting Ford specification WSK-M2G349-A1. 

Apply four or five drops of Stud and Bearing Mount EOAZ-19554-BA or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification WSK-M2G349-A1 to threaded holes only. 
Make sure the adhesive is on the threads.

[FIGURE: E78611A.gif]

Tighten the fasteners to the required torque value for that size 
fastener. There is no special procedure or torque value required. Refer to the 
torque specifications chart in Section 05-02A , Section 05-02B or Section 05-02C .

[FIGURE: E65941A.gif]

 Check Torque Values of Dri-Loc® Fasteners Not 
Requiring Removal 

 CAUTION: If Dri-Loc® fasteners do not require removal from 
components, check the fasteners for correct torque value as follows: 

Apply the minimum amount of torque required for that size fastener. 
Refer to the torque specifications chart in Section 05-02A , Section 05-02B or 
 Section 05-02C .

Remove the fastener from the component and apply adhesive to the 
threaded hole if the fastener rotates any amount. Follow the procedure for 
installing old Dri-Loc® fasteners. 

 Remove Dri-Loc® Fasteners 

If it is difficult to remove fasteners from components, the strength of 
Dri-Loc® and Stud and Bearing Mount EOAZ-19554-BA or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification WSK-M2G349-A1 can be decreased by 
heating. Use the following procedure: 

Heat the fastener for three to five seconds only and try to loosen the 
fastener with a wrench. Do not use an impact wrench to loosen the fastener or 
hit the fastener with a hammer. 

 CAUTION: Do not exceed 177°C (350°F) maximum. 
Heating must be done slowly to prevent thermal stresses in the other 
components. 

Repeat Step 1 until the fastener can be removed.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Application of Stud and Bearing Mount in Bearing Bores for Differential 

Use adhesive Stud and Bearing Mount EOAZ-19554-BA or equivalent meeting 
Ford specification WSK-M2G349-A1.

Clean the oil and dirt from outer diameters of bearing cups and bearing 
bores in the carrier and bearing caps. There is no special cleaning required. 

Apply axle lubricant to the bearing cones and the inner diameters of 
the bearing cups of the main differential. Do not get oil on the outer 
diameter of the bearing cup and do not permit oil to drip on the bearing 
bores. 

Apply a single continuous bead of the adhesive to the bearing bores in 
the carrier and bearing caps. Apply the adhesive 360 degrees around the 
smooth, ground surfaces only. Do not put adhesive on threaded areas.

[FIGURE: E78231A.gif]

 NOTE: The stud and bearing mount adhesive will become hard (dry) in 
approximately two hours. The following two steps of the procedure must be done 
in two hours from the time the adhesive was applied. If two hours have passed 
since application, clean the parts again and apply new adhesive. 

Install the main differential assembly, bearing cups and bearing caps 
into the carrier. 

Adjust preload of the differential bearings, backlash and tooth contact 
patterns of the gearset as required using the normal procedures.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Application of Silicone Gasket Material 

 WARNING: SMALL AMOUNTS OF ACID VAPOR ARE PRESENT WHEN APPLYING SILICONE GASKET 
MATERIAL. FOR THIS REASON, MAKE SURE THERE IS GOOD VENTILATION IN THE WORK 
AREA. IF THE SILICONE GASKET MATERIAL GETS IN THE EYES, FLUSH WITH WATER FOR 
15 MINUTES. HAVE THE EYES CHECKED BY A DOCTOR. 

 NOTE: The following silicone gasket products or the equivalents can be used 
on Rockwell components. 

Dow Corning Silicone Rubber Sealant, No. 732 Black

Ford Black Non-Acid Cure Silicone Rubber Sealant E7TZ-19562-A or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESL-M4G273-A

From Rockwell International: 

40-pound containers, Part No. 1199-Q-2981 

Ten-ounce tubes, Part No. 1250-X-388 

Three-ounce tubes, Part No. 1199-T-3842

Remove all old gasket material from both surfaces.

[FIGURE: E78621A.gif]

Clean the surfaces where silicone gasket material will be applied. 

Dry both surfaces. 

 CAUTION: The amount of silicone gasket material applied must not exceed a 
1/8-inch diameter bead. Too much gasket material can block lubrication 
passages. 

Apply a 1/8-inch diameter continuous bead of the silicone gasket 
material around one surface. Also apply the gasket material around the edge of 
all fastener holes in that surface.

[FIGURE: E70811A.gif]

Assemble the components immediately to permit the silicone gasket 
material to compress evenly between the parts. Tighten fasteners to the 
required torque value for that size fastener. Refer to the torque 
specifications chart in Section 05-02A , Section 05-02B or Section 05-02C .

Wait 20 minutes before the assembly is filled with lubricant.

For complete information on lubricating drive axles and carriers, refer 
to Lubrication in this section.

ADJUSTMENTS

U-Joint Phasing 

When U-joint yokes are assembled to their shafts in the same plane, 
they are in phase. When they are assembled to the shafts in different planes, 
they are out of phase. 

To obtain vibration-free operation, check and correct as necessary 
according to the following specifications. 

On vehicles with a slip-spline on the last coupling shaft, the yoke, 
which is part of the slip-yoke assembly, should be considered part of the 
coupling shaft. 

The U-joints between the rear axle and transmission must be in phase. 

The U-joints between tandem rear axles must be in phase (parallel).

Mark splined main driveline components prior to disassembly, to ensure 
reassembly in the same relative orientation.

ADJUSTMENTS

Driveline Support Plate Position, Adjustable 

An adjustable driveline support plate is used on some applications. 
Although it can be mounted in any one of several positions, only one position 
is correct for a specific application. The correct position can be determined 
from the support plate part number shown on the Truck Specification List 
attached to each vehicle. 

The numerical digit in the adjustable support plate part number suffix 
indicates the hole set to be used. For example, EOHT-CA1 requires that the 
EOHT-4831-CA support plate be bolted to the crossmember (or 4691 bracket —
 some installations) through support plate hole set number 1. 

The hole sets are identified by the numbers 1 through 4 or 5 stamped 
into the support plate or four numbers between 1 and 16 on 4691 bracket.

Leg of support plate must always face rear of vehicle as shown. 
Assemble 4831 support plate to 5028 crossmember (or 4691 bracket) through the 
hole set identified in the support plate part number suffix.

ADJUSTMENTS

Driveshaft Alignment 

Before adjusting components for correct driveshaft alignment, be sure 
to check the following: 

Inflate all tires to the pressure at which they are normally operated. 

Park empty vehicle on a surface which is as nearly level as possible 
both from front-to-rear and side-to-side. 

The tractor must be in its normal operating position. Do not attempt to 
level the truck by jacking up the front or rear axles to obtain a level 
condition. 

All angles should be read within one-quarter degree and they should be 
measured with the protractor held plumb on a clean flat surface.

To determine driveshaft angles, a spirit level protractor is required. 
When angles are read from the 0 degree mark (horizontally on the driveshaft), 
record and use the angle shown on the protractor.

Protractor Indexing Marks

When angles are read from either of the 90 degree marks (vertically —
 on the flange), such as when measuring yoke angles, do not 
record the angle shown on the protractor since the 90 degree marks must be 
understood to be the same as 0 degrees on a horizontal plane. Thus, if a 
vertical reading is 85 degrees, the angle being measured is 5 degrees (90 
degrees - 85 degrees = 5 degrees).

ADJUSTMENTS

Driveshaft Angles, Single Rear Axles, Check and Adjustment 

Check and record the angle of the engine and main transmission. This 
reading can be taken at the rear of the main transmission on the output yoke 
or flange. Record this reading. 

EXAMPLE: 1 degree (down from horizontal) 

Check the angle of the driveshaft. Record this reading. 

EXAMPLE: 4 degrees 30 min. (down from horizontal) 

Check the axle yoke angle. Record this reading. 

EXAMPLE: 2 degrees (down from horizontal) 

Subtract the angle measured in Step 1 of this procedure from the angle 
measured in Step 2 of this procedure.

Example:

4° 30 min.

(driveshaft angle down from horizontal)

-1°

(engine and main transmission down from horizontal)

= 3° 30 min.

(transmission output shaft U-joint operating angle down from horizontal)

Use the angle measured in Step 3, and subtract it from the angle 
measured in Step 2.

Example:

4° 30 min.

(driveshaft angle down from horizontal)

-2°

(axle yoke angle down from horizontal)

= 2° 30 min.

(axle yoke U-joint operating angle down from horizontal)

Now, subtract the answer found in Step 4 from the answer found in Step 5.

Example:

3° 30 min.

(transmission output shaft U-joint operating angle down from horizontal)

-2° 30 min.

(axle yoke U-joint operating angle down from horizontal)

= 1°

(U-joint operating angle difference)

ADJUSTMENTS

Driveshaft Angles, Tandem Axles, Check and Adjustment

This procedure must be performed for all tandem axle suspensions in 
which both axle pinion angles are set by longitudinal torque rod lengths and 
adjusted by varying the number of shims under the torque rod mounting brackets 
at the frame crossmember. 

Before measurements are made, make sure the vehicle is in cab-chassis 
condition and tires are inflated to normal pressure ± 69 
kPa (10 psi). 

Before any angles are measured, the vehicle must be standing on a level 
surface (labeled Horizontal in the illustration).

With the forward torque arm installed, measure the forward axle pinion 
angle vs. the horizontal to the nearest 5 minutes, using a vernier 
inclinometer or electronic level gauge. The measuring instrument should be 
calibrated to provide repeated readings within ± 5 minutes 
of 0 degrees when placed on the level surface. 

Measure the slope of the engine and transmission vs. the horizontal 
(labeled Angle 1 in the figure) with the same inclinometer resting against a 
machined surface known to be parallel to the crankshaft (the manufacturing 
pads on some transmission cases are a suitable surface). Subtract this angle 
from the forward axle pinion angle measured in Step 3 to obtain the difference 
angle (labeled Angle 4 in the figure). 

Compare the calculated difference angle to the range shown for the 
suspension in the chart Tandem Axle Angle Settings. If the measurement is 
within the specified range, the forward pinion angle is correct (omit Step 6). 

Add or remove shims from the forward torque rod bracket to bring the 
measured forward axle pinion angle within the range specified for the 
suspension in the chart. Each thick shim (Part No. E4HT-4N002-CA or 
equivalent, 0.12-in. thick) will subtract approximately 22 minutes from the 
forward axle pinion angle (reverse for Neway air suspensions). Each thin shim 
(Part No. E4HT-4N002-BA or equivalent, 0.06-in. thick) will subtract 
approximately 11 minutes from the forward pinion angle. Repeat Step 3 
following any change in the number of shims under the forward torque rod 
bracket. 

With the rear torque arm installed, measure the rear axle pinion angle 
vs. the horizontal (labeled Angle 6 in the figure) to the nearest 5 minutes, 
using the same gauge as for the forward axle. 

Compare the measured rear pinion angle to the range shown for the 
suspension in the chart. If the measurement is within the specified range, the 
rear pinion angle is correct (omit Step 9). 

Add or remove shims from the rear torque rod bracket to bring the 
measured rear axle pinion angle within the range specified for the suspension 
in the chart. Each thick (0.12-in.) shim will add approximately 22 minutes to 
the rear axle pinion angle. Each thin shim (0.06 in.) will add approximately 
11 minutes to the rear pinion angle. Repeat Steps 7-9 following any change in 
the number of shims under the rear torque rod bracket.

ADJUSTMENTS

Driveshaft Runout and Balance 

 Driveshaft and Yoke Runout Check 

 NOTE: With transmission in NEUTRAL, turn the rear wheel/drum to rotate the 
coupling shaft and driveshaft when checking runouts. 

Check coupling shaft for proper phasing. Refer to Adjustments, U-Joint 
Phasing in this section. Check all U-joint to yoke installations for 
improperly seated U-joint bearing caps. 

Check the runouts at the front and rear of the coupling shaft and the 
front, center and rear of the driveshaft. The runout check at the rear of the 
driveshaft should be made on the tube as close to the universal joint as 
possible.

 NOTE: The runout at the rear of the driveshaft can be caused by either the 
driveshaft or the rear axle yoke. 

Mark the points of the greatest runouts on the coupling shaft and 
driveshaft.

If the runout is 0.889 mm (0.035 inch) or more on the coupling shaft or 
at the front or center of the driveshaft, replace the shaft. 

If the runout at the rear of the driveshaft is less than 0.889 mm 
(0.035 inch) and the front and center runouts are also less than 0.889 mm 
(0.035 inch), proceed to Driveshaft Balancing. 

If the runout at the rear is more than 0.889 mm (0.035 inch) and the 
front and center runouts are less than 0.889 mm (0.035 inch), mark the point 
of greatest runout on the shaft.

To determine the cause of the runout at the rear of the driveshaft, 
mark the U-joint and yoke, remove and rotate the driveshaft 180 degrees to the 
rear axle yoke and check and mark the greatest runout at the rear of the 
driveshaft. If the runout is less than 0.889 mm (0.035 inch), evaluate on the 
hoist. Road test if the vibration is not present. Proceed to driveshaft 
balance if vibration is present. If runout is more than 0.889 mm (0.035 inch), 
proceed to Step 5. 

Compare the first and second marks at the rear of the driveshaft to 
determine the cause of the runout. If the marks are within approximately 25.4 
mm (1 inch), replace the driveshaft. If the marks are approximately on 
opposite sides of the shaft, replace the yoke.

[FIGURE: E2722D.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

4602

Driveshaft

2

—

First Runout Mark

3

—

Second Runout Mark

After replacing either the driveshaft or rear axle yoke, recheck 
runouts. If the excessive runout is still evident after replacement of the 
rear axle yoke, it will be necessary to replace the ring gear and pinion and 
repeat the above checks until runout is within specifications. 

Evaluate on hoist. If the vibration is still present, proceed to 
Driveshaft Balancing procedure. 

 Driveshaft Balancing 

Vibration or shudder that is noticeable either on fast acceleration, 
when coasting, or when using the engine for braking may be caused by the rear 
axle housing being loose on the rear springs, improper tire balance, improper 
driveline installation, or driveline imbalance. 

If detailed parts of the driveshaft are replaced and shaft vibration is 
encountered after installation, disconnect the shaft at the slip-spline. 
Rotate the slip-spline 180 degrees. Reconnect the shaft to the slip-spline. If 
the vibration persists, disconnect the shaft at the rear axle yoke. Rotate the 
rear axle yoke 180 degrees and reconnect the shaft to the yoke. 

If rotating the driveshaft 180 degrees does not eliminate vibration, 
the driveshaft may be balanced, using the following procedure. Two people are 
required to perform this operation: one in the vehicle, and one under the 
vehicle making adjustments.

Raise the vehicle on a twin-post hoist so that both the front and rear 
axles are safely supported with all wheels free to rotate.

With the transmission in gear, increase the vehicle speed to the 
maximum vibration level. Note and record the speedometer speed of this 
vibration period as a baseline speed.

Check the attachment of all U-joint bearing caps of the driveshaft or 
coupling shaft to the transmission yoke, front or rear axle pinion yokes and 
all transfer unit drive yokes for improper installation or damaged U-joint 
bearing cap locating lugs. All yokes with worn, shaved, or damaged locating 
lugs must be replaced.

Check the driveshaft and coupling shaft for correct phasing. Refer to U-joint Phasing 
 under Adjustments in this section.

 WARNING: DO NOT WEAR LOOSE CLOTHING THAT COULD GET CAUGHT ON THE ROTATING SHAFT. 

With the transmission (and transfer unit) in gear, run the vehicle with 
the driveshaft and coupling shaft rotating at a speedometer speed of 65-80 
km/h (40-50 mph), carefully bring a crayon, piece of chalk, or colored pencil 
up until it just barely contacts the rear end, center and front end of the 
driveshaft. The chalk marks will indicate the heavy side of the driveshaft. 
Use caution when checking the driveshaft near the balance weights to prevent 
injury to the hands.

[FIGURE: E1685D.gif]

Install two screw-type hose clamps on the driveshaft so that their 
heads are located 180 degrees from the chalk mark, starting at the pinion yoke 
end of the driveshaft. Tighten the clamps and cut off the excess band from the 
clamps.

[FIGURE: E16861B.gif]

Run the vehicle up to the baseline speed. If vibration is still 
evidenced, rotate the clamps approximately 45 degrees away from each other and 
test for correction of vibration.

If necessary, continue to rotate the clamps apart in smaller increments 
until the vibration is eliminated or begins to be reduced.

If the vibration is not completely eliminated, repeat the foregoing 
procedure and balance the front end of the driveshaft, checking for 
elimination or reduction in the vibration level.

[FIGURE: E16871B.gif]

To completely eliminate the driveline vibration, it may be necessary to 
balance the coupling shaft, following the same procedure as for the 
driveshaft. To prevent overheating, do not run the vehicle on the hoist for an 
extended period.

Remove the vehicle from the hoist and road test.

 Alternate Procedure 

Road Test — Evaluate and record road speed at which 
vibration occurs. 

Raise vehicle on a twin-post hoist or jack stands and re-evaluate by 
starting the engine, engaging the transmission and accelerating to the 
indicated speeds at which the vibration was most severe during the road test. 

Disconnect the driveshaft from the axle yoke. Rotate the driveshaft 180 
degrees from its original position and reinstall. Repeat evaluation per Step 2 
above. In some cases, rotating the driveshaft 180 degrees may decrease the 
vibration to an acceptable level. However, if the vibration level is 
increased, install the driveshaft in its original position and proceed to Step 
4. 

A vehicle is more sensitive to excessive imbalance and runout at the 
rearward end of the driveshaft; therefore, locate the heavy side of the 
driveshaft by the use of the strobe light, such as Rotunda Electronic Strobe 
Balancer 006-01399 or equivalent and transducer, as follows: 

Remove rear wheels and tires, reinstall all the wheel lug nuts in 
reverse, flat side of the nuts toward the drum or disc to avoid lug nut 
imbalance and to prevent the drum or disc from dislodging.

Scribe an axial chalk line (at any radial location) approximately 101 
mm (4 inches) long at the rear of the driveshaft.

Locate the transducer so it is contacting the bottom side of the 
differential carrier and secure it in place.

Run the engine and driveline at the worst vibration speed noted and 
visually note the position of the chalk line by use of the strobe light. This 
provides a starting point for the initial location of the hose clamps. 

Stop the engine and rotate the driveshaft so that the chalk line is in 
the same location as it was noted under the strobe light.

[FIGURE: E27231B.gif]

[FIGURE: E27241B.gif]

Install two screw-type (stainless steel) hose clamps on the driveshaft. 
Position the clamp heads 180 degrees from the transducer and tighten the 
clamps. 

 CAUTION: Do not run the engine with the transmission engaged on the hoist for 
extended periods due to the danger of overheating the engine and transmission. 

Run the engine and driveline through the speed range. If no vibration 
is felt, remove the lug nuts, install the wheels and tires and reinstall the 
lug nuts in the correct position and proceed to Step 9. However, if any 
vibration still exists, the combined weight of the two hose clamp heads may be 
in excess. To reduce this excess weight, rotate the clamp heads away from each 
other approximately 15 degrees (one each way from the original position). Run 
the engine and driveline and note if the vibration has been reduced.

[FIGURE: E55901A.gif]

Continue to rotate the clamp heads apart in smaller angular increments 
until the feel of balance is best. At this point, install the wheels and tires 
as described in Step 7 and road test the vehicle to determine the actual 
degree of improvement. If satisfactory improvement has been obtained, proceed 
to Step 9. If no improvement has been obtained, the clamps must be removed and 
diagnosis should be redirected to other areas, such as wheels, tires, 
driveline angle, and yoke runout. 

When the vehicle has been corrected to a satisfactory level, as 
determined by a road test evaluation, tighten the clamps securely. Clean 
thoroughly with lacquer thinner, and spray the clamps with a commercially 
available black paint for a finished appearance.

ADJUSTMENTS

Ring Gear Backlash Adjustment

 Specifications 

 NOTE: Measure the outer diameter of ring gear for approximate pitch diameter. 

Ring gears that have a pitch diameter of less than 431.8 mm (17 inches).

Range of backlash setting — 0.20-0.46 mm (0.008-0.018 inch). 

Backlash setting for new gearsets — 0.30 mm (0.012 inch). 

Ring gears that have a pitch diameter of 431.8 mm (17 inches) or 
greater. 

Range of backlash setting — 0.25-0.51 mm (0.010-0.020 inch). 

Backlash setting for new gearsets — 0.38 mm (0.015 inch).

[FIGURE: E78321A.gif]

If the old gearset is installed, adjust the backlash to the setting 
that was measured before the carrier was disassembled. 

If a new gearset is installed, adjust the backlash to the correct 
specification for new gearsets. 

During the check of tooth contact patterns, the backlash can be 
adjusted within specification limits, if needed, to change the location of the 
pattern. 

Attach Dial Indicator with Bracketry TOOL-4201-C or equivalent on the 
mounting flange of the carrier.

[FIGURE: E5348D.gif]

Adjust the dial indicator so that the plunger or pointer is against the 
tooth surface. 

Adjust the dial of the indicator to zero (0). 

Hold the drive pinion in position. 

 NOTE: Backlash is increased by moving the ring gear away from the drive 
pinion. Backlash is decreased by moving the ring gear toward the drive pinion. 
When you adjust backlash, move the ring gear only. Do not move the drive 
pinion. 

Read the dial indicator, while rotating the differential and ring gear 
a small amount in both directions, against teeth of the drive pinion. If the 
backlash reading is within specification, continue by checking tooth contact 
patterns. If the backlash reading is not within specifications, adjust 
backlash as needed. Continue by following Steps 6 and 7.

[FIGURE: E78331A.gif]

Loosen one bearing adjusting ring one notch, then tighten the opposite 
ring the same amount.

[FIGURE: E78341A.gif]

Repeat Steps 2 to 6 until the backlash is within specifications.

Check tooth contact patterns of the gearset. Refer to Tooth Contact 
Patterns Check of Gearset under Component Tests in the Diagnosis and Testing 
portion of this section.

Install cotter keys, pins or lock plates that hold the two bearing 
adjusting rings in position. Use the following procedures.

Cotter keys — Install cotter keys between lugs of the 
adjusting ring and through the boss of the bearing cap. Bend the two ends of 
the cotter key around the boss.

Pins — Install pin through boss of the bearing cap 
until the pin is between lugs of the adjusting ring. Use a drift and hammer to 
install the pin.

Lock plates — Install lock plate on bearing cap so that 
the tab is between lugs of the adjusting ring. Install the two capscrews that 
hold the lock plate to the bearing cap. Tighten the capscrews to correct 
torque value as listed under the Specifications 
portion of Section 05-02A.

[FIGURE: E7835B.gif]
