Section 06-02: Brake Drum

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake System, Drum

A brake drum's function is to provide a friction surface for the brake 
lining and to absorb and dissipate the heat generated by the braking action.

The full cast brake drum is machined from a single iron casting and is 
a uniform material throughout. The full cast brake drums feature a mill 
balance or machine-to-balance process. In this process, the brake drums are 
cast with a thicker band around the perimeter near the open face of the brake 
drum. This band is approximately 51 mm (2 inches) wide and 13 mm (0.5 inch) 
thick. This band can then be precisely machined to bring the brake drum into 
balance. This process will greatly reduce "hot spots" caused by balance 
weights welded to the brake drum. 

 Brake Drum, Full Cast 

[FIGURE: H10265A.gif]

PAGE 3104

Section 06-02: Brake Drum

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake, Service

The cam-type brake is an air-operated, two-shoe brake. 

As the brake pedal is applied, air pressure is routed to the brake air 
chamber. The brake air chamber has an internal diaphragm that will push 
against the brake air chamber push rod with a force proportional to the air 
pressure being applied to the brake air chamber. The brake air chamber push 
rod then pushes on the slack adjuster arm, which causes rotation of the brake 
camshaft. Rollers riding on the brake cam lobes are forced apart with rotation 
of the brake camshaft. The brake shoes riding on the rollers are then forced 
apart and into contact with the brake drum.

When the brake pedal is released, return springs in the brake air 
chamber and brake shoe assembly pull the components back to the at-rest 
position.

================================================================================
PAGE 3105
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 06-02: Brake Drum

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake, Parking

The parking brake system is composed of a parking brake control valve, 
double check valve, quick release valves and spring brake air chambers. The 
spring brake air chambers use a powerful spring to mechanically apply the 
service brakes. Brake system air pressure in the spring brake air chambers 
keeps the spring brakes from being applied. Therefore, the spring brakes will 
be applied whenever brake system air pressure falls below a preset level, 
whether intentionally or unintentionally.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake Shoe Automatic Adjustment

Brake shoe automatic adjustment design uses both brake air chamber push 
rod travel and shoe-to-brake drum force to maintain proper brake adjustment. 
Upon brake application, the brake air chamber push rod rotates the slack 
adjuster until the adjusting link engages a one-way cone clutch on the 
wormshaft within the slack adjuster. At this point, if the brake shoes are not 
in contact with the brake drum, the cone clutch will remain engaged with the 
wormshaft and the link will rotate the wormshaft. This wormshaft rotation 
adjusts the brake shoes by reducing shoe-to-brake drum clearance. Adjustment 
continues until the brake linings are forced against the brake drum. The 
shoe-to-brake drum force creates a resistance torque that exceeds the slip 
torque of the cone clutch and allows the clutch to slip on the wormshaft for 
the remainder of the slack adjuster travel. During the return stroke the 
one-way cone clutch allows the link to return without wormshaft movement. The 
adjustment cycle will repeat until shoe-to-brake drum contact force occurs 
simultaneously with the link-to-clutch engagement.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake Drum Mounting

 Outboard 

The outboard-mounted brake drum is mounted on the outboard face of the 
hub and fits over the wheel mounting studs. The wheel is mounted on the face 
of the brake drum, providing access to brakes without disturbing bearings or 
seals. Make sure the brake drum pilot diameter does not interfere with the 
mating hub pilot diameter.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Wheels, Disc, Outboard-Mounted Drums

 WARNING: AFTERMARKET WHEEL ASSEMBLIES MAY NOT BE COMPATIBLE WITH THE VEHICLE. 
USE OF INCOMPATIBLE WHEEL ASSEMBLIES MAY RESULT IN EQUIPMENT FAILURE AND 
POSSIBLE INJURY. USE ONLY APPROVED WHEEL ASSEMBLIES. 

 WARNING: DO NOT PAINT DISC WHEEL MOUNTING SURFACE OR WHEEL STUDS. EXCESS PAINT 
CAN ADVERSELY AFFECT DISC WHEEL MOUNTING SYSTEM. 

 WARNING: USE ONLY FLANGED, INTEGRAL TWO-PIECE SWIVELING WHEEL NUTS ON VEHICLES 
EQUIPPED WITH DUAL REAR WHEELS. DO NOT ATTEMPT TO USE BALL SEAT ONE-PIECE 
WHEEL NUTS ON THESE VEHICLES. IF USED, BALL SEAT ONE-PIECE WHEEL NUTS CAN COME 
LOOSE DURING VEHICLE OPERATION. DO NOT ATTEMPT TO USE PAST MODEL WHEELS THAT 
HAVE BALL SEATS ON THIS VEHICLE. DO NOT ATTEMPT TO USE PRESENT DESIGN WHEELS 
AND WHEEL NUTS ON PAST MODEL WHEEL HUBS. ATTEMPTED USE OF INTERMIXED WHEELS 
CAN LEAD TO DAMAGE TO THE WHEEL MOUNTING SYSTEM AND COULD RESULT IN WHEELS 
COMING LOOSE. 

 Removal 

Remove the tire and wheel assembly. 

[FIGURE: H33351B.gif]

Remove the brake drum from the hub.

 CAUTION: Replace brake drums with brake drums of the same type. Failure to do so 
will affect vehicle track and performance. Replace cast brake drums only with 
cast brake drums. 

Check the brake drum for damage or wear and service or replace as 
necessary. If a new brake drum is installed, be sure to remove the protective 
coating with degreaser.

Check wheel seals for leakage. If the hub is removed from the axle, 
install new wheel seals. Refer to Section 04-01 for front wheel seals or to 
 Section 04-02B for rear wheel seals.

 Installation 

 WARNING: MAKE SURE THE BRAKE DRUM SLIDES OVER THE PILOT LOCATORS WITH REASONABLE 
EFFORT AND THAT BRAKE DRUM FLANGE IS FULLY SUPPORTED BY THE MATING HUB FLANGE. 

Install the brake drum on the hub.

Mount inside wheel on rear hub with wheel dish facing inboard. Make 
sure wheel is flush with hub mounting surface so there is no gap between hub 
and wheel.

Install outside rear wheel with wheel dish facing outboard so it is 
flush against inner wheel.

Install and tighten 8 or 10 integral two-piece wheel nuts (nut and 
washer assembly), as required, until snug.

With wheel nuts loosely installed, turn wheel until one wheel nut is at 
top of bolt circle. Tighten until snug. In criss-cross manner, tighten 
remaining wheel nuts until snug to minimize runout. Remove safety stands and 
lower vehicle to floor.

Observing tightening sequence and torque specifications, evenly tighten 
the wheel nuts. Refer to Section 04-04 .

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Wheel Hub Bolt 

 Disc Wheel 

 WARNING: DO NOT USE OXYACETYLENE OR SIMILAR EQUIPMENT TO HEAT THE HUB. THIS MAY 
CAUSE OVERHEATING IN LOCALIZED AREAS, WHICH WILL RESULT IN LOSS OF STRENGTH 
THAT MAY CAUSE FAILURE OF THE HUB ASSEMBLY AND, ULTIMATELY, LOSS OF VEHICLE 
CONTROL. 

 WARNING: WHEN ONE BROKEN STUD IS REPLACED, THE STUD ON EACH SIDE OF IT MUST BE 
REPLACED. IF MORE THAN ONE STUD IS BROKEN, ALL STUDS MUST BE REPLACED. 

 Removal 

Remove the tire and wheel. 

Remove the hub and brake drum assembly from the front or rear axle. 
Refer to Section 04-01 for front wheel or Section 04-02B for rear wheels.

Separate the hub and brake drum assembly.

Position the hub on a suitable press with the inner bearing cup facing 
down.

Support the hub flange evenly, and adjacent to the mounting stud being 
removed.

Using a steady, uninterrupted movement, press the damaged mounting stud 
out of the hub.

 Installation 

 WARNING: WHEEL MOUNTING HARDWARE SPECIFICATIONS ARE CRITICAL. ALWAYS CHECK AND 
OBSERVE MANUFACTURER'S RECOMMENDATIONS FOR DIMENSIONS AND QUALITY. FAILURE TO 
USE CORRECT PARTS CAN CAUSE COMPONENT FAILURE LEADING TO SERIOUS INJURY OR 
DEATH. 

 CAUTION: Metric fasteners are right-hand threaded only. 

Position the hub on the press with the inner bearing cup facing up.

Support the hub evenly and adjacent to the mounting stud hole.

Insert the new mounting stud in the hub.

 CAUTION: Make sure the flat edges on the mounting stud are in line with the 
groove or shoulder on the hub. Make sure the mounting stud is fully seated and 
that the shoulder does not become embedded in the hub. If the mounting stud is 
embedded into the hub, the hub must be replaced. 

With a steady, uninterrupted movement, press the new mounting stud all 
the way into the hub.

Remove the hub from the press.

Reassemble the hub and brake drum assembly.

Observing tightening sequence and torque specifications, install the 
wheel and tire. Refer to Section 04-04 .

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Brake Drum Refinishing

 NOTE: All production brake drum tolerances are as follows: 15-inch diameter ±
0.254 mm (0.010 inch) maximum. 16.5-inch diameter ±
0.254 mm (0.010 inch) maximum.

For safety, the following rebore and wear limitations are recommended:

 REBORE AND WEAR LIMITS

Brake Drum Original Inside Diameter Size

Rebore Limits

Permissible Additional Wear

Total Rebore and Wear Limits

Over 14 Inches Standard

2.032 mm

 (0.080 Inch)

1.016 mm

 (0.040 Inch)

3.048 mm

 (0.120 Inch)

Brake drums should be machined or replaced in axle pairs to get the 
same braking on both sides of the vehicle.

Minor scores on a brake drum can be removed with fine emery cloth, 
provided the emery is thoroughly cleaned off the brake drum after the operation.

A badly scored, rough, or out-of-round brake drum should be ground or 
turned on a drum lathe. Turn brake drums only when necessary and remove only 
as much material as necessary. Do not remove any more material from the brake 
drum than is necessary to provide a smooth surface for brake shoe contact. 
Brake drum maximum braking surface diameter is shown on each brake drum. Brake 
drums which exceed the maximum braking surface diameter shown on the brake 
drum, caused either by wear or refinishing, must be replaced. The replacement 
brake drum should be of the same type, size and shape. It is not necessary to 
turn a replacement brake drum on installation. The brake drum pilot will 
accurately locate the braking surface.

[FIGURE: H4152B.gif]

After refinishing the brake surface, runout must not exceed 0.25 mm 
(0.010 inch) total indicator reading, measured from the bearing cups.

Fade resistance and strength of brake drums rebored in excess of the 
above limits are reduced to a point approaching a safety hazard. All brake 
drums exceeding the maximum brake (drum) face diameter should be replaced.

Oversize brake drums will result in rough or chattering brakes and a 
pulsating ride. They produce fast fade.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Cleaning

 WARNING: DO NOT INHALE THE DUST FROM BRAKES , CLUTCHES OR ASSOCIATED COMPONENTS. 
INHALATION OF DUST FROM THESE COMPONENTS COULD BE INJURIOUS TO YOUR HEALTH AND 
COULD CAUSE CANCER OR ASBESTOSIS. COMPRESSED AIR OR BRUSHES MUST NOT BE USED 
TO CLEAN BRAKES, BRAKE DRUMS, CLUTCHES OR ASSOCIATED COMPONENTS. USE A VACUUM 
CLEANER SUCH AS ROTUNDA BRAKE/CLUTCH/SERVICE VACUUM 164-R3600 OR EQUIVALENT 
EQUIPPED FOR THIS PURPOSE TO CAREFULLY REMOVE ANY DUST. ADHERENT DUST SHOULD 
BE REMOVED WITH A DAMP RAG. ANY DUST SHOULD BE CONTAINED IN A SEALED AND 
LABELED BAG FOR DISPOSAL. WEAR AN APPROVED HIGH-EFFICIENCY CARTRIDGE OR AIR 
LINE RESPIRATOR AND USE EXTRA CAUTION TO AVOID BREATHING THIS DUST. USE 
NON-ASBESTOS REPLACEMENT PARTS WHENEVER POSSIBLE. 

Removal of dust and dirt from brake assemblies should be done with 
Rotunda Brake/Clutch/Service Vacuum 164-R3600 or equivalent, or Rotunda Brake 
Washer 065-00016 or equivalent. Brake assembly dust and dirt should not be 
removed by blowing off with an air gun or by vacuuming with a standard 
industrial vacuum.

ADJUSTMENTS

Hub and Drum Balancing

If conventional wheel balancing methods do not correct cab pitch or 
steering wheel vibration that occurs between 68-90 km/h (42-56 mph), the hub 
and brake drum or cast spoke wheel and brake drum assembly must be balanced 
separately from the wheel and tire assembly. Use the following procedure to 
statically balance the assembly. (The hub and brake drum assembly is used as 
an example.)

Mark all tires and hub assemblies as to their respective positions on 
the vehicle.

Remove the hub and brake drum. Refer to Wheels, Disc, Outboard-Mounted 
Drums , in the Removal and Installation portion of this section.

Clean all loose dirt and rust from the hub and brake drum assembly.

Drain all excess oil from the inside of the hub cavity.

Mount the assembly on a suitable brake drum balancing mandrel. Use 
Rotunda Truck Arbor Set 104-00034 and Truck Hub/Hubless Adapter Set 104-00014 
or equivalent to center the assembly (leave the wheel bearings installed in 
the hub). Tighten the large nut.

Place the mandrel and the hub and brake drum assembly onto two safety 
stands. Install a support bearing (C3AZ-7025-C or equivalent) on each end of 
the mandrel.

 Brake Drum Balancing Setup, Typical 

[FIGURE: H10342A.gif]

Rotate the mandrel and the assembly to make sure it turns freely on the 
support bearings. If required, apply light lubricating oil to the two support 
bearings to reduce friction.

Rotate the assembly several times and allow it to come to a stop. If 
the assembly remains stationary at all positions, it does not require 
balancing. If the assembly does not remain stationary at all positions, the 
assembly requires balancing. The heaviest part will normally rest at the 
bottom. Refer to Steps 9-11 for balancing procedures.

Mark the top of the brake drum, which will be the lightest part. Rotate 
the assembly a few times to verify that the mark always appears at the top of 
the brake drum.

Tape small pieces of flat, mild steel on the light area of the brake 
drum. Experiment with different weights until hub and brake drum will not 
rotate when stopped at any position. When adding weights, remember to allow 
for clearance between the brake drum and wheel during installation.

 CAUTION: Under no condition should any welding method be used other than arc 
welding. To prevent brake drum distortion, do not use a current setting of 
more than 100 amps. 

 NOTE: Do not add balance weights to the 8-hole brake drums on 8 bolt hubs for 
rear axles.

After determining the proper weight to balance the hub and brake drum 
assembly, tack weld the weight to the brake drum. Use a 3-mm (1/8-inch) 
welding rod, either silver-nickel or chrome-nickel.

Install the hub and brake drum, and the tire and wheel assembly.

Rebalance the wheel and tire assembly using an appropriate electronic 
balancer.

Road test the vehicle for several miles to verify that vibration or cab 
pitch has been reduced to an acceptable level.

Section 06-05: Brake, Air, Parking/Emergency System

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Parking/Emergency System 

 WARNING: IN THE EVENT OF PARKING BRAKE SYSTEM DAMAGE, THE VEHICLE SHOULD NOT BE 
OPERATED UNTIL THE SYSTEM IS REPAIRED. 

The parking brake system is composed of a parking brake control valve, 
a modulating valve (trucks) or double check valve (tractors), quick release 
valves and spring brakes. The spring brake chambers use a powerful spring to 
mechanically apply the brakes when air pressure is not available (provided the 
brakes are properly adjusted). 

Air pressure compresses the spring in the brake air chamber when the 
parking brake control is in the release position. The air pressure is 
delivered to the brake air chamber by modulating valve or a double check 
valve. The modulating valve is controlled by an air pressure signal from the 
parking brake control valve on the instrument panel. The modulating valve or 
double check valve also functions to prevent the application of the spring 
brakes and service brakes at the same time, thus preventing brake system 
damage. 

 Emergency Stopping, Tractors 

For emergency stopping, tractors use a vertically split brake system. 
If an air pressure loss occurs somewhere in the front brake system (hose, air 
line, etc.), the rear (primary) brake system will continue to operate until 
the supply air is depleted by several brake applications. An air pressure loss 
in the rear brake system makes the front (secondary) brake system responsible 
for stopping the vehicle until the air supply in the reservoir(s) is depleted. 

 WARNING: IN THE EVENT OF BRAKE SYSTEM DAMAGE, THE VEHICLE SHOULD NOT BE OPERATED 
UNTIL THE SYSTEM IS REPAIRED. 

 Emergency Stopping, Trucks 

Emergency brake systems on trucks are different than brake systems on 
tractors. The rear (primary) brake system operates similarly to a tractor-type 
system when there is a failure in the front brake system. A failure in the 
rear brake system leaves the front brakes continuing to function, but 
additional braking power is provided by the modulation of the rear spring 
brakes application. This is done by the modulating valve. 

For either truck or tractor emergency systems, the stopping 
capabilities of the brakes are reduced during a brake failure since not all of 
the brakes are functional. Upon service of the component, the system should 
return to normal operation.

 WARNING: IN THE EVENT OF BRAKE SYSTEM DAMAGE, THE VEHICLE SHOULD NOT BE OPERATED 
UNTIL THE SYSTEM IS REPAIRED. 

The brake air chamber assembly consists of two separate air chambers, 
each having its own application and release mechanism. The only difference 
between the two chambers is that the service chamber applies the brake by air 
pressure and releases it by spring pressure; the spring brake chamber applies 
the brake by spring pressure and releases it by air pressure. 

 Parking/Emergency Stopping 

During normal driving (brakes released), the service brakes are held in 
the released position by the diaphragm return spring in the service air 
chamber assembly. Air reservoir pressure against the spring brake chamber 
piston and diaphragm keeps the parking-emergency spring compressed. 

During normal braking (service brakes applied), air pressure from the 
foot control valve pressing on the service brake diaphragm applies the brakes. 
Air reservoir pressure in the spring brake chamber keeps the parking-emergency 
spring compressed. Normal service brake operation is not affected by the 
spring brake. 

During parking or an emergency brake application, air is exhausted from 
the spring brake chamber permitting the parking-emergency spring to expand, 
moving the spring brake piston and the brake air chamber push rod against the 
slack adjuster assembly to apply the brakes. 

Loss of air pressure at the spring brake chamber will result in 
automatic application of the brakes. If it is necessary to move the vehicle 
before air pressure can be restored, the parking-emergency spring must be 
manually compressed. Refer to Section 06-08E or to Section 06-08F for the 
procedure to manually release the spring brake and then reset the spring brake 
after service has been performed. The vehicle should not be driven until the 
brake system is repaired. 

Two types of spring brake chambers are used: Maxi-Brake II and MGM.

Section 06-05: Brake, Air, Parking/Emergency System

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Maxi-Brake II 

The Midland Maxi-Brake II brake air chambers are standard. The Maxi has 
an emergency chamber, a service chamber and a bulkhead assembly. 

The service chamber applies the brake by air pressure and releases it 
by spring pressure when air is exhausted from the service brake chamber. The 
emergency brake in the end cap is applied by spring pressure and released by 
air pressure. 

A safe level of air pressure within the system holds spring brakes 
released, but always ready for parking or emergency application.

[FIGURE: H8914B.gif]

Since the service section and spring brake section are isolated from 
each other by seals, the spring brake cannot interfere with the operation of 
the normal service brake.

[FIGURE: H9702A.gif]

A hand operated parking brake control valve in the cab to exhaust air 
pressure from the spring brake air chamber gives the driver foolproof and 
positive parking brakes.

[FIGURE: H9703A.gif]

For Maxi-Brake II brake chamber service procedures, refer to Section 06-08E .

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Valve, Parking Brake Control 

The parking brake control valve is a push-pull, manually operated air 
control valve. It is pressure- sensitive and will automatically move from the 
parking brake released position to the apply position if both primary and 
secondary air reservoirs are reduced to below 241-310 kPa (35-45 psi).

Air pressure is constantly supplied to the supply port from the air 
reservoirs. As the parking brake control valve is pushed in, air is supplied 
to the spring chambers releasing the parking brakes. This air pressure also 
acts on the surface area of the inlet and exhaust valve to keep the valve in. 
If the air supply pressure to the valve is reduced to a pressure of 241-310 
kPa (35-45 psi), a spring will overcome the force created by the air pressure 
on the inlet and exhaust valve and the valve will pop out. This will apply the 
parking brakes by releasing the air from the brake air chambers out through 
the parking brake control valve exhaust port. 

The parking brakes are normally applied by manually pulling out the 
parking brake control valve and releasing the air from the spring chambers.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Valve, Modulating

The modulating valve is used on the parking system for truck-type 
vehicles only. 

The modulating valve is used in conjunction with a dual air brake 
system and spring brakes and performs four functions: 

limits hold-off pressure to the spring brake air chambers to 655-724 
kPa (95-105 psi) 

provides for quick release of air pressure from the spring cavity of 
the spring brake air chamber allowing a fast application of the spring brake

modulates spring brake application should a failure occur in the 
service brake system

prevents compounding of service and spring forces

Brake Air Chamber

 NOTE: The force of the spring below the balance piston is adjustable by an 
external screw on the modulating valve. The adjustment is set at the factory 
so the inlet valve will close at a slightly greater pressure, 655 kPa (95 
psi), than the hold-off pressure of the spring brake actuator, but below the 
maximum system pressure. 

When air pressure in the spring brake compartment of the brake air 
chamber has released the spring brake and when air pressure on top of the 
balance piston is sufficient to overcome the force of the balance piston 
spring, the balance piston moves. When the balance piston moves, it allows the 
inlet valve spring to close the inlet valve, shutting off further air pressure 
from the reservoir that supplies the modulating valve.

When the parking brakes are released and a normal service brake 
application is made by actuating the foot control valve, air from the primary 
circuit is delivered to the lower side of the control piston through the 
balance port. Air from the secondary circuit is delivered to the top of the 
control piston through the control port. Because air pressure from the primary 
and secondary circuits are not equal, there will be a slight movement of the 
control piston but the modulating valve does not operate.

The pressure differential between the primary and secondary circuits 
regulates the amount of air pressure released from the spring cavity of the 
spring brake air chamber. This results in a brake application on the rear axle 
which is proportionate to the braking on the other axles. 

Should a failure in the secondary air system occur, causing loss of air 
pressure and requiring an emergency foot control valve application, reduced 
air pressure would be delivered to the top of the control piston. However, the 
inlet and exhaust valve and balance piston would not move and the braking on 
the rear axle(s) is made sure by the primary circuit supplying rear axle 
service brakes. The spring brakes would not be actuated.

Circuit

Brake Air Chamber 

When the knob of the parking brake control valve is pulled to the park 
(exhaust) position, the modulating valve's supply air pressure and the air 
pressure in the brake air chamber is exhausted. The single check valve speeds 
the exhaust of air from the brake air chamber cavities by allowing the air on 
top of the balance piston to exhaust by the double check valve through the 
supply port to the atmosphere. When air pressure drops sufficiently, the 
balance piston opens the inlet valve, opening the larger passage in the 
modulating valve. This makes sure the balance of air pressure in the spring 
cavity of the brake air chamber exhausts rapidly.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Valve, Quick Release 

The quick release valve is used for several functions in the brake 
system. It is mounted near the brake air chambers to provide a close exit 
point for exhausted air. The nearer the air exhaust port, the quicker the 
application of the spring brake or release of the service brake.

It is used in tractors to release air pressure in the service line. It 
is used in the parking brake system to provide a faster brake application and 
to eliminate the undesirable exhausting of large quantities of air into the cab.

[FIGURE: H4959E.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

2A095

Quick Release Valve

2

—

Supply Port (Part of 2A095)

3

—

Delivery Port (Part of 2A095)

4

—

Exhaust Port (Not Threaded) (Part of 2A095)

When a brake application is made, air pressure enters the supply port. 
The diaphragm moves down and seals the exhaust. At the same time, air pressure 
forces the edges of the diaphragm down and air flows out the delivery port. 

When air pressure being delivered (beneath the diaphragm) equals the 
pressure being delivered by the brake valve (above the diaphragm), the 
diaphragm outer edge will seal against the body seat. The exhaust port is 
still sealed by the center portion of the diaphragm when the foot control 
valve application is released. When the air pressure above the diaphragm is 
released back through the foot control valve exhaust port, air pressure 
beneath the diaphragm forces the diaphragm to rise, opening the exhaust port 
and allowing air to exhaust.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Valve, Double Check 

The double check valve is used in an air brake system to direct a flow 
of air into a common line from either of two sources, whichever is at the 
higher pressure. It may be used for directing airflow for specific functions 
or to select the higher pressure of either of two sources of air as a supply 
source. 

 Double Check Valve 

[FIGURE: H4167D.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

—

Inlet Port (Part of 2K119)

2

—

Delivery Port (Part of 2K119)

3

—

Shuttle (Part of 2K119)

4

—

Body (Part of 2K119)

5

—

Shuttle Guide (Part of 2K119)

6

—

O-Ring (Part of 2K119)

The double check valve is used in several parts of the brake system. It 
is used in the brake system for tractors to make sure both the service brake 
force and the spring force of a brake air chamber are not applied at the same 
time, which could damage the brake system. If the parking brakes are applied, 
the air is released from the spring hold-off side of the brake air chamber to 
provide spring application of the brakes. To make sure the service chamber 
force is not applied at the same time, the double check valve routes air 
pressure to the spring brake hold-off side of the brake air chamber during a 
service brake application, relieving the spring force proportional to the 
service brake application. 

The double check valve used in the parking brake supply line serves to 
make sure if a failure occurs in either the primary or secondary air supply 
system, the remaining system will provide sufficient air for control of the 
spring brake release. It is used with the tractor hand control valve to allow 
either foot control valve control or tractor control valve application of the 
trailer brakes. 

The double check valve operates as follows: air under pressure enters 
either of the double check valve inlet ports. The moving shuttle is pushed 
away from a higher pressure inlet port to seal a lower pressure inlet port. 
The airflow continues out the delivery port of the double check valve. The 
position of the shuttle will reverse if the pressure levels are reversed.

Section 06-05: Brake, Air, Parking/Emergency System

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Low-Pressure Indicator Switch 

The low air pressure switch is a safety device designed to give an 
automatic warning to the driver whenever air pressure in the air brake system 
is below 414 kPa (60 psi), the safe minimum for normal vehicle operation. It 
is used to operate an electrical buzzer and warning lamp, which are audible 
and visible to the driver. The low air pressure switch is located on the 
parking brake control valve. 

The low air pressure switch is also used in the primary and secondary 
air supply lines. 

The low air pressure switch is designed so that the electrical contacts 
remain closed by the spring force until the air brake system pressure is above 
the spring set point (force). The setting and piece number are marked on a 
label on the low air pressure switch body. If a label is not present, the 
vehicle manual should be consulted for the proper setting. The minimum setting 
of the low air pressure switch is 511-593 kPa (74-86 psi). 

The low air pressure switch operates as follows: when air pressure at 
the supply port and under the diaphragm is above 552 kPa (80 psi), the 
electrical contacts remain open because the force exerted by air pressure 
underneath the diaphragm overcomes the force exerted by the spring above the 
diaphragm. 

When air pressure below the diaphragm drops below 552 kPa (80 psi), the 
spring exerts a force that is greater than the force exerted by the air 
pressure below the diaphragm. This causes a piston to move and allows the 
electrical contacts to close. When the ignition switch is on, this closes the 
electrical circuit to the warning device, warning the driver of low air 
pressure in the system.

 Low Air Pressure Switch 

[FIGURE: H8324B.gif]

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Brake, Air, Parking/Emergency System

 Inspection and Verification 

 WARNING: BEFORE ATTEMPTING TO WORK ON AN AIR BRAKE SYSTEM, CERTAIN PRECAUTIONS 
SHOULD BE OBSERVED. AIR UNDER COMPRESSION MAY BE COMPARED TO THE ENERGY IN A 
COILED SPRING AND WHEN RELEASED, MAY PRESENT A HAZARD IF NOT PROPERLY 
RECOGNIZED. 

Follow the safety measures listed below.

The wheels of the vehicle should always be blocked by some means other 
than the air brake system so that depletion of air will not permit the vehicle 
to roll.

In draining the system, do not look into the air jets or direct them 
toward a person as dirt or sludge particles may be carried in the air stream. 
Hoses which contain air pressure should not be disconnected under pressure 
since they will whip as air escapes from the line.

Follow the manufacturers' recommended procedures in working on any air 
device so as to avoid injury or damage from parts which, when released, are 
subject to mechanical (spring) or pneumatic propulsion.

As system pressure is drained and the emergency brakes applied, hands 
should be away from brake air chamber push rods and slack adjusters which will 
apply automatically with the loss of pressure. This also applies when checking 
a service brake system.

Reservoirs that are closest to the source of compressed air (compressor 
or auxiliary source) should contain a safety valve in known working order and 
sufficient capacity to limit the reservoir pressure to a safe maximum level.

Old, used reservoirs should not be used as replacements. The safety 
valves should not be reset higher than specified by the reservoir 
manufacturer, vehicle manufacturer, or code to which the reservoir had been 
manufactured.

Brake air chambers contain large internal steel springs that require 
special disassembly procedures. Note and be guided by the warning tags on such 
units.

 Symptom Chart — Air, Parking/Emergency System 

 AIR, PARKING/EMERGENCY SYSTEM 

Condition

Possible Source

Action

Braking Is Uneven. Vehicle Pulls to One Side

 NOTE: Brake-pull evaluation should be conducted on a smooth, level surface.

Low tire pressure or worn tires.

INFLATE tires to recommended pressure. REPLACE worn tires. REFER to 
 Section 04-04 .

Improperly adjusted brakes.

 NOTE: VERIFY that the air chamber push rod clevis position is to 
specifications.

ADJUST brakes to recommended specifications. REFER to Section 06-08D .

Worn or damaged brake air chambers.

APPLY brakes and CHECK brake air chamber operation. CHECK for leaking 
diaphragm, bent push rod or other damage. SERVICE brake air chamber components 
as required. REFER to Section 06-08D , Section 06-08E or Section 06-08F .

Improper push rod-to-slack adjuster connection.

CHECK connection from push rod to slack adjuster. Connections must be 
the same on both ends of the axle. Clevis should be free moving. Lengths from 
clevis pin to center of brake camshaft must be the same.

Worn or damaged brake camshaft.

 NOTE: Do not use heat to free brake camshaft. The brake camshaft contains 
nylon bushings that might be damaged.

CHECK for frozen or restricted brake camshaft. LUBRICATE brake camshaft 
and WORK free or DISASSEMBLE and SERVICE. REFER to Section 06-08D .

Worn or damaged brake components.

CHECK for contaminated brake linings or damaged hoses, rollers, brake 
shoes and return springs. If linings are contaminated, REPLACE linings. 
SERVICE worn or damaged components as required. REFER to Section 06-08D .

Worn or damaged air lines.

CHECK for equal air pressure delivery to the brake air chambers at both 
ends of the axle. SERVICE leaking, collapsed or damaged air lines. CHECK for 
internal restrictions in the air lines, fittings or valve ports. REFER to 
 Section 06-08A or Section 06-08B .

Worn or damaged bearing or overtightened wheel bearing nut.

RAISE each wheel with brakes released. CHECK for free wheel rotation. 
If wheels do not rotate freely, CHECK for worn or damaged bearings. CHECK 
bearing nut torque. TIGHTEN to specifications. REFER to Section 04-01 or 
 Section 04-02B .

Low Air Pressure Buzzer Is Sounding or Dual Air Pressure Gauge Reading 
Is Above 414 kPa (60 psi)

Damaged or worn low air pressure switch.

DISCONNECT terminal to low air pressure switch. If buzzer continues, 
CHECK for other electrical wiring ground. SERVICE wiring. If buzzer stops with 
terminal disconnected, CHECK instrument panel air gauge. SERVICE or REPLACE 
low air pressure switch. REFER to Section 06-08A .

Damaged or worn air pressure gauge.

CHECK air pressure at inlet to dual air pressure gauge with a test 
gauge. If pressure is below 414 kPa (60 psi), REPLACE the instrument panel air 
gauge. REFER to Section 13-10 .

Braking Inadequate

Excessive brake air chamber push rod travel.

ADJUST slack adjuster. Refer to Section 06-08D .

Glazed or worn brake linings.

REPLACE brake shoe and linings. REFER to Section 06-08D .

Grease or oil on brake linings.

REPLACE brake shoe and linings.

Worn, heat-spotted or cracked brake drums.

REPLACE brake drums. REFER to Section 06-02 .

Excessive brake air chamber push rod length.

ADJUST slack adjuster. Refer to Section 06-08D .

Brake air chamber improperly positioned in bracket slot.

REPOSITION brake air chamber. REFER to Section 06-08E or Section 06-08F .

Broken or bent cam brake components.

REPLACE components. REFER to Section 06-08D .

Brake linings do not contact brake drum during brake application.

SERVICE foundation brake system. REFER to Section 06-08D .

Flat spot on brake camshaft or rollers.

REPLACE brake camshaft or rollers. REFER to Section 06-08D .

Parking Brake Is Inoperative or Slow to Apply

Damaged or worn parking brake control valve.

 WARNING: BEFORE ATTEMPTING TO REPAIR A BRAKE AIR CHAMBER, READ AND FOLLOW THE 
SERVICE PROCEDURES IN THE APPROPRIATE BRAKE AIR CHAMBER SECTION. THE SPRING 
BRAKE CHAMBERS CONTAIN A POWERFUL SPRING THAT MUST BE DISENGAGED CAREFULLY. 
DISCONNECT the air line from the delivery port of the parking control 
valve carefully — air and debris may come out. ALLOW air to 
exhaust from the line and CHECK if parking brakes apply. If parking brakes 
apply, SERVICE or REPLACE the parking brake control valve. REFER to Valve, 
Parking Brake Control in the Removal and Installation portion of this section.

Damaged or worn double check valve.

REMOVE the jounce hose to axle at double check valve. PUSH the parking 
brake control valve to the release or off position and CHECK if air escapes 
from the double check valve. SERVICE or REPLACE the double check valve. REFER 
to Valve, Double Check in the Removal and Installation portion of this section.

Damaged or worn brake air chamber.

DISCONNECT the slack adjuster clevis pin and MOVE the slack adjuster 
arm out of the way. APPLY the parking brake control and CHECK if the brake air 
chamber push rod moves to the fully extended position. If not, SERVICE or 
REPLACE the brake air chamber. (VERIFY spring brakes are not held off with 
cage bolts.) REFER to Section 06-08E and Section 06-08F .

Damaged or worn foundation brake.

APPLY the parking brake control (on position), and CHECK for movement 
of the slack adjuster. MOVE the parking brake control to the released or off 
position and APPLY the service brakes. If the brakes do not apply, SERVICE or 
LUBRICATE the foundation brakes. REFER to Section 06-08D .

Parking Brake Will Not Release or Is Slow to Release

Leaking air lines.

With the parking brake in the released position, CHECK for leakage in 
the parking brake system. Leakage could be from lines and hoses to the brake 
air chambers from the double check valve, or the lines to the double check 
valve from the parking brake control valve. SERVICE leakage as required. REFER 
to Removal and Installation in this section.

Leaking brake air chamber.

SERVICE or REPLACE the brake air chamber. Diaphragm may require 
replacement. REFER to Section 06-08E</

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Valve, Modulating

The modulating valve should be replaced if it is leaking or operating 
improperly. If disassembly is required, observe the following procedure: 

 Disassembly 

Remove exhaust cover screw, exhaust cover and exhaust diaphragm. 

Remove four capscrews and lockwashers and cover. Remove O-ring from 
cover. 

Remove control piston and remove three O-rings from control piston. 

Remove large retaining ring from body and remove inlet/exhaust valve 
assembly. 

Remove ring from inlet/exhaust valve assembly. Remove O-ring retainer 
and remove O-ring from O-ring retainer. Remove washer and spring. Remove valve 
retainer and valve from modulating valve body. 

 CAUTION: Do not disturb adjusting screws unless adjusting spring brake hold-off 
pressure. 

Remove bottom cover and inner and outer springs. 

Remove balance piston. Remove O-ring from balance piston. 

 NOTE: To ease removal of supply adapter, a pipe nipple can be screwed into 
the adapter. 

Remove retaining ring from supply port and remove supply adapter and 
double check valve assembly. Remove O-ring from supply adapter. Remove double 
check valve from shuttle guide.

 NOTE: If single check valve is difficult to remove, it can be dislodged 
inside bore of modulating valve body. 

Remove Allen head plug from single check valve service port. Remove 
single check valve assembly. 

 Assembly 

Before assembly, lightly lubricate all O-rings, bores and mating 
surfaces with Silicone Lubricant COAZ-19553-AA or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESR-M13P4-A. 

Install single check valve assembly and Allen head plug. Tighten 
securely. 

Install O-ring on supply adapter, shuttle guide over supply adapter and 
double check valve in shuttle guide. 

Install adapter and double check valve assembly in supply port. Install 
retaining ring, making sure the retaining ring is engaged in groove. 

Install O-ring on balance piston and install balance piston in bore of 
body. 

 NOTE: Cone shaped protrusion on spring seat faces springs. 

Install inner and outer springs and spring seat.

Install bottom cover. Tighten screws to 5 Nm (44 lb-in).

Assemble the inlet/exhaust valve assembly. Install valve retainer, 
spring and washer. Install O-ring on O-ring retainer. Install O-ring retainer, 
compress retainer and install retaining ring, making certain retaining ring is 
engaged in groove of valve body. 

Install inlet/exhaust valve assembly in body. Install retaining ring 
making sure the retaining ring is engaged in groove in bore of body. 

 NOTE: Large diameter stem should point up.

Install three O-rings on control piston. Install control piston in body. 

Install O-ring on upper cover. Install upper cover with four capscrews 
and lockwashers. Tighten to approximately 11 Nm (8 lb-ft). 

Install exhaust diaphragm and exhaust cover.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake System, Air 

The air brake system consists of three subsystems: the air supply 
system (refer to Section 06-08A ), the air delivery system (refer to Section 06-08B ) and the parking/emergency system (refer to Section 06-05 ). The 
components that make up the air brake systems of Cargo and other series 
vehicles may differ, but all systems operate in basically the same manner. 

On CF-8000 series vehicles, a tractor trailer air brake system is 
available (refer to Section 06-08C ) as a regular production option.

Schematics of the air brake systems for the vehicle are illustrated in 
the Diagnosis and Testing portion of this section.

================================================================================
PAGE 3145
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 06-08: Brake System, Air, Service

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake System Balance 

The air brake system on the truck must provide balanced braking at all 
wheels and axles of the unit. This will provide for optimum brake system 
performance and life. The braking effort produced at each wheel and axle of 
the unit must be capable of doing its share of the work in controlling the 
speed of the unit or units. 

Brake system balance can be adversely affected by worn, damaged, or 
inoperative components, contaminants in the air supply and delivery system, 
poor system maintenance, or the use of incorrect replacement parts. 
Maintenance and service of the air brake systems should be performed with 
these considerations kept clearly in mind. When performance difficulties are 
encountered in the air brake system, the information contained in this section 
can be used to identify and correct the source of the problem.

================================================================================
PAGE 3146
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 06-08: Brake System, Air, Service

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Supply System 

The air supply system is the source of air pressure for the air brake 
system. It consists of the compressor, reservoirs (supply, primary and 
secondary), governor, low pressure indicator, dash gauge, safety valve, drain 
cock, optional air dryer, single check valves, double check valves and the 
tank valve. 

The compressor is driven by the engine and is controlled by a governor. 
When the reservoir air pressure reaches 793-861 kPa (115-125 psi), the 
governor cuts out the compressor. When the reservoir pressure drops to 82-179 
kPa (12-26 psi) below the cutout pressure, the governor allows the compressor 
to cut in again. When reservoir air pressure drops below 414 kPa (60 psi), the 
low pressure indicator switch closes an electrical circuit to the warning 
buzzer and the warning lamp. If the air reservoir pressure exceeds 1034 kPa 
(150 psi), the safety valve will release the pressure. The single check valves 
between the supply reservoir and the primary and secondary service reservoirs 
keep the air from flowing from the protected service air reservoir should an 
air loss occur in the other service system, supply reservoir, or air 
compressor plumbing. 

The air reservoir is equipped with a manual drain valve. This allows 
for the removal of moisture from the air brake system. 

The tank valve in the supply reservoir can be used to fill the air 
system if the engine is inoperative and the vehicle must be moved.

================================================================================
PAGE 3147
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 06-08: Brake System, Air, Service

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Delivery System 

The air delivery system delivers the air brake pressure from the air 
supply system service reservoirs to the brake chambers. It controls the amount 
of air pressure that is delivered to the brake chambers and thus controls the 
amount of braking during a stop. It consists of the foot control valve, the 
relay valve, the quick release valve and the brake chamber. 

The foot control valve meters the air pressure delivery to the front 
brake chamber and the rear relay valve, relative to the amount the foot pedal 
is depressed. The rear relay valve is constantly supplied with full system 
pressure from the primary service reservoir. As the foot control valve meters 
the pressure to the relay valve, the relay valve controls and delivers air 
pressure to the rear brake chambers. 

The relay valve's main function is to speed up the delivery and release 
of air pressure to the rear chambers. This is attained by having full system 
pressure available at the rear of the vehicle and controlling the delivery and 
release of this air pressure near the chambers. The brake chamber functions to 
convert air pressure into a mechanical force to apply the brakes. 

The bobtail proportioning relay valve functions as a standard service 
relay valve during operation of a tractor trailer combination. During bobtail 
tractor operation, the proportioning relay valve improves controllability and 
reduces stopping distances by reducing air pressure to the rear 
actuator/chambers, whose axle load has been greatly reduced.

================================================================================
PAGE 3148
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 06-08: Brake System, Air, Service

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake System, Parking/Emergency 

The parking brake system is composed of a PP-1 parking brake control 
valve, an inverting relay valve, quick release valves, and spring brake 
chambers. The spring brake chambers use a powerful spring to mechanically 
apply the brakes when air pressure is not available (provided the brakes are 
properly adjusted). 

Air pressure compresses the spring in the spring brake chamber when the 
parking brake control valve is in the release position. The inverting relay 
valve also functions to prevent the application of the spring brakes and 
service brakes at the same time, thus preventing brake system damage. 

For emergency stopping, trucks use a vertically split brake system. If 
air pressure is lost in the front brake system (hose, air line, etc.), the 
rear (primary) brake system will continue to operate until the supply air is 
depleted by several brake applications. An air pressure loss in the rear brake 
system lets the front (secondary) brakes continue to function, but additional 
braking power is provided by the modulation of the rear spring brakes 
application. This is controlled by the R-7 inverting relay valve. 

For truck emergency systems, the stopping capabilities of the brakes 
are reduced during a brake problem since not all of the brakes are functional. 
Upon service of the component, the system should return to normal operation. 

The MGM and Maxi-II service spring (parking) brake assemblies are 
standard on all vehicles with S-cam brakes. The brake chamber assembly is a 
spring applied parking brake that acts as an emergency brake in case of air 
pressure loss. The brake chamber assembly consists of two separate air 
chambers, each having its own application and release mechanism. The only 
difference between the two chambers is that the service chamber applies the 
service brakes by air pressure and releases it by spring pressure; the spring 
brake chamber applies the parking brakes by spring pressure and releases it by 
air pressure.

================================================================================
PAGE 3149
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 06-08: Brake System, Air, Service

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake System, Air — Tractor Trailer 

The tractor trailer air brake system is available as a regular 
production option. Its function is to provide air supply to the trailer for 
its braking system and control the trailer brakes during normal and emergency 
stops. It also protects a tractor's brake system should a failure occur in the 
trailer's air system and provides operation of the trailer brakes independent 
of the tractor brakes using the trailer brake hand control valve. The 
following components are part of this system: trailer air supply control 
valve, tractor protection valve, trailer brake hand control valve, bobtail 
proportioning relay valve and the hoses, hanger and connectors. 

The trailer air supply control valve supplies air through the tractor 
protection valve to the trailer air brake system. It works in conjunction with 
the parking brake control valve to park the trailer if the tractor is parked. 
The air supplied through the tractor protection valve opens the service 
portion of the tractor protection valve. As the supply pressure reaches a 
predetermined setting, it allows service brake application on the trailer. 
This is controlled by the foot control valve or trailer brake hand control 
valve. The trailer brake hand control valve can be used to apply the trailer 
brakes independent of the tractor brakes. 

The bobtail proportioning relay valve functions as a standard service 
relay valve during operation of a tractor trailer combination. During bobtail 
tractor operation, the bobtail proportioning relay valve improves 
controllability and reduces stopping distances by reducing air pressure to the 
rear actuator/chambers, whose axle load has been greatly reduced.

ADJUSTMENTS

Brake Hose

Replace a flexible brake hose if it shows signs of softening, cracking

SAE J1401 rayon braid, low expansion brake hose or equivalent. 

When installing a new brake hose, position the hose to avoid contact 
with other vehicle parts.

Section 06-08A: Brake, Air Supply

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Supply System 

The air supply system is the source of air pressure for the brake 
system. It consists of the compressor, reservoirs, governor, low air pressure 
switch, dash mounted dual air pressure gauge, safety valve, drain cock or 
automatic moisture ejector valve, air dryer (optional), tank valve, single 
check valve and double check valve. 

The compressor is engine-driven and controlled by a governor. When 
reservoir air pressure reaches 793-861 kPa (115-125 psi), the governor cuts 
out the compressor. When reservoir pressure drops to 82-179 kPa (12-26 psi) 
below the cutout pressure, the governor allows the compressor to cut in again. 
When reservoir air pressure drops below 414 kPa (60 psi), the low air pressure 
switch closes an electrical circuit to the warning buzzer and the warning 
light. If the air reservoir pressure exceeds 1034 kPa (150 psi), the safety 
valve will release the pressure. 

The air reservoir is equipped with a manual, lanyard operated, drain 
cock or an automatic moisture ejector valve, which can be drained for the 
removal of moisture from the air brake system.

================================================================================
PAGE 3155
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 06-08A: Brake, Air Supply

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Compressor 

The function of the air compressor is to build up and maintain the 
required amount of air pressure in the air reservoirs of the supply system. 
The rated capacity of a compressor is based on the piston displacement in 
cubic feet per minute when operating at 1250 rpm.

[FIGURE: H5465D.gif]

Compressors are of the one- or two-cylinder, single-stage, 
reciprocating piston design. The compressor is constructed from two major 
assemblies, the head and the crankcase. The head houses the discharge valving 
and is installed on the upper portion of the crankcase. The crankcase is a 
one-piece casting combining the cylinder block and the crankcase. The upper 
portion of the casting houses the cylinder bores and inlet valving; and the 
lower portion, the crankshaft and main bearings. Various mounting and drive 
configurations, required by vehicle engine designs, are obtained by bolting 
different mounting flanges, end covers, and base adapters to the compressor 
crankcase.

 Compressor/Governor System, Typical 

[FIGURE: H1341G.gif]

Piston (Compression) (Part of 2875)

Since all compressors are connected to the engine's pressurized oil 
system, a continuous flow of oil is provided to the compressor, which is 
eventually returned to the engine. Oil is fed into the compressor in various 
ways. Two examples are through the rear end cover, the drive end of the 
crankshaft or through the front flange adapter. An oil passage in the 
crankshaft conducts pressurized oil to the precision sleeve main bearings and 
to the connecting rod bearings. Splash lubrication of the cylinder bores, 
connecting rod wrist pin bushings, and the ball type main bearings, on some 
models, is obtained as oil is forced out around the crankshaft journals by 
engine oil pressure. 

Air flowing through the engine compartment from the action of the 
engine's fan and the movement of the vehicle assists in cooling the crankcase. 
Coolant flowing from the engine's cooling system enters the head, goes through 
the head's water jacket, and then returns to the engine. Proper cooling is 
important in maintaining discharge air temperatures below the maximum 204°
C (400°F) recommended. 

The compressor operates as follows: 

The unloader piston is in the retracted (non-pressurized) position. 

As the compressor piston is retracted (moved downward), air is drawn 
into the cylinder through the inlet valve which operates like a check valve. 

When the piston moves upward, the air is compressed. The air inlet 
valve is seated thus keeping the air from leaving the cylinder through the 
inlet valve. As the air is compressed further, it overcomes the spring force 
of the discharge valve and allows the compressed air into the discharge line 
and to the reservoir. 

As the compressor piston moves downward, the discharge valve is 
returned to its seat and air is drawn into the cylinder by way of the inlet 
valve and the cycle begins again. 

When air pressure in the air reservoir reaches the governor cutout 
setting of 793-861 kPa (115-125 psi), the governor opens and allows air to the 
compressor unloader piston. The unloader piston is lifted, thus moving the air 
inlet valve off its seat. With the inlet valves unseated, air is pumped back 
and forth between the cylinder or cylinders and the inlet valve cavity. As 
reservoir air pressure is used up, the governor pressure drops to its cut-in 
pressure setting, the governor closes and exhausts the air below the unloader 
piston. The spring then moves the unloader piston downward, the inlet valve is 
seated, and the compressor cycle is restarted.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Governor 

The governor operates in conjunction with the compressor unloading 
mechanism to keep air pressure in the supply system within specifications. The 
compressor runs continually with the engine but the compression of air is 
controlled by the governor which starts or stops compression when the maximum 
or minimum governor settings are reached. The governor is non-adjustable.

Air pressure from the reservoir to the reservoir port of the governor 
forces the governor piston to overcome the resistance of the pressure setting 
spring. (The governor piston and the inlet and exhaust valve move up as 
reservoir air pressure reaches the governor cutout setting.) The exhaust stem 
seats on the inlet and exhaust valve and opens the inlet passage. Reservoir 
air pressure then flows by the open inlet valve, through the passage in the 
governor piston and out the unloader port to the compressor unloading 
mechanism. 

As air pressure in the reservoir drops to the governor cut-in setting, 
the force exerted by air pressure on the governor piston is reduced and the 
pressure spring will move it downward. The inlet valve will close and the 
exhaust valve will open. With the exhaust valve open, air in the unloader line 
will escape through the exhaust stem and out the exhaust port. 

The governors are mounted directly to the compressor, allowing direct 
connection between the compressor unloader and the governor unloader port.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Reservoir 

The reservoir is a storage tank; its function is to provide a volume of 
compressed air for braking which will be adequate in relation to the volume 
used by the brake chambers and auxiliary devices. It also provides a location 
in the system where the air, heated by compression, may be cooled and the 
water vapor condensed. 

 Single Reservoir, Typical 

[FIGURE: H41651A.gif]

The primary reservoir is the air source for the rear brakes, and the 
front brakes are supplied by the secondary reservoir. The combined volumes of 
all service reservoirs and supply reservoirs are 12 times, or more than the 
combined volumes of all service brake air chambers at maximum travel of the 
pistons or diaphragms. The reservoirs are made from steel sheet, with stamped 
heads and rolled shells. The seams are electrically welded, and each reservoir 
is internally coated for corrosion resistance. 

All reservoirs should be drained to 0 kPa (0 psi) daily. If an 
automatic drain device is used, it should be checked periodically for proper 
functioning. If an air dryer or aftercooler is used, the reservoirs should be 
manually drained periodically to verify the proper function of the drying 
device. Reservoirs that have collected a considerable oily emulsion can be 
drained by opening a drain cock and allowing them to drain until all drainage 
stops. 

Minor service to the reservoir consists of examining the reservoir 
mounting, and the inspection of the outside for corrosion or damage. The 
outside should be kept painted to reduce the possibility of corrosion causing 
a failure. 

Service involving welding should never be performed on reservoirs. If a 
reservoir has been damaged so as to be unfit for use, it should be replaced 
with a new one.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Safety Valve 

The safety valve protects the air brake system against excessive air 
pressure buildup. The safety valve consists of a spring-loaded ball valve 
subjected to reservoir pressure, which will permit air to exhaust from the 
reservoir to the atmosphere if the reservoir pressure rises above the safety 
valve pressure setting. The safety valve pressure setting is determined by the 
force of the spring.

[FIGURE: H3339C.gif]

Item

 NOTE: It is recommended that the safety valve be installed in a vertical 
position. If it must be mounted horizontally, the exhaust port must point 
downward and the safety valve stem must face the rear of the vehicle. 

The safety valve should be installed in the same reservoir that the 
compressor discharge line is connected to. It can be installed in a convenient 
location in a top port of the reservoir.

A safety valve setting of 985-1082 kPa (143-157 psi) is used, and is 
not adjustable. Should system pressure rise to approximately 1034 kPa (150 
psi), air pressure would force the ball valve off its seat, and allow 
reservoir pressure to vent to the atmosphere through the exhaust port in the 
spring cage. 

When reservoir pressure decreases sufficiently, the spring force will 
seat the ball valve, sealing off reservoir pressure. This occurs at 930 kPa 
(135 psi) for the 1034 kPa (150 psi) setting. It is important to note that the 
desired pressure setting of the safety valve is determined by the governor 
cutout pressure. The opening and closing pressures of the safety valve must 
always be in excess of the governor cutout pressure setting. The pressure 
setting is stamped on a wrench flat of the safety valve. 

Normally, the safety valve remains inoperative and only functions when 
reservoir pressure rises above the setting of the valve. Constant popping off 
or exhausting of the safety valve can be caused by a faulty safety valve, 
governor, compressor unloader mechanism, or a combination of any of the 
preceding items.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Drain Cock 

A drain cock is provided as standard on air reservoirs that do not have 
the automatic moisture ejector valves. Drain cocks have a brass body fitted 
with a lanyard. The drain cock is open when the lanyard is pulled and closed 
when the lanyard is released. Drain cocks are installed in the bottom of each 
reservoir in the air brake system to provide a convenient means of draining 
the condensation and contamination that normally collects in the reservoirs. 

Air reservoirs should be drained daily to 0 kPa (0 psi). If they are 
not drained to 0 kPa (0 psi), the moisture and contamination may not be 
drained fully. High-pressure air will blow through the water, keeping the 
moisture in the reservoir while air is being released.

Always open a drain cock by hand. 

To prevent damage and leakage, never strike the handle with hammer or 
any other instrument. 

[FIGURE: H49891B.gif]

The automatic moisture ejector valve may also be drained manually by 
depressing the stem wire located in the exhaust port.

The automatic moisture ejector valve has a die cast aluminum body and 
cover, and is mounted in the bottom or lower end port of the air system 
reservoir.

With no air pressure in the system, the inlet and exhaust valves are 
closed. Upon charging the air system, a slight pressure opens the inlet valve 
which permits air and contaminants to collect in the sump. The inlet valve 
remains open when pressure is increasing in the system until (governor) cutout 
pressure is reached. The spring action of the valve guide in the sump cavity 
closes the inlet valve. The inlet valve and the exhaust valve are now closed.

When reservoir pressure drops approximately 13 kPa (2 psi), air 
pressure in the sump cavity opens the exhaust valve and allows moisture and 
contaminants to be ejected from the sump cavity until pressure in the sump 
cavity drops sufficiently to close the exhaust valve. The length of time the 
exhaust valve remains open and the amount of moisture and contaminants ejected 
depends upon the sump pressure and the reservoir pressure drop that occurs 
each time air is used from the system.

To drain the automatic moisture ejector valve manually, use a tool to 
move the wire in the exhaust port upward and hold it in until draining is 
completed to 0 kPa (0 psi).

Tank Valve 

A tank valve is provided in the supply reservoir to allow air pressure

similar to a tire valve stem and operates similarly.

Air Gauge 

Air brake systems have either dual or split brake systems which provide

provides a direct reading of each service system's air pressure.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Check Valve

 Single 

Single check valves are used in the air brake supply systems on all 
vehicles. They protect the primary and secondary air reservoirs against air 
pressure loss in the compressor or the supply tank. They protect against a 
loss of either primary or secondary system pressure by sealing off the 
remaining system's operation to allow an emergency stop. The single check 
valve is located in the air line from the supply tank to each reservoir. It 
allows air to flow in one direction only and prevents the flow of air in the 
reverse direction. Airflow in the normal direction moves the check valve disc 
from its seat, and the flow is unobstructed. Flow in the reverse direction is 
prevented by the seating of the disc, which is caused by a drop in the 
up-stream air pressure and assisted by the spring.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Dryer 

The purpose of the air dryer is to collect and remove solid, liquid and 
vapor contaminants from the air brake system. It provides clean, dry air to 
brake system components, increasing the life of the system and reducing 
maintenance cost. 

The Bendix AD-9 Air Dryer consists of a desiccant cartridge and a die 
cast aluminum end cover that is attached to an outer cylinder by capscrews and 
nuts. The end cover contains a purge valve mechanism, a check valve, a 
pressure relief valve and three threaded air connections. 

A cast-in heater element, a screw-in desiccant cartridge and an 
external electrical terminal are also included in the air dryer. The 
electrical requirements of the heater and thermostat are shown in the recess 
near the port marked CON. 

Air dryer operation consists of two cycles, the charge cycle and the 
purge cycle. 

For ease of serviceability, a replaceable desiccant cartridge, 
discharge valve and a heater and thermostat assembly with an external 
electrical connector are provided. The heater and thermostat are only 
serviceable as part of the purge valve assembly.

 Charge Cycle 

When the air compressor is operating, air, along with oil vapor, water 
and water vapor flows through the compressor discharge line to the air dryer 
supply port. As the air enters the port and moves through a baffle system, the 
flow direction changes by 180 degrees several times. These changes in 
direction cause air contaminants to condense and drop into the air dryer end 
cover sump. After leaving the air cover baffle system, the air flows into a 
desiccant cartridge that removes oil, oil vapor and solid contaminants.

[FIGURE: H72551A.gif]

Air leaves the oil separator and enters the desiccant drying bed. The 
air is still 100 percent saturated with water vapor. Air flowing through the 
column of desiccant becomes progressively drier as water vapor adheres to the 
desiccant material. The desiccant material removes 95 percent of the water 
vapor from the air. 

The dry air leaves the desiccant cartridge through an integral single 
check valve. Some air also exits the cartridge through the purge orifice next 
to the check valve. 

Dry air flows through the single check valve and out the delivery port 
to the air system supply reservoir. 

The air dryer will remain in the charge cycle until the air brake 
system pressure builds to the governor cutout setting. 

 Purge Cycle 

When the air brake system pressure reaches the governor cutout setting, 
the compressor continues to turn but stops compressing. This is the point at 
which the air dryer purge cycle begins. The governor unloader port-to-air 
dryer control port line becomes pressurized when the governor unloads the 
compressor. Air pressure at the air dryer end cover control port is also 
present on the purge valve piston. The purge valve piston moves and causes the 
purge valve to open to the atmosphere. Contaminants in the end cover sump are 
expelled immediately. In addition, air which was flowing through the desiccant 
cartridge changes direction and begins to flow toward the open purge valve. 
Oil and solid contaminants collected by the oil separator are removed by air 
flowing from the desiccant drying bed to the open purge valve.

[FIGURE: H72561A.gif]

The initial purge and desiccant cartridge decompression lasts only a 
few seconds. It can be heard as a burst of air at the air dryer exhaust. 

Dry air flows from the purge volume through the desiccant cartridge 
purge orifice and into the desiccant drying bed. Pressurized air from the 
purge volume expands after passing through the purge orifice. Its pressure is 
lowered and its volume is increased. The flow of dry air through the drying 
bed reactivates the desiccant material by removing the water vapor that 
adheres to it. It usually takes 15 to 30 seconds for the entire purge volume 
of a standard air dryer to flow through the desiccant drying bed. 

The end cover single check valve prevents air pressure in the brake 
system from returning to the air dryer during the purge cycle. After the purge 
cycle is complete, the air dryer is ready for the next charge cycle to begin. 
The purge valve will remain open after the purge cycle is completed and will 
not close until air brake system pressure is reduced and the governor allows 
the compressor to begin compressing.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Low Air Pressure Switch 

The low air pressure switch is a safety device designed to give an 
automatic warning to the driver whenever air pressure in the air brake system 
is below 414 kPa (60 psi), the safe minimum for normal vehicle operation. It 
is usually used to operate an electrical buzzer or warning lamp, or both, that 
are audible or visible to the driver. Low air pressure switches are located in 
both the primary and secondary air supply lines.

[FIGURE: H8176A.gif]
