DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Brake, Air Supply

 Inspection and Verification 

Before testing the air brakes, operate the engine until the air 
pressure builds up to 621 kPa (90 psi). Then open the drain cocks and drain 
the air pressure to zero in each reservoir. Close the drain cocks. Some models 
may have automatic moisture ejector valves which can be manually operated to 
completely drain the reservoirs. 

If the air supply system is not properly maintained, the system can 
become filled with moisture and other contaminants which can cause damage to 
the brake system internal components (diaphragms, valve seats, seats, etc.). 
Daily draining of the air reservoir to 0 kPa (0 psi) or periodic maintenance 
of the automatic moisture ejectors is very important to make sure brake system 
performance is trouble-free. More frequent maintenance is required in dusty, 
high humidity or low temperature environments. 

 Symptom Chart — Air Supply Brake 

 AIR SUPPLY BRAKE 

Condition

Possible Source

Action

Air Dryer Constantly Cycling or Purging

Excessive system air leaks.

TEST for excessive air leaks and SERVICE as necessary. Allowable air 
leaks are: Single vehicle, 7 kPa/minute (1 psi/minute); Tractor trailer, 21 
kPa/minute (3 psi/minute)

Excessive air leaks in fittings, hoses and tubing connected to the 
compressor, air dryer and supply reservoir.

Using soap solution, TEST for leaks at fittings, drain cock (if used) 
and pressure relief valve in supply reservoir. SERVICE or REPLACE as necessary.

Worn or damaged check valve in the air dryer cover.

TEST check valve. START the engine, ALLOW pressure to build in the 
system to the governor cutout. WAIT two minutes for the purge cycle to 
complete. Using soap solution, CHECK for air at the purge valve exhaust. Air 
leaks should not exceed a 25-mm (1-inch) bubble in five seconds. REPLACE check 
valve if necessary.

Worn or damaged air compressor governor.

TEST governor for proper cut-in or cutout pressures and excessive leaks 
in both positions. REPLACE or SERVICE governor or compressor as necessary.

Leaking purge valve in the air dryer end cover on the control side.

REMOVE air dryer end cover. APPLY 827 kPa (120 psi) at the control 
port. SOAP both sides around the purge valve to test for control piston leaks. 
Air leaks should not exceed a 25-mm (1-inch) bubble in five seconds.

Compressor unloader mechanism leaking excessively.

REMOVE compressor air strainer or fitting at inlet cavity. With 
compressor unloaded, CHECK for unloader piston air leaks. Slight air leaks are 
allowed.

Air Dryer Pressure Relief Valve Popping or Exhausting Air

Desiccant cartridge plugged or saturated.

CHECK for proper compressor installation. CHECK for excessive oil 
passing the compressor piston rings. SERVICE or REPLACE as necessary. REBUILD 
or REPLACE cartridge.

Worn or damaged end cover check valve.

CHECK if air passes through the check valve. SERVICE or REPLACE.

Worn or damaged fittings, hose or tubing between air dryer and the 
supply reservoir.

CHECK if air reaches supply reservoir. INSPECT for kinked tubing or 
hoses, undrilled or restricted hose and tube fittings.

Constant Exhaust of Air at Air Dryer Purge Valve Exhaust or Unable to 
Build System Pressure

Air dryer purge valve leaking excessively.

With compressor loaded, APPLY soap solution to purge valve exhaust and 
CHECK for excessive leaks. SERVICE purge valve if necessary.

Worn or damaged air compressor governor.

CHECK governor for proper cut-in, cutout pressure and excessive leaks 
in both positions. SERVICE or REPLACE as necessary.

Purge control line connected to reservoir or governor exhaust port.

CONNECT purge control line to the governor unloader port.

Purge valve stuck open, worn or damaged heater and thermostat, wiring, 
blown fuse.

TEST heater and thermostat. REFER to the Air Dryer Component
Test procedure in this section.

Inlet and outlet connections reversed.

CONNECT lines properly. The compressor discharge line must enter the 
air dryer at the inlet port.

Worn or damaged check valve between air dryer and supply reservoir.

CHECK if air passes through the check valve. SERVICE or REPLACE.

Kinked or plugged discharge line.

CLEAR line. STRAIGHTEN or REROUTE line as necessary.

Excessive bends in discharge line, water collects and freezes.

REROUTE discharge line to slope away from compressor to air dryer, with 
as few bends as possible.

Excessive system air leaks.

REFER to "Air Dryer Constantly Cycling or Purging."

Air Dryer Does Not Purge or Exhaust Air

Broken, kinked, frozen, plugged or disconnected purge control, input or 
output lines.

When the compressor is unloaded, TEST to determine if air flows through 
the purge control line. CHECK for undrilled fittings.

Worn or damaged air dryer purge valve.

SERVICE purge valve.

Worn or damaged compressor governor.

CHECK governor for proper cut-in, cutout pressure and excessive leaks 
in both positions. SERVICE or REPLACE as necessary. CONNECT lines properly. 
The compressor discharge line must enter the air dryer at the inlet port. 
CHECK if air passes through the check valve. SERVICE or REPLACE. CHECK 
discharge line. STRAIGHTEN or REROUTE the discharge line as necessary. REROUTE 
discharge line to slope away from compressor to air dryer, with as few bends 
as possible. REFER to "Air Dryer Constantly Cycling or Purging".

Desiccant Material, Whitish Liquid or Paste or Small Beads Expelled 
from Air Dryer Purge Valve Exhaust or Unsatisfactory Desiccant Life

This symptom is almost always accompanied by one or more of the above 
symptoms. See related causes for these symptoms.

SEE possible cause and remedy for all preceding symptoms.

Air dryer not securely mounted, excessive vibration.

ADD bracket supports or CHANGE the air dryer mounting location if 
necessary to minimize vibration.

Worn or damaged cloth-covered perforated plate in air dryer desiccant 
cartridge or improperly rebuilt desiccant cartridge.

REPLACE desiccant cartridge.

Compressor passing excessive oil.

CHECK for proper compressor installation. If symptoms persist, REPLACE 
the compressor.

Ice blocking the purge orifice — cold weather operation.

CHECK air dryer fuse. TEST heater and thermostat. REFER to procedure in 
the Air Dryer Component Test in this section.

Water in Air Reservoir

Desiccant needs replacement.

REPLACE the desiccant cartridge.

Improper discharge line length or improper line material.

USE a minimum 1.8 m (6 feet) of metal tubing between the compressor 
discharge port and the air dryer supply port.

Air system charged from outside air source, outside air not passing 
through the air dryer.

Outside air must pass through the air dryer if system has an outside 
air fill provision. An outside air fill system is not recommended.

Air dryer not purging.

REFER to "Air Dryer Does Not Purge or Exhaust Air."

Purge time is insufficient because of excessive system air leaks.

REFER to "Air Dryer Constantly Cycling or Purging."

Air dryer/vehicle application requires additional purge volume.

Additional purge volume may be necessary when the compressor is 
operating longer than 90 seconds during normal operation.

Air dryer not compatible with vehicle air system requirements. Improper 
air dryer/vehicle application.

Air dryer requires a minimum purge time of approximately 30 seconds. If 
the air compressor stays loaded longer than 90 seconds, and additional purge 
volume is added, a longer purge time is required. Air dryer efficiency will 
decrease as compressor loaded time increases beyond 120 seconds, during the 
normal operation of the vehicle. This limitation assumes that the compressor 
is approximately 12CFM and engine operation is 1600-1900 rpm. The air dryer 
will accommodate occasional longer loaded times, such as system initial 
pressure buildup.

 Component Tests 

 Compressor 

 NOTE: Tractor must be disconnected from the trailer to run this test. 

Bleed both the primary and secondary reservoirs down to 586 kPa (85 
psi) as measured with a test gauge. Run the engine at full governed rpm until 
the air pressure in the reservoirs reaches 689 kPa (100 psi). If the pressure 
buildup time exceeds 40 seconds, the compressor is not operating properly and 
one or more of the following conditions may exist. 

clogged engine air cleaner or compressor inlet hose

excessive air system leakage

drive belt slipping

restricted discharge cavity in compressor or restricted discharge line 

discharge valve stuck or broken

unloader piston inside the compressor stuck 

excessively worn compressor piston rings or cylinder walls 

governor out of adjustment or fouled 

 Governor 

Install a test gauge in the air lines, in the supply or service 
reservoir. Run the engine to build up air pressure. Note the reading on the 
test gauge at which the pressure stops rising. This is the point that the 
governor shuttles the compressor unloader piston and stops the compression 
cycle of the compressor. This is the compressor cutout pressure. The 
compressor cutout pressure should be between 793-861 kPa (115-125 psi). If the 
instrument panel dual air pressure gauge is used, the pressure should range 
between 752-903 kPa (109-131 psi), allowing for dual air pressure gauge 
accuracy. 

With the engine running, slowly reduce the amount of air pressure in 
the system by applying and releasing the brakes. Note on the dual air pres

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Air Compressor

 NOTE: The air compressor is flange-mounted to the accessory drive and is belt 
driven.

 Removal 

Drain cooling system. Open air reservoir drain cocks to exhaust air 
pressure from system. 

Loosen air outlet line at air compressor. Disconnect air outlet line. 
Disconnect governor air line at air compressor governor. 

Disconnect air inlet, coolant supply and return lines at air compressor. 

Disconnect oil supply line at air compressor. 

Loosen drive belt tension. Remove compressor mounting bolts. Disengage 
belt from pulley, and remove compressor. 

 Installation 

Position air compressor and new gasket on mounting bracket attached to 
engine. 

Position air compressor belt on pulley and adjust belt tension. 

Connect oil supply line to compressor. 

Connect air inlet, coolant supply and return lines to compressor. 

Connect governor air line and air outlet line to compressor. 

Fill and bleed cooling system. 

Close air reservoir drain cocks. 

Start engine and check for air, coolant, and oil leaks.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Governor

The governor is mounted to the compressor with two attaching bolts. 
Mating ports in the governor and compressor bodies connect governor pressure 
to the unloading pistons in the compressor. Reservoir pressure is connected to 
the governor through a hose or tube.

 Removal 

Exhaust the air brake system.

Disconnect the pressure lines at governor.

Remove the attaching bolts and remove the governor.

 Installation 

Apply Pipe Sealant with Teflon® D8AZ-19554-A or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification WSK-M2G350-AZ and ESR-M18P7-A to the 
governor bolt threads.

Using a new gasket, position the governor and bolts on the compressor. 
Tighten the governor bolts to 20-25 Nm (15-18 lb-ft).

Transfer the pressure lines to replacement governor.

Test the governor as described in Component Tests in the Diagnosis and 
Testing portion of this section.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Heater and Thermostat Assembly 

 Removal 

Unplug the wiring harness from the heater and thermostat assembly 
connector on the purge valve housing. Make sure connector seal is present on 
vehicle wiring harness connector.

 NOTE: Mark the relationship of the purge valve assembly to the air dryer.

Remove the three self-tapping screws securing the purge valve housing 
assembly to the end cover assembly. Remove the purge valve assembly from the 
end cover assembly. 

Remove and discard the three (two in certain assemblies) O-rings from 
the purge valve assembly.

Remove and discard the two screws securing the heater and thermostat 
assembly to the purge valve assembly.

 CAUTION: Do not pull the heater and thermostat assembly straight out of the 
purge valve body. Read this step before attempting removal. 

Remove the heater and thermostat assembly by gently rotating the 
connector to the left until the thermostat clears the purge valve housing. 
Then, slide the heater element out, to the right and up. Discard the heater 
and thermostat assembly along with its sealing ring(s).

[FIGURE: H9946A.gif]

 Installation 

Make sure that the square-cut sealing ring(s) on the back side of the 
connector has not slipped off or twisted.

Position the heater and thermostat.

First install the heater element into the heater element slot until the 
connector contacts the purge valve housing. 

Gently move the connector and thermostat to the left until the 
thermostat clears the cavity in the housing. 

Gently rotate the connector to the right while inserting the thermostat 
down into the cavity until the thermostat is inside the cavity and the 
connector seats against the housing. 

Make sure that the sealing ring(s) is not pinched.

While holding the connector against the purge valve housing, install 
the two heater connector-to-purge valve housing screws that secure the 
connector to the housing. Torque to 1.13-2.26 Nm (10-20 lb-in).

Lubricate the O-rings and the respective grooves on the purge valve 
assembly. Install the O-rings on the purge valve.

Install the purge valve assembly, with the O-rings, into the air dryer 
end cover using the relationship mark made during the removal to align the 
parts.

Install the three exhaust cover screws and flatwashers or extended 
exhaust cover if present at removal. Start screws by hand then tighten to 6-9 Nm
 (53-80 lb-in).

With the key on, test for vehicle power and ground at the two pins of 
the vehicle wiring harness connector. If voltage is not detected, check for a 
blown fuse, broken or pinched wiring.

Reconnect the vehicle wiring harness connector to the purge valve 
assembly. Make sure that the seal is present on the vehicle wiring harness, 
then plug the wiring harness connector into the purge valve assembly connector 
until the lock tab snaps in place.

Charge the system and test for leaks.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Moisture Ejector Valve, Automatic 

The automatic moisture ejector valve is used in place of the reservoir 
drain cock on some models, and must be disassembled and cleaned every 80450 km 
(50,000 miles) or six months. The automatic moisture ejector valve must be 
removed from the air reservoir for cleaning. 

 Disassembly 

Remove the capscrews and lockwashers. 

Remove the cover and sealing rings. 

Remove the valve guide. 

Remove the inlet and exhaust valve. 

Wash metal parts with solvent. Wipe rubber parts with a clean cloth. 

Inspect all parts for wear or deterioration. 

Replace all worn or damaged parts. 

 Assembly 

 CAUTION: Do not apply oil to the inlet and exhaust valve. 

Before assembling the valve, apply a light film of grease to inlet 
valve seat. 

Place the sealing ring in groove of cover. 

Place the valve guide over the inlet and exhaust valve. 

Place the valve guide over the inlet and exhaust assembly into the 
cover. The manual release wire will project through the exhaust port. 

Place the body on the cover and install the capscrews and lockwashers.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Safety Valve 

 Disassembly 

Clamp lower wrench flat in vise (flat nearest pipe thread). 

Using upper wrench flat, unscrew lock nut. Unscrew and remove spring 
cage from body of safety valve. 

Remove ball valve, spring and release pin from spring cage. 

Clean all parts in mineral spirits. Inspect all parts. All parts 
requiring replacement should be replaced with genuine Bendix replacement 
parts. 

 Assembly 

Place the ball valve in body. 

Install spring and release pin in spring cage with adjusting screw. 

Position the release pin over ball valve. Screw body with ball into the 
spring cage. Tighten securely. The safety valve is not adjustable.

Air Dryer 

 NOTE: The desiccant change interval may vary from vehicle to vehicle.

In order to take maximum advantage of desiccant life and to make sure

 CAUTION: Do not use any clamping device to hold the end cover as damage may 
occur. The end cover may be held by installing a pipe nipple into the supply 
port and clamping the nipple in a vise. 

Using a machinist's scribe, matchmark the air dryer housing and end 
cover. Remove the three self-tapping screws retaining the purge valve assembly 
to the end cover. Remove the purge valve assembly from the end cover. 

Remove the three O-rings from the exterior of the purge valve assembly.

Remove the six 3/8-inch air dryer housing bolts, air dryer housing nuts 
and twelve special washers and remove the end cover and desiccant cartridge 
assembly.

Remove and discard the end cover O-ring. 

Place a strap or chain wrench around the desiccant cartridge 
approximately two to three inches away from the end cover. Rotate the 
dessicant cartridge counterclockwise and separate it from the end cover. 

Remove the desiccant cartridge O-ring from the end cover. 

 NOTE: Do not remove the heater and thermostat assembly unless proven damaged. 
Refer to Air Dryer in Component Tests in the Diagnosis and Testing portion of 
this section. 

 NOTE: A Torx® head socket or a twelve point 1/4-inch socket 
is required.

Disassemble the purge valve assembly. 

Remove the 1/4-inch purge piston nut from the bottom of the purge valve 
assembly with a socket wrench and one of the sockets mentioned above to hold 
the purge piston bolt head. Remove the exhaust diaphragm, diaphragm (if used) 
and purge valve. 

Remove the 1/4-inch Torx® head purge piston bolt, 
purge piston, spring and the O-rings; one from the inside and one from the 
outside of the purge piston.

 Assembly 

Wash all parts thoroughly in a quality commercial solvent such as 
mineral spirits. Make sure that all parts are thoroughly dry before assembly.

Inspect all components for wear and damage. Replace as necessary. 

Lubricate the new O-rings and bores with a barium-base lubricant. 

Install the O-rings in the purge piston inside and outside O-ring 
grooves. 

Install the spring into the top inside diameter of the purge valve 
housing. Install the purge piston in the inside diameter of the spring. 
Install the 1/4-inch Torx® head purge piston bolt in the 
purge piston. Depress the purge piston into the exhaust cover. 

Hold the purge piston and, from the opposite end of the exhaust cover, 
install the purge valve, rubber side up on the purge piston bolt. Install the 
diaphragm and diaphragm washer (if used) or the flatwasher and purge piston 
nut. Tighten the purge piston nut to 7-9 Nm (60-80 lb-in). 

Install the three O-rings on the exhaust cover and install the exhaust 
cover into the end cover aligning the scribe marks. Install the three 1/4-inch 
self-tapping exhaust cover screws and tighten to 6-9 Nm 
(53-80 lb-in). 

Install the O-ring on the check valve assembly and install the assembly 
in the end cover. Tighten to 23-28 Nm (17-21 lb-ft). 

Install the desiccant cartridge sealing ring in the end cover. 
Lubricate the bottom of the cartridge at the O-ring seal and end cover contact 
area with a light coating of barium grease. 

Screw the desiccant cartridge into the end cover until it contacts the 
O-ring. With a strap or chain wrench positioned two to three inches from the 
bottom of the cartridge, turn the cartridge clockwise 180-225 degrees. Do not 
overtighten. 

Install the end cover O-ring on the end cover, place the housing over 
the cartridge and align the holes. 

 NOTE: The longer 3/8-inch capscrews are used to secure the dryer assembly to 
its support bracket. 

Install the six 3/8-inch capscrews, lock nuts and 12 special washers 
making sure they are in proper position as removed. Tighten the capscrews 
using a cross pattern. Tighten to 31-43 Nm (23-32 lb-ft).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Delivery System 

The air delivery system delivers the air brake pressure from the air 
supply system to the brake chambers. It controls the amount of air pressure 
that is delivered to the brake chambers, and controls the amount of braking 
during a stop. It consists of the foot control valve, the relay valve, quick 
release valve and the brake air chamber.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Foot Control Valve 

The foot control valve is mounted to the dash panel and uses a 
suspended brake pedal. The foot control valve is the dual brake valve type 
which provides two separate circuits to control the primary and secondary 
systems of the dual (or split) systems.

Air Exhaust Port (Secondary) (Part of 2A270)

The foot control valve is connected to each of the air supply systems. 
The air from supply tanks is metered by the foot control valve as the driver 
applies the brake pedal during a brake stop. The metered air pressure is then 
delivered to a rear axle relay valve which controls the amount of air to the 
brake air chambers. This amount of air is proportional to the air delivered 
from the foot control valve. 

The front brakes are supplied directly from the foot control valve. 

The circuits in the foot control valve are identified as follows: 

The number one (primary) circuit is the portion of the valve between 
the spring seat which contacts the plunger and the relay piston.

The number two (secondary) circuit consists of that portion between the 
relay piston and the exhaust cavity. 

The primary circuit of the foot control valve is similar in operation 
to a standard single circuit air brake valve. Under normal operating 
conditions the secondary circuit is similar in operation to a relay valve. 

Both the primary and secondary circuits use a common exhaust, protected 
by an exhaust diaphragm.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Relay Valve 

The R-12 relay valve speeds up the application and release of the air 
at the rear brake air chambers. The valve is constantly supplied with air 
pressure from the air reservoir to its supply port. As an application is made 
to the foot control valve, air pressure is delivered to the relay valve 
service port. The air supply to the relay valve is then metered to the rear 
brakes from the valve delivery port proportional to the air pressure at the 
service port.

Capscrew (4 Req'd) (Part of 2A449)

Air pressure delivered to the service port enters the small cavity 
above the piston and moves the piston down. The exhaust seat moves down with 
the piston and seats on the inner or exhaust portion of the inlet/exhaust 
valve and seals off the exhaust passage. At the same time, the outer or inlet 
portion of the inlet/exhaust valve moves off its seat, permitting supply air 
to flow from the reservoir, past the open inlet valve and into the brake air 
chambers. 

The air pressure being delivered by the open inlet valve also is 
effective on the bottom area of the relay piston. When air pressure beneath 
the piston equals the service air pressure from above, the piston lifts 
slightly and the inlet spring returns the inlet valve to its seat. The exhaust 
remains closed as the service line pressure balances the delivery pressure. 
The R-12 relay valve is equipped with a piston return spring which will assist 
the lifting of the piston. As delivered air pressure is changed, the relay 
valve reacts instantly to the change and holds brake application at that 
level. 

When air pressure is released from the service port as the foot control 
valve is released, and air pressure in the cavity above the piston is 
exhausted, air pressure beneath the piston lifts the piston and the exhaust 
seat moves away from the exhaust valve, opening the exhaust passage. With the 
exhaust passage open, the air pressure in the brake air chambers is permitted 
to exhaust through the exhaust port and releases the brakes.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Service Brake Air Chamber 

A brake air chamber converts the energy of air pressure into mechanical 
force. This force is used to push a lever to rotate a brake camshaft, forcing 
the brake shoes against the brake drum. Air pressure delivered to the brake 
air chambers (delivered through the inlet port) acts on the diaphragm, moving 
the push rod and plate. The amount of force coming from the brake air chamber 
is equal to the air pressure multiplied by the effective area of the 
diaphragm. This force is proportional to the air pressure delivered to the 
brake air chambers.

When air pressure is released from the brake air chamber, the push rod 
return spring and the brake shoe return spring return all the affected 
components (push rod and plate, diaphragm, brake camshaft) to their released 
position, releasing the brakes. 

Spring brake air chambers also have an integral service chamber which 
applies the spring brakes the same as the service chamber above. Refer to 
 Section 06-05 for spring brake air chamber operation.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Quick Release Valve 

The quick release valve is used for several functions in the brake 
system. Its function is to speed up the exhaust of air from a particular part 
of the brake system. It is used to exhaust air from brake air chambers, front 
and rear, near the brake air chamber, to speed up the release of air without 
the air traveling all the way back to the source of air. It is used in 
tractors to release air pressure in the service line to the trailer. It is 
used in the parking brake system to provide a faster brake application and to 
eliminate the undesirable exhausting of large quantities of air into the cab.

[FIGURE: H4959E.gif]

Item

Quick Release Valve

Exhaust Port (Not Threaded) (Part of 2A095)

When a brake application is made, air pressure enters the supply port. 
The diaphragm moves down and seals the exhaust port. At the same time, air 
pressure forces the edges of the diaphragm down and air flows out the delivery 
port. 

When the air pressure being delivered (beneath the diaphragm) equals 
the pressure being delivered by the foot control valve (above the diaphragm), 
the diaphragm outer edge will seal against the body seat. The exhaust port is 
still sealed by the center portion of the diaphragm. When the foot control 
valve application is released, the air pressure above the diaphragm is 
released back through the foot control valve exhaust. Air pressure beneath the 
diaphragm forces the diaphragm to rise, opening the exhaust and allowing air 
to exhaust.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Service Brakes 

Cam air brakes are used on the front and rear axles. The cam-type brake 
is an air-operated, two-shoe brake. The front brake shoes each use a one-piece 
shoe lining. The rear shoes each use a two-piece lining. Air applied to the 
brake air chamber push rod causes a cam to rotate against the rollers, forcing 
the brake shoes outward against the brake drum. For more information, refer to 
 Section 06-08D .

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Brake, Air Delivery

 Inspection and Verification 

Since most air leaks occur at the fittings and connections, these areas 
should be checked before any other part is replaced. For diagnostic and 
testing procedures for individual components, refer to the Diagnosis and 
Testing portion of each air brake section.

 WARNING: WHEN DRAINING THE SYSTEM, DO NOT LOOK INTO THE AIR JETS OR DIRECT THEM 
TOWARD A PERSON, AS DIRT OR SLUDGE PARTICLES MAY BE CARRIED IN THE AIR STREAM. 
HOSES WHICH CONTAIN AIR PRESSURE SHOULD NOT BE DISCONNECTED UNDER PRESSURE 
SINCE THEY WILL WHIP AS AIR ESCAPES FROM THE LINE. FOLLOW THE MANUFACTURERS' 
RECOMMENDED PROCEDURES IN WORKING ON ANY AIR DEVICE SO AS TO AVOID INJURY OR 
DAMAGE FROM PARTS WHICH, WHEN RELEASED, ARE SUBJECT TO MECHANICAL (SPRING) OR 
PNEUMATIC PROPULSION. AS SYSTEM PRESSURE IS DRAINED AND THE EMERGENCY BRAKE 
APPLIES, HANDS SHOULD BE AWAY FROM BRAKE CHAMBER PUSH RODS AND SPRING 
ACTUATORS WHICH WILL APPLY AUTOMATICALLY WITH THE LOSS OF PRESSURE. THIS ALSO 
APPLIES WHEN CHECKING SERVICE BRAKE SYSTEM. 

Reservoirs which are closest to the sources of compressed air 
(compressors or auxiliary sources) should contain a safety valve in known 
working order and sufficient capacity to limit the reservoir pressure to a 
safe maximum level. Old, used reservoirs should not be used as replacements. 
The safety valves should not reset higher than specified by the reservoir 
manufacturer, vehicle manufacturer, or code to which the reservoir had been 
manufactured. Various brake air chambers contain large internal steel springs 
that require special disassembly procedures. Note and be guided by the warning 
tags on such units.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Foot Control Valve 

 Removal 

Chock the wheels or hold the vehicle by means other than air brakes and 
exhaust air pressure from reservoirs supplying air to the foot control valve. 

To remove the foot control valve from the dash panel, identify and tag 
the two supply and two delivery lines to their respective ports as connected 
to the foot control valve. There may also be air lines to other brake devices 
inside the cab, which should be properly identified and tagged before 
disconnecting. 

 Installation 

Install brake pedal assembly using three capscrews. Check to be certain 
plunger is in contact with spring seat. The stop button should be adjusted so 
that the roller and plunger contact after adjustment. Roller should be able to 
be turned freely by thumb. 

Connect the two supply and delivery lines to their respective ports and 
the other air lines to their ports as they were tagged at removal. 

Charge up system with air. Check for leakage and correct operation.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Relay Valve 

 Removal 

Chock and hold vehicle by means other than air brakes. 

Drain air brake system reservoirs to 0 kPa (0 psi). 

If entire relay valve is to be removed, identify air lines to 
facilitate installation. 

 CAUTION: Drain reservoirs before removing insert. Use care so as not to damage 
inlet/exhaust valve or guide O-ring. 

Disconnect air lines from relay valve. 

 NOTE: It is generally not necessary to remove entire relay valve to service 
the inlet/exhaust valve. The inlet/exhaust valve insert can be removed by 
removing the retaining ring, two exhaust cover capscrews and cover. 
Inlet/exhaust valve can then be pulled out.

Remove mounting bolts, then relay valve. 

 Installation 

Clean air lines connecting to relay valve. 

Inspect all lines and hoses for damage and replace as necessary. 

Install relay valve and tighten mounting bolts. 

Connect air lines to relay valve (plug any unused ports). 

Check relay valve for proper operation. Refer to Component Tests in the 
Diagnosis and Testing portion of this section.

Foot Control Valve 

 NOTE: The body of the foot control valve is serviced as an assembly. The

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Relay Valve 

It is recommended to replace all rubber parts. Make sure correct 
replacement parts are available before disassembly.

 Disassembly 

 NOTE: Prior to disassembly, mark the locations of the mounting bracket to the 
cover and cover to the body. 

Remove the four capscrews and lockwashers securing the cover to the 
body. 

Remove the cover, sealing ring and mounting bracket. 

Remove the piston and O-ring from the body. 

While depressing the exhaust cover, remove the retaining ring and 
slowly relax the spring beneath the exhaust cover. 

Remove the exhaust cover assembly and O-rings. 

Remove the inlet/exhaust valve return spring from the body. 

Remove the inlet/exhaust valve from the body. 

Remove the valve retainer from the inlet/exhaust valve. 

Discard rubber parts.

Wash all metal parts in mineral spirits. Inspect all parts for signs of 
wear or deterioration. Inspect springs for cracks, distortion or corrosion. 

Inspect inlet seat and exhaust seat for nicks and burrs and replace as 
necessary. It is recommended that any part showing signs of wear or 
deterioration be replaced.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Relay Valve

While disassembled, wash all metal parts in mineral spirits. Inspect 
all parts for signs of wear or deterioration. Inspect springs for cracks, 
distortion or corrosion. Inspect inlet seal and exhaust seat for nicks and 
burrs and replace as necessary. It is recommended that all rubber parts be 
replaced, and that any part showing signs of wear or deterioration be replaced.

Section 06-08C: Brake, Air, Tractor/Trailer

1997 CF-8000 Series Cargo Tractor Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Tractor Trailer Air Brake System 

The tractor trailer air brake system is available as a regular 
production option. Its function is to provide air supply to the trailer for 
its braking system and control the trailer brakes during normal and emergency 
stops. It also protects a tractor's brake system should a failure occur in the 
trailer's air system and provides operation of the trailer brakes independent 
of the tractor brakes. The following components are part of this system: 
trailer air supply control valve (also known as the PP-7 valve), tractor 
protection valve (also known as the TP-5 valve), trailer brake hand control 
valve (also known as the TC-6 valve), bobtail proportioning relay valve (also 
known as the BP-R1 valve) and the hoses, hanger and connectors. 

The trailer air supply control valve supplies air through the tractor 
protection valve to the trailer air brake system. It works in conjunction with 
the parking brake control valve to park the trailer if the tractor is parked. 
The air supplied through the tractor protection valve opens the service 
portion of the tractor protection valve. As the supply pressure reaches a 
predetermined setting, it will allow service brake application on the trailer. 
The bobtail proportioning relay valve functions as a standard service relay 
valve during operation of a tractor trailer combination. During bobtail 
tractor operation, the bobtail proportioning relay valve improves 
controllability and reduces stopping distances by reducing air pressure to the 
rear actuator/chambers, whose axle load has been greatly reduced. This is 
controlled by the foot control valve or trailer brake hand control valve. The 
trailer brake hand control valve can be used to apply the trailer brakes 
independent of the tractor brakes.

 Operation 

The button of the trailer air supply control valve must be manually 
depressed but will automatically pop out and exhaust if the air supply is 
below 276 kPa (40 psi). Air supply of 345 kPa (50 psi) or greater is required 
for the button to remain in after it is depressed and it will remain in until 
supply air pressure falls below 276 kPa (40 psi) or until the trailer air 
supply control valve is manually actuated. 

 Normal Operating Position 

When system air pressure at the valve supply port is greater than 345 
kPa (50 psi), the button of the trailer air supply control valve can be 
depressed and will stay in. If the parking brake control valve is in the 
release position, the parking brake control valve will deliver air pressure to 
the control port of the trailer air supply control valve. 

With the button of the trailer air supply control valve depressed, the 
plunger inlet will be open and the exhaust valve will be seated, thus sealing 
the exhaust vent. Supply air is permitted to flow through the body to the 
control inlet and exhaust valve. With the parking brake control valve 
delivering full system pressure to the control port of the trailer air supply 
control valve, the control piston moves into contact with the control valve, 
closing the exhaust passage through the piston and opening the inlet. Opening 
the control inlet permits supply air to flow out the delivery port of the 
trailer air supply control valve to the tractor protection valve.

 NOTE: If the vehicle is parked and the system air pressure is above 345 kPa 
(50 psi), the parking brake control valve will not be delivering air to the 
trailer air supply control valve control port and the control inlet valve will 
be closed. In this case, no air will be flowing from the delivery port to the 
trailer air supply control valve.

Supply Port (Part of 2B200)

With air pressure removed from the control port of the trailer air 
supply control valve, the control piston moves away from the control inlet and 
exhaust valve. The inlet valve seats and the exhaust passage through the 
control piston is open. Air at the delivery port of the trailer air supply 
control valve is exhausted at the exhaust port of the trailer air supply 
control valve.

 Automatic Application 

The trailer air supply control valve will operate automatically in case 
of an emergency. In the event of trailer breakaway or a sudden complete 
failure of the trailer supply line, the button of the trailer air supply 
control valve will pop out. In this situation, the air pressure retained in 
the tractor air system should be approximately 69 kPa (10 psi) of the 
registered air pressure just prior to the breakaway or failure. The reason for 
this reaction is that air escaping from the failed supply line cannot be 
replaced through the supply port of the trailer air supply control valve as 
fast as it is lost. The rapid loss of air pressure in the trailer air supply 
control valve results in a momentary reduction below the 276 kPa (40 psi) 
pop-out pressure of the trailer air supply control valve plunger. 

If a leak develops that is not as severe as a broken line, the trailer 
air supply control valve button will pop out when air pressure in the supply 
line falls below 276 kPa (40 psi). 

In case of automatic exhaust (override), the driver holds the trailer 
air supply control valve button in after supply air pressure has dropped below 
the 276 kPa (40 psi) automatic pop-out pressure. The control piston will then 
move into the exhaust position when control port pressure falls below 138 kPa 
(20 psi).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Tractor Protection Valve 

The tractor protection valve contains a service line shutoff valve with 
exhaust function, a service line QRV and two double-check valves. 

The function of the tractor protection valve is to receive all 
pneumatic signals pertinent to the operation of the trailer braking system, 
transmit same to the trailer and also to protect the tractor air supply in 
case of separation of the connecting lines to the trailer. 

Air from the trailer air supply control valve in the cab enters at the 
tractor protection delivery port and passes out the trailer supply port, 
simultaneously acting upon the service line shutoff plunger, moving the 
service line inlet valve off its seat and opening the service line passage. 
With common air to the supply side and service side of the manifold, the 
tractor protection valve should open at approximately 310 kPa (45 psi). 

If the trailer air supply control valve is manually or automatically 
moved to the exhaust position, the service line shut off valve will close at 
approximately 69 kPa (10 psi) and the exhaust passage in the plunger will vent 
the trailer service line.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Double-Check Valves 

Double-check valves are used in an air brake system to direct a flow of 
air into a common line from either of two sources, whichever is at the higher 
pressure. They may be used for directing airflow for specific functions or to 
select the higher pressure of either of two sources of air as a supply source.

[FIGURE: H4167D.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

—

Inlet Port (Part of 2K119)

2

—

Delivery Port (Part of 2K119)

3

—

Shuttle (Part of 2K119)

4

—

Body (Part of 2K119)

5

—

Shuttle Guide (Part of 2K119)

6

—

O-Ring (Part of 2K119)

Double-check valves are used in several parts of the brake system for 
tractors to make sure both the service brake force and the spring force of a 
brake chamber are not applied at the same time, which could damage the brake 
system. If the parking brakes are applied, the air is released from the spring 
hold-off side of the chamber to provide spring application of the brakes. To 
make sure that the service chamber force is not applied at the same time, the 
double-check valve routes air pressure to the spring brake hold-off side of 
the chamber upon a service application, relieving the spring force 
proportional to the service operation procedure. 

The double-check valve used in the parking brake supply line serves to 
make sure that if a failure occurs in either the primary or secondary air 
supply system, the remaining system will provide sufficient air for spring 
brake release. It is used with the tractor brake hand control valve to allow 
either foot control valve or trailer brake hand control valve applications of 
the trailer brakes. 

The double-check valve operates as follows: air under pressure enters 
either end of the double-check valve (supply port). The moving shuttle 
responds to the pressure and seals the opposite port, assuming it is at a 
lower pressure level than the other. The airflow continues out the delivery 
port of the double check valve. The position of the shuttle will reverse if 
the pressure levels are reversed.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Trailer Brake Hand Control Valve

The TC-6 trailer brake hand control valve is normally used to operate 
the trailer brakes independently of the tractor brakes. It may be used, 
however, wherever a hand-controlled pressure graduation function is desired.

[FIGURE: H70591A.gif]

The trailer brake hand control valve is handle-operated and is mounted 
to the instrument panel. The trailer brake hand control valve is not designed 
for use as a parking brake control and should never be used to hold the brakes 
applied when the operator leaves the vehicle.

When the handle is pulled through its 75-degree arc, the roller cam is 
rotated accordingly. The cam action forces the cam follower downward, 
compressing the graduating spring and creating a force on the plunger which 
depresses the inlet valve and delivers air under pressure to the delivery port.

As delivery pressure builds up in the delivery port, it is also 
effective under the plunger, causing it to balance the force of the graduating 
spring until the inlet valve is seated against its seat in the body and is 
also seated against the plunger. This prevents the delivery air from 
exhausting through the center of the plunger, maintaining the desired pressure 
in the delivery line. 

When the handle is released or moved to its release position, the cam 
follower is permitted to rise, opening the exhaust passage and allowing the 
air pressure in the delivery line to exhaust out the exhaust port.

Section 06-08C: Brake, Air, Tractor/Trailer

1997 CF-8000 Series Cargo Tractor Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Quick Release Valve 

The quick release valve is used for several functions in the brake 
system. Its function is to speed up the exhaust of air from a particular part 
of the brake system. It is used to exhaust air from brake chambers, front and 
rear, near the chamber, to speed up the release of air without the air 
traveling all the way back to the source of air. It is used in tractors to 
release air pressure in the service line. It is used in the parking brake 
system to provide a faster brake application and to eliminate the undesirable 
exhausting of large quantities of air into the cab.

[FIGURE: H70681A.gif]

Its operation is very simple. When a brake application is made, air 
pressure enters the supply port. The diaphragm moves down and seals the 
exhaust. At the same time, air pressure forces the edges of the diaphragm down 
and air flows out the delivery port. 

When air pressure being delivered (beneath the diaphragm) equals the 
pressure being delivered by the brake valve (above the diaphragm), the 
diaphragm outer edge will seal against the body seat. The exhaust port is 
still sealed by the center portion of the diaphragm when the brake valve 
application is released. The air pressure above the diaphragm is released back 
through the brake valve exhaust. Air pressure beneath the diaphragm forces the 
diaphragm to rise, opening the exhaust and allowing air to exhaust.

================================================================================
PAGE 3208
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 06-08C: Brake, Air, Tractor/Trailer

1997 CF-8000 Series Cargo Tractor Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Bobtail Proportioning Relay Valve

The bobtail proportioning relay valve is a combination of two 
individual valves in a single housing. The lower portion, or body of the 
bobtail proportioning relay valve contains a standard service brake relay 
valve, which functions as a relay station to speed up brake application and 
release. The upper portion, or cover, houses a brake proportioning valve, 
which reduces normal service brake application pressure when the tractor is 
not towing a trailer. 

Used in tractor air brake systems only, the bobtail proportioning relay 
valve is installed in place of a standard relay valve. It functions as a 
standard service relay during operation of a tractor trailer combination. 
During bobtail tractor operation, the bobtail proportioning relay valve 
improves controllability and reduces stopping distances by reducing air 
pressure to the rear actuators/chambers, whose axle load has been greatly 
reduced. 

The bobtail proportioning relay valve has a crack pressure of 28 kPa (4 
psi).

1997 CF-8000 Series Cargo Tractor Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

BP-R1 Tractor Air System

 Initial Charging 

During the initial buildup of tractor system air pressure, supply air 
flows through internal body and cover passages in the bobtail proportioning 
relay valve to the blend back piston. 

Activating the trailer air supply control valve (dash control with red 
octagonal button), simultaneously charges the trailer and the bobtail 
proportioning relay valve control port. Air entering the bobtail proportioning 
relay valve control port causes the proportioning piston to move toward its 
stop in the cover. The integral inlet and exhaust valve is carried along with 
the piston until it seats and seals the exhaust passage. Continued movement of 
the proportioning piston opens the inlet valve. With the tractor and trailer 
air system fully charged, the vehicle may be operated.

 BP-R1 Tractor Air System

Foot Control Valve

 Service Application 

Brake application air enters the bobtail proportioning relay valve 
service port and is conducted through the service piston to the exhaust 
diaphragm which flexes in response to the incoming air and seals the exhaust 
passage in the exhaust piston. Air flows around the exhaust diaphragm and then 
through the center of both the blend back and proportioning pistons to the 
inlet and exhaust valve. Flowing around the inlet valve, application air moves 
through a passage in the cover to the top of the service relay piston. In 
response to air pressure, the relay piston moves in to contact with the 
exhaust portion of the inlet and exhaust valve. With the exhaust passage 
sealed, continued movement of the piston unseats the inlet portion of the 
inlet and exhaust valve, allowing supply air from the reservoir to flow out 
the bobtail proportioning relay valve delivery ports to the brake actuators.

 Service Brakes Holding 

The air pressure being delivered to the brake actuators is also present 
beneath the relay piston. 

When the air pressure above and below the relay piston is equal, the 
piston moves slightly, allowing the inlet valve to return to its seat. The 
exhaust valve remains closed. With both the inlet and exhaust valves closed, 
air pressure in the brake actuators is held stable and neither increases nor 
decreases.

Proportioning Piston (Part of 2A449)

 Service Brakes Releasing 

When the brake application is released, air pressure in the service 
port of the bobtail proportioning relay valve returns to the foot control 
valve and is exhausted. Air from above the relay piston flows back through the 
proportioning, blend back and service pistons to the exhaust diaphragm. If the 
service brakes are rapidly released, the diaphragm flexes in response to the 
returning air and opens the exhaust. If the brakes are slowly released, 
service air pressure will flow through the slot behind the diaphragm and back 
to the foot control valve. As air pressure is reduced above the relay piston, 
pressure beneath it lifts the piston away from the exhaust valve and opens the 
exhaust passage. Air from the service brake actuators returns to the bobtail 
proportioning relay valve and flows out the open exhaust.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Tractor/Trailer Air Brake System

 Inspection and Verification 

 End Cap Inspection 

 WARNING: FAILURE TO KEEP THE WEATHER SEAL PLUG IN PLACE ON DOUBLE DIAPHRAGM 
SPRING PARKING BRAKE CHAMBERS ALLOWS ROAD SALT AND OTHER CONTAMINANTS TO ENTER 
THE SPRING CHAMBER. THIS MAY CAUSE INTERNAL CORROSION AND POSSIBLY WEAKEN THE 
PARKING BRAKE SPRING, SPRING SUPPORT PLATE AND THE INSIDE SURFACE OF THE END 
CAP. THE CORROSION IS NOT VISIBLE FROM THE OUTSIDE OF THE SPRING BRAKE CHAMBER 
AND COULD EVENTUALLY RESULT IN A FRACTURE OF THE SPRING, SUPPORT PLATE OR THE 
END CAP, WHICH COULD ALSO LEAD TO PROPERTY DAMAGE OR PERSONAL INJURY. 

Whenever an inspection or service operation is performed on a spring 
brake chamber, check for the presence of the weather seal plug. Install a new 
plug if it is missing.

 Component Tests 

 Trailer Air Supply Control Valve 

 Operation and Leakage Test 

To perform the following test, an accurate vehicle test gauge is 
required. The vehicle dash gauge(s), if used, should be checked for accuracy 
against the test gauge prior to making these tests.

Block or hold the vehicle by means other than the service air brakes. 

With the trailer air supply control valve button out and the parking 
brake control valve in the exhaust, or brakes applied position, build the air 
system pressure to governor cutout. 

Apply a soap solution to the exhaust vent and the plunger stem of the 
trailer air supply control valve to check for leakage. Leakage should not 
exceed a 25.4 mm (1-inch) bubble in five seconds at either point. 

Depress the control button of the trailer air supply control valve and 
apply a soap solution to the exhaust vent and the exhaust port. Leakage should 
not exceed a 25.4 mm (1-inch) bubble in five seconds at either point.

Install the test gauge and coupling on the trailer supply coupling 
(tractor emergency hose coupling) at the rear of the tractor. 

Place the tractor parking brake control valve in the "brakes released" 
position and observe an immediate rise in pressure on the test gauge. The 
pressure registered on the test gauge should equal dash gauge or system 
pressure.

Apply a soap solution to the exhaust port of the trailer air supply 
control valve. Leakage should not exceed a 25.4-mm (1-inch) bubble in five 
seconds. 

With the tractor air system at governor cutout pressure, shut off the 
engine and note the dash gauge pressure. Quickly disconnect the test gauge and 
hose coupling from the tractor trailer supply line coupling. Leakage from the 
tractor trailer supply line should cease immediately and trailer air supply 
control valve button should be out. Dash gauge air pressure after performing 
the preceding test should be within approximately 69 kPa (10 psi) of the 
initial pressure. 

Reconnect the test gauge to the tractor trailer supply line and depress 
the trailer air supply control valve button. Open the drain cock's primary 
(green) and secondary (red) service reservoirs slightly. Note at what pressure 
(descending) the button of the trailer air supply control valve pops out and 
exhausts the tractor trailer supply line. This should occur between 138-310 
kPa (20-45 psi) air system pressure. 

If the trailer air supply control valve fails to function as described 
or if leakage is excessive, it is recommended that it be disassembled and 
cleaned, or replaced if necessary. If this is not possible, the trailer air 
supply control valve should be repaired using only genuine Bendix replacement 
parts.

 Tractor Protection Valve 

 Operation and Leakage Test 

Perform test as follows.

Charge air brake system to governor cutout, block the wheels, and place 
trailer air supply control valve in the emergency position. 

Disconnect the trailer service line hose coupling. Make a trailer brake 
hand control valve application. Hold a finger over the 1.6 mm (1/16-inch) vent 
hole in the service line shutoff valve area of the tractor protection valve 
casting. Check for leakage at hose coupling and at exhaust port at the tractor 
protection valve. Excessive leakage at either port indicates a faulty inlet 
valve.

With trailer brake hand control valve still applied, key to run and 
check for stoplight function. 

Release trailer brake hand control valve application and place trailer 
air supply control valve in normal position. 

Connect the tractor service hose coupling to a test gauge, reapply the 
trailer brake hand control valve and note that there is pressure at the 
service hose coupling.

Check for leakage at the service line QRV. Excessive leakage would 
indicate a worn or damaged diaphragm. 

With service line pressure still applied through the trailer brake hand 
control valve, check for leakage at the brake valve exhaust. Excessive leakage 
indicates a worn or damaged double-check valve shuttle. 

Check for leakage at the 1.6-mm (1/16-inch) vent hole. Leakage 
indicates that one of the two O-rings is worn or damaged.

Release the trailer brake hand control valve application and recheck 
for leakage at the vent hole. If the leakage continues, it is the large O-ring 
that is leaking. If the leakage stops, it was the smaller O-ring that was 
leaking.

Make and hold a foot control valve application. Check for leakage at 
exhaust of trailer brake hand control valve. Excessive leakage indicates a 
faulty double-check valve shuttle. 

Release foot control valve application, disconnect line from primary 
service brake circuit at tractor protection valve delivery port (PCD) and 
block off the end of the line from the brake valve. Make a foot control valve 
application and observe for leakage at the PCD delivery port. 

Reconnect the primary circuit line and reverse the procedure with the 
secondary circuit line (SCD). Excessive leakage in either the front service 
port or stoplamp switch indicates a faulty double-check valve shuttle. Restore 
the secondary circuit connection to the tractor protection valve. 

If the tractor protection valve does not function as described above or 
if leakage is excessive, the tractor protection valve should be exchanged or 
replaced at the nearest Bendix HVSG authorized distributor. If this is not 
possible, the following should prove helpful.

 Trailer Brake Hand Control Valve 

 Operation Test 

Connect an accurate test gauge to the trailer service line hose and 
leave the trailer emergency or supply hose connected to the trailer. If a 
trailer is not available, connect the trailer supply hose to an unvented dummy 
coupling or to a plugged hose fitting. The trailer air supply control valve 
should be in the normal position. 

When the operating lever is moved to the fully applied position, the 
gauge should register full reservoir pressure. Intermediate positions should 
deliver proportional intermediate pressures. Upon release, the gauge should 
immediately register zero. The location of the atmospheric end of the exhaust 
line from the trailer brake hand control valve should be found, probably in 
the engine compartment.

 Leakage Test 

With the trailer brake hand control valve in the release position, no 
pressure should register on the test gauge, and leakage at the end of the 
exhaust line should not be greater than a 25.4-mm (1-inch) bubble in five 
seconds. With the trailer brake hand control valve fully applied, leakage at 
the exhaust line should not be greater than a 25.4-mm (1-inch) bubble in three 
seconds. If the trailer brake hand control valve does not function as 
described, or if the leakage is excessive, it is recommended that it be 
serviced or replaced.

 Quick Release Valve 

 Operation Test 

With the air brake system fully charged, apply the brakes. Observe the 
brake action on the wheels controlled by the quick release valve or relay 
valve in question. The brakes should apply promptly. 

Release the brakes and inspect to be sure that air pressure is 
exhausted rapidly from the exhaust port. Be sure the exhaust port is not 
restricted. 

Disassemble and clean the quick release valve, if required and retest. 
If the valve does not seat or operates improperly, replace the quick release 
valve.

 Leakage Test 

With brakes applied, coat the exhaust port with a soap solution and 
inspect for leaks. Leakage is not permissible.

Disassemble and clean the quick release valve, if required. If the 
valve does not seat or operates improperly, replace the quick release valve.

 Double-Check Valve 

 Operation and Leakage Test 

If double-check valve is to be bench tested or tested on the vehicle, 
two separately controlled air supplies must be connected to the inlet ports. 

Install an accurate test gauge in the outlet port or in a line from 
outlet port. 

Apply and release air to one inlet port and note that gauge registers 
application and release. 

Repeat by applying and releasing air to other inlet port. 

Leakage check should be performed at inlet ports of the double-check 
valve in the following manner: 

Disconnect line from one inlet port. 

Apply air to other inlet port and coat opposite inlet port with soap 
solution. Permissible leakage is a 25.4-mm (1-inch) bubble in five seconds. 

Repeat Step b, applying air to other inlet port while checking opposite 
inlet port for leakage. If double-check valve does not function as described, 
replace double-check valve.

 Bobtail Proportioning Relay Valve 

 Operation and Leakage Test 

To properly test the function of the bobtail proportioning relay valve, 
a pair of test gauges or gauges of known accuracy must be used. 

Park the vehicle on a level surface and chock the wheels or hold the 
vehicle by means other than the air brakes. 

Drain air pressure from all vehicle reservoirs. 

Install a tee at the bobtail proportioning relay valve service port and 
at one of the delivery ports, then install a gauge in each. 

Connect the tractor service and emergency "glad hands" (hose couplings) 
to hose couplings that have been plugged, or alternatively, to a trailer. 
Build the tractor system air pressure to governor cutout and make four to five 
full brake applications. Check the air fittings at the bobtail proportioning 
relay valve for leakage. Tighten as needed. 

 NOTE: A prompt application occurs during the following procedure and can be 
held then promptly released. 

With the trailer air supply control valve (dash control with red 
octagonal button) and parking brake control valve (dash control with yellow 
diamond button) activated for tractor trailer operation, apply, hold, then 
release the brakes several times varying the application pressures while 
watching the reaction of the gauges installed on the bobtail proportioning 
relay valve.

 NOTE: The measured differential obtained during the following procedure 
should be approximately 28 kPa (4 psi).

Check the bobtail proportioning relay valve differential pressure by 
applying 6

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Trailer Air Supply Control Valve

 Disassembly 

Mark the upper and lower body halves to show their relationship to each 
other. 

Remove the two 1/4-inch 20 capscrews that secure the lower valve body 
to the upper valve body, using a 7/16-inch wrench. Separate the two body 
halves. 

Remove and discard the square cut sealing ring between the upper and 
lower body halves. 

Remove the end plate and O-ring from the lower body and discard the 
O-ring.

Remove the control piston and piston return spring. 

Remove the large and small diameter O-rings from the piston and discard 
them. 

Remove the internal Truarc® retaining ring from the 
lower body. 

Remove the O-ring retainer, remove and discard the O-ring. 

Remove the inlet and exhaust valve return spring. 

Using a 7/16-inch wrench, remove the special hex nut from the plunger 
inlet, exhaust valve and washer. 

Remove the plunger inlet and exhaust valve and washer. 

Remove the plunger and plunger return spring from the body. 

Remove and discard the plunger O-ring.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Tractor Protection Valve

 Disassembly 

Chock the wheels and drain the air brake systems. 

Remove all air lines and stoplight switch from the manifold and remove 
the unit from the vehicle. 

Remove the four capnuts from the body. Identify the cap nuts to their 
respective ports before removing. Remove the O-rings. 

Remove the double-check guides and double-check shuttles. 

Reach into the port marked BLK-SLS with a set of snap ring pliers and 
remove the snap ring, spring, and valve. 

Remove the two screws which hold the cover to the body. Remove the two 
small O-rings and one large O-ring. Remove the quick release valve diaphragm. 

Remove the 6-32 panhead screw and remove the exhaust check valve 
diaphragm. 

Clean all parts, bores, and passages with a solvent equivalent to 
mineral spirits.

 Assembly 

 NOTE: Before assembly, lubricate all O-rings, bores, pistons, etc., with 
Silicone Lubricant COAZ-19553-AA or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESR-M13P4-A. Replace all worn or deteriorated parts.

Reinstall inlet valve, spring and lock ring in body. 

Install shuttle guides and shuttles and their respective capnuts. 

Install the O-rings on the service line shut off plunger, and install 
spring, plunger and corresponding capnut with O-ring. 

Position the quick release valve diaphragm in the body and the one 
large and two small O-rings on the cover and install the cover in its cavity 
in the body. 

Replace the exhaust seal diaphragm in the cover.

Reinstall air lines and stoplight switch into the manifold.

Test the reassembled tractor protection valve per Tractor 
Protection Valve Operation and Leakage Test procedures under Diagnosis and Testing.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Trailer Brake Hand Control Valve 

 Disassembly 

Remove the trailer brake hand control valve from the panel. Place the 
lever in a vise and with a firm pull remove rubber handle. Remove the two 
slotted head capscrews which hold the mounting bracket in place and remove the 
mounting bracket.

Drive the pivot pin out of the body with a drift punch. Remove the 
handle, roller cam and torsion spring. Remove the roller cam from the handle.

Remove the cam follower, graduating spring, plunger, and plunger return 
spring through the top of the valve. Care should be taken not to lose washer.

Place the body in a soft-jawed vise and remove capnut. Remove O-ring 
from capnut.

Remove valve spring and inlet valve.

 Assembly 

Before assembling the valve, all bores, cam, pivot pin, plungers, and 
O-rings should be lubricated with Silicone Lubricant COAZ-19553-AA or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESR-M13P4-A.

Place body in a soft-jawed vise with ports pointing up. Place inlet 
valve in inlet cavity and install inlet valve spring. Place O-ring on capnut 
and assemble capnut in body. Tighten capnut to 6-16 Nm 
(53-141 lb-in).

 NOTE: O-rings are different sizes and must not be interchanged.

Install O-rings on plunger and cam follower.

 NOTE: The cam follower must be positioned so that the projection on the side 
of the body matches the corresponding groove in the body.

Reverse position of body in vise and install plunger return spring, 
plunger, washer, graduating spring, and cam follower.

Position the torsion spring in its approximate position in the body so 
that the end which engages the handle rests against the side of the body 
opposite the bracket retaining screw holes. Place the roller cam in position 
and insert pivot pin through the torsion spring and partially through the 
roller cam, leaving room to insert the wedge shaped end of the handle.

With a small screwdriver or similar tool, force the tang of the torsion 
spring towards the opposite wall of the body far enough so the handle may be 
inserted into the roller cam. The pivot pin may then be tapped on through 
until the ends of the pin are flush with either side of the body.

Place the mounting bracket in position and secure with two slotted-head 
capscrews. 

Place the rubber knob back on the handle. Reinstall the trailer brake 
hand control valve on the vehicle and test per Trailer 
Brake Hand Valve Operation Test and Leakage Test procedures under Diagnosis and Testing.

 Disassembly 

 CAUTION: The bobtail proportioning relay valve may be lightly clamped in a bench 
vise during disassembly; however, overclamping will cause damage to the valve 
and result in leakage. If a vise is to be used, position the valve so that the 
jaws bear on the supply ports on opposing sides of the valve's body. 

Remove all air fittings and plugs from the bobtail proportioning relay 
valve. 

Mark the relationship of the valve cover to the body and if the bobtail 
proportioning relay valve is equipped with a mounting bracket, mark the 
relationship of the bracket to the cover. 

While holding the exhaust cover, remove and discard the retaining ring 
that secures it to the body. 

Remove and discard the exhaust cover along with both O-rings. 

Remove and discard the valve spring, valve retainer, and the valve 
assembly from the body. 

Remove and retain the four capscrews that secure the cover to the body. 

Separate the cover from the body, then remove and discard the sealing 
ring and O-ring. 

Remove and retain the relay piston from the body. 

Remove and discard the O-ring from the relay piston. 

Remove and discard the dust shield and the retaining ring from the 
valve cover, then remove and retain the exhaust piston. 

Remove and discard the exhaust piston O-ring and the exhaust diaphragm. 

Remove and retain the service piston from the valve cover, then remove 
and discard the service piston O-ring. 

Remove the spring and spring cage from the valve cover. Discard the 
spring and retain the spring cage. 

Remove and retain the blend back piston from the valve cover, then 
remove and discard both O-rings. 

Remove and retain the proportioning piston from the valve cover, then 
remove and discard both O-rings. 

While holding the inlet valve seat in place, remove and discard the 
retaining ring from the proportioning piston. 

Remove the inlet seat, the inlet valve, and the valve spring from the 
proportioning piston, then remove and discard the O-ring from the valve seat. 
Discard the valve and spring also. 

Remove and discard the exhaust cover screw and exhaust cover. 

 Assembly 

Prior to assembly, lubricate all O-ring(s), seals, and pistons as well 
as body and cover bores, using the lubricant provided with the Bendix 
maintenance kit. Use all of the lubricant and spread it evenly on the rubbing 
surfaces. 

Install the O-ring on the inlet valve seat. 

Install the small end of the inlet/exhaust valve spring over the rubber 
of the valve, making sure the spring coils rest on the valve's four tabs. 

Insert the spring and valve into the valve seat, making sure the four 
tabs are within the seat's bore. 

Insert the valve, seat and spring assembly into the proportioning 
piston, large end of the spring first. 

While holding the seat in place, install the retaining ring to secure 
it in the piston. Make sure the retaining ring is fully seated in its groove. 
Make sure the valve is straight against the exhaust seat and free to move. 

Install both the large and small diameter O-rings on the proportioning 
piston. 

Install both the large and small diameter O-rings on the blend back 
piston, then insert the small diameter of the proportioning piston into the 
small diameter end of the blend back piston. 

Carefully insert the assembled proportioning and blend back pistons to 
the edge of the bore in the cover. Do not cut or pinch the O-rings. 

With the bore of the cover facing up, install the spring cage in the 
blend back piston so that its flat side rests against the blend back piston 
(its depressed side out toward the spring.) 

Install the O-ring on the service piston, then install the spring in 
the cage so that its coils are within the inside diameter of the cage. 

Install O-ring on exhaust piston, and place exhaust diaphragm between 
the six posts of the service piston. 

Place exhaust piston on service piston with its six-ribbed side facing 
the service piston. Then install both pistons while pushing the proportioning 
and blend back pistons all the way into the cover. 

Install the dust shield in the cover. 

While holding the dust shield in the cover, install the retaining ring, 
making sure it is fully seated in its groove. 

Install the exhaust cover using screw to retain it. Tighten the screw 
to 1-1.6 Nm (8-14 lb-in). 

Install the valve retainer on the inlet and exhaust valve so that the 
flange of the retainer surrounds the rubber portion of the valve. Install the 
inlet and exhaust valve in the body. 

Install the inlet and exhaust valve return spring in the body. 

Install the large and small diameter O-rings in the exhaust cover. Then 
install the exhaust cover in the body, taking care not to damage the O-rings. 
Hold the exhaust cover in place. 

While depressing the exhaust cover, install the retaining ring in the 
body. Make sure the retainer is fully seated in its groove in the body. 

Using lubricant to hold them in place, install the large and small 
sealing rings on the cover. 

Install the O-ring on the relay piston, then install the piston in the 
body. 

After noting the relationship marks made prior to disassembly, install 
the mounting bracket (not illustrated) on the cover, then secure the cover and 
mounting bracket on the body using the four capscrews. Tighten the capscrews 
to 14-16 Nm (10-12 lb-ft). 

Install all air line fittings and plugs, making sure thread sealing 
material does not enter the bobtail proportioning relay valve. 

Install the bobtail proportioning relay valve on the vehicle and 
perform the Bobtail Proportioning 
Relay Valve Operation and Leakage Tests under Diagnosis and Testing before 
returning the vehicle to service.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Bobtail Proportioning Relay Valve

Using mineral spirits or an equivalent solvent, clean and thoroughly 
dry all metal parts. Do not damage bores with metal tools. 

Wash all nonmetallic components in a soap and water solution, making 
sure to rinse and dry thoroughly. 

Inspect the interior and exterior of all metal parts that will be 
reused for severe corrosion, pitting and cracks. Superficial corrosion or 
pitting on the exterior portion of the body and cover is acceptable. Replace 
the entire bobtail proportioning relay valve if the interior of the body or 
cover exhibits signs of corrosion or pitting. 

Inspect each nonmetallic component for cracks, wear or distortion. 
Replace the entire bobtail proportioning relay valve if these conditions are 
found. 

Inspect the bores of both the body and cover for deep scuffing or 
gouges. Replace the entire bobtail proportioning relay valve if either are 
found. 

Make sure the air channel running between the top surface of the body 
and its supply port is clear and free of obstruction. 

Make sure all air channels and exhaust passages in the valve cover are 
clear and free of obstruction. 

Inspect the pipe threads in the body and valve cover. Make sure they 
are clean and free of thread sealant. 

Inspect all air line fittings for corrosion and replace as necessary. 
Make sure to remove all old thread sealant before reuse.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brakes, Cam

 WARNING: DO NOT INHALE DUST FROM BRAKES, CLUTCHES OR ASSOCIATED COMPONENTS. 
INHALATION OF DUST CAN BE INJURIOUS TO YOUR HEALTH. COMPRESSED AIR OR BRUSHES 
MUST NOT BE USED TO CLEAN BRAKES, BRAKE DRUMS, CLUTCHES AND ASSOCIATED 
COMPONENTS. USE BRAKE AND CLUTCH SERVICE VACUUM, MODEL 164-R3600 OR EQUIVALENT 
EQUIPPED FOR THIS PURPOSE TO CAREFULLY REMOVE ANY DUST. ADHERENT DUST SHOULD 
BE REMOVED WITH A DAMP RAG. ANY DUST SHOULD BE CONTAINED IN A SEALED AND 
LABELED BAG FOR DISPOSAL. WEAR AN APPROVED HIGH EFFICIENCY CARTRIDGE OR AIR 
LINE RESPIRATOR AND USE EXTRA CAUTION TO AVOID BREATHING THIS DUST. 

The cam-type brake is an air-operated two-shoe brake. The front brake 
shoes each use a one-piece shoe lining. The rear shoes each use two-piece 
lining.

 Front Brake Assembly, Rockwell Q-Series 

[FIGURE: H7405B.gif]

Item

Camshaft Bracket

As the brake pedal application is made, air pressure is applied to the 
brake air chamber. The brake air chamber has an internal diaphragm that will 
push against the brake chamber push rod with a force proportional to the air 
pressure being applied. The push rod then pushes on the automatic slack 
adjuster arm, which causes rotation of the brake camshaft. The rotation causes 
the rollers of the brake shoes to roll up the cam ramp forcing the brake shoes 
against the brake drum. When the brake pedal is released, the retracting (or 
return) spring of the brake pulls the shoes away from the brake drum, and a 
return spring in the brake air chamber returns the slack adjuster to the 
released position.

================================================================================
PAGE 3230
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 06-08D: Brake, Air, Cam-Type

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Slack Adjuster, Automatic 

The automatic slack adjuster design uses both brake chamber push rod 
travel and shoe-to-brake drum force to maintain proper brake adjustment. On 
brake application, the brake chamber push rod rotates the slack adjuster until 
the adjusting link engages a one-way cone clutch on the wormshaft. At this 
point, if the brake shoes are not in contact with the brake drum, the cone 
clutch will remain engaged with the shaft and the link will rotate the 
wormshaft. This shaft rotation adjusts the brake shoes by reducing 
shoe-to-drum clearance. Adjustment continues until the brake linings are 
forced against the brake drum. The shoe-to-brake drum force creates a 
resistance torque that exceeds the slip torque of the clutch, and allows the 
clutch to slip on the wormshaft for the remainder of the slack travel. During 
the return stroke the one-way cone clutch allows the link to return without 
shaft movement. The adjustment cycle will repeat until shoe-to-brake drum 
contact force occurs simultaneously with the initial link to clutch engagement.

[FIGURE: DH0176A.gif]

Section 06-08D: Brake, Air, Cam-Type

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Brake, Air, Cam-Type

 Inspection and Verification 

It is important that a careful parts inspection be made before 
assembly. Check all parts for wear or damage and service or replace as required.

Check the brake backing plate for expanded anchor pin holes and for 
cracks. Replace damaged backing plate and anchor pin bushings.

Check the camshaft bracket for broken welds, cracks and correct 
alignment. Replace damaged brackets.

Check anchor pins for corrosion and wear. Replace damaged anchor pins.

Check brake shoes for rust that can impair operation, expanded rivet 
holes, broken welds and incorrect alignment. Service or replace as necessary.

On 16.5 inch brake shoes only: anchor pin holes must not exceed 25.63 
mm (1.009 inches) in diameter. The distance from the center of the anchor pin 
hole to the center of the roller hole must not exceed 324.59 mm (12.779 
inches). Replace any shoe whose measurements are not to specifications.

Check the brake camshaft for cracks, wear and corrosion. Check the cam 
head, bearing journals and splines. Replace damaged brake camshafts.

Check the slack adjusters:

For slack adjusters with "quick connect" type clevis, check the gap 
between the clevis and the collar. If the gap exceeds 1.52 mm (0.060 inch) 
replace the clevis.

Check the clevis pins and the bushing in the arm of the slack adjuster. 
Replace the pins if they are worn. Replace the bushing if its diameter exceeds 
16.7 mm (0.656 inch).
