DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Manual Transmission

 Inspection and Verification 

 Vibration 

Although the effects of vibration will show up in the transmission, 
vibration usually originates somewhere else in the drivetrain. Vibration can 
usually be felt and can be accompanied by noise. 

Some of the problems found in the transmission due to drivetrain 
vibration are: 

gear rattle at idle 

gear and shaft splines fretted

[FIGURE: C94901A.gif]

noise 

fretted bearings 

repeated rear seal leakage 

broken or loose synchronizer pins

[FIGURE: C94911A.gif]

continuous loosening of capscrews, brackets and mountings 

input shaft spline wear

[FIGURE: C94921A.gif]

worn universal joints (not a transmission symptom, but an indicator of 
vibration) 

driveline imbalance or misalignment 

unbalanced wheels or brake drums 

rough running engine 

broken or worn engine mounts 

worn suspension 

 Gear Slipout and Jumpout 

 Front Section 

When a sliding clutch is moved to engage with a mainshaft gear, the 
mating teeth must be parallel. Tapered or worn clutching teeth will try to 
"walk" apart as the gears rotate. Under the right conditions, slipout will 
result. Some of these conditions are as follows: 

transmission mounted eccentrically with engine flywheel pilot 

excessive gear clashing which shortens clutching teeth 

gear clutching teeth wearing to a taper

[FIGURE: C94931A.gif]

insufficient pressure on detent ball from weak or broken detent spring

[FIGURE: C94941A.gif]

excessive wear on detent notch of yoke bar

[FIGURE: C94951A.gif]

incorrect adjustment of remote shift control linkage resulting in 
partial engagement (also check for loose connections and worn bushings) 

Slipout will generally occur when pulling with full power or 
decelerating with the load pushing. 

Jumpout will occur when a force sufficient to overcome the detent 
spring pressure is applied to the yoke bar, moving the clutch gear to a 
neutral position.

[FIGURE: C94961A.gif]

Some conditions contributing to jumpout are:

Extra-heavy and long shift levers which swing, pendulum-fashion, from 
operating over uneven terrain. Whipping action of the lever overcomes detent 
spring tension. 

Mechanical remote controls with the master mounted to the frame. 
Relative movement between engine-transmission package and frame can force 
transmission out of gear. Worn or broken engine mounts increase the effects of 
this condition. 

 Auxiliary Section 

Slipout in the auxiliary section can be caused by the clutching teeth 
being worn, tapered, or not fully engaged. These conditions cause the clutch 
gear to "walk" out of engagement as the gears turn. Causes of these clutching 
defects are clashing or normal wear after long life. Vibrations set up by an 
improperly aligned driveline and low air pressure add to the slipout problem.

[FIGURE: C94971A.gif]

Jumpout in the auxiliary section usually occurs with the splitter gear 
set. If torque is not sufficiently broken during splitter shifts, the sliding 
clutch gear may not have enough time to complete the shift before torque is 
reapplied to the gears. As torque is reapplied, the partially engaged clutch 
gear "jumps" out of the splitter gear. Since the gears have torque applied to 
them, damage will be done to the clutching teeth of the mating gears. 

 Hard Shifting 

Before checking the transmission for hard shifting, the remote linkage 
should be inspected. Linkage problems stem from worn connections or bushings, 
binding, improper adjustment, lack of lubrication on the joints or an 
obstruction which restricts free movement. 

To determine if the transmission itself is the cause of hard shifting, 
remove the shift lever or linkage from the top of the transmission. Move the 
shift blocks into each gear position using a pry bar or screwdriver. If the 
yoke bars slide easily, the trouble is with the linkage assembly. If the 
trouble is in the transmission, it will generally be caused by one of the 
following: 

Splines of the sliding clutch gear binding on the mainshaft as a result 
of a twisted mainshaft, bent shift yoke or bowed mainshaft key.

[FIGURE: C94981A.gif]

Yoke bars binding in the bar housing as a result of cracked housing, 
overtorqued shift block lock screw, sprung yoke bar, or swelled areas of the 
yoke bar. 

If hard shifting occurs only in first and reverse, the shift block 
detent plunger movement may be restricted. This can result from burrs on the 
plunger or from overtightening the plunger spring plug. With the plunger 
blocked in the depressed position, the plug should be tightened until it 
bottoms out against the spring and then backed out one-quarter to one-half 
turn. 

Gear clashing should not be confused with hard shifting. Gear clashing 
occurs when an attempt is made to engage the clutch gear before it has reached 
synchronization with the mainshaft gear. 

 Heat 

The transmission operating temperature must never exceed 120°
C (248°F) for an extended period of time. 
If it does, the oil will break down and shorten transmission life. 

Because of the friction of moving parts, transmissions will produce a 
certain amount of heat. In most cases normal operating temperature is 
approximately 40°C (104°F) above ambient. 
Heat is dissipated through the transmission case. When conditions prevent the 
proper dissipation of heat, overheating occurs. 

Before checking for possible causes of overheating, the oil temperature 
gauge and sending unit should be inspected to make sure they are giving 
correct readings. 

Some of the causes for overheating are as follows: 

improper lubrication (oil level too low or too high, wrong type of oil, 
or an operating angle of more than 12 degrees) 

operating consistently under 32 km/h (20 mph) 

high engine rpm 

restricted airflow around the transmission, due to the transmission 
being boxed in by frame rails, deck lids, fuel tanks and mounting brackets, or 
by a large bumper assembly

exhaust system too close to transmission

high ambient temperature 

high horsepower, overdrive operation 

coasting downhill with the clutch depressed 

 Noise 

 Knocking or Thudding Gears 

Knocking or thudding can be a result of bumps or swells on gear teeth. 
Such bumps or swells can be removed with a hone or small hand grinder. These 
areas can be identified as highly polished spots on the face of the gear 
tooth. Generally, this noise is more prominent when the gear is loaded. The 
problem gear can be located as the noise occurs in a specific gear position. 
Bumps or swells are caused by improper handling of gears before or during 
assembly.

[FIGURE: C94991A.gif]

 Cracked Gear 

A gear cracked or broken by shock loading or by pressing on a shaft 
during installation will produce a knocking or thudding sound at low speeds. 
At high speeds a howl will be present.

[FIGURE: C95001A.gif]

 High Pitched Whine or Squeal 

A high-pitched whine or squeal is the result of normal gear wear, 
including gear tooth pitting from excessive use. In advanced deterioration a 
howl will result. 

 Mismatched Gear Sets 

Such gear sets are identified by an uneven wear pattern on the face of 
gear teeth. 

 Bearings 

Noise comes in at low shaft speeds in any position. It is caused by 
bearings with damaged balls or rollers or with pitted and spalled raceways. 

Pinched bearings, having insufficient axial or radial clearance can be 
a cause of whining or squealing noise. 

 Growling 

A growling noise may be produced by improper timing of the transmission 
during reassembly, or improper timing due to gear turning on the countershaft. 
Both conditions produce error in tooth spacing. 

 Causes or Types of Noise Other Than Transmission 

rough idling engine 

engine operating noise 

clutch driven plates in which the dampening action of springs or rubber 
blocks has been eliminated by wear set or fracture 

driveline out of balance 

unequal joint working angles 

worn crosses in universal joints 

loose or worn center bearings 

worn or pitted teeth on ring gear and pinion of driving axle (rear axle 
bearing failure) 

wheels out of balance 

worn spring pivot bearing 

loose U-bolts 

brake drums warped or out of balance 

 Clashing 

Snubbing and clashing gears while shifting are frequent abuses to which 
unsynchronized transmissions are subjected. Light snubbing will do little 
damage. The real damage is done by the hard clash shift caused by engaging 
gears which are far out of synchronization. This can break pieces of metal 
from the ends of the clutching teeth.

[FIGURE: C95011A.gif]

Clashing gears can be traced to one of three causes: 

Improper shifting — This applies to drivers who are not 
familiar with the shift pattern or have not learned the rpm spread between 
shifts. 

Clutch — Clashing when starting up in first or reverse 
gear can be caused by insufficient clutch clearance or a dragging clutch not 
releasing properly. This makes the transmission countershafts and mainshaft 
gears continue rotating while the clutch pedal is depressed. Clashing results 
when the nonrotating sliding clutch is forced to mesh with a rotating 
mainshaft gear. Double clutching during lever shifts will also reduce snubbing 
and clashing. 

Inertia force — Countershafts and mainshaft gears 
usually take from three to five seconds to stop rotating after the clutch has 
been disengaged. Attempting to mesh a clutch gear with a mainshaft gear before 
the mainshaft gear stops will result in clashing. If the transmission is not 
equipped with a clutch brake or countershaft brake, pause a few seconds after 
depressing the clutch pedal before attempting initial engagement of the 
transmission. 

 Gear Rattle at Idle 

Mainshaft gears are designed to have a specified amount of axial 
clearance which allows them to rotate freely on the mainshaft. The amount of 
clearance is governed by the use of washers. A rough idling engine can set up 
vibrations, causing the mainshaft gears to rattle as they strike mating gears. 
This condition can usually be cured by improving the idling characteristics of 
the engine. Tolerance washers may have to be changed to bring the axial gear 
clearance to within tolerance on high mileage units. 

 Gear Manufacturing Marks 

Sometimes gears are replaced or thought to be damaged because of marks 
left on the gear by manufacturing processes. These blemishes, however, do not 
contribute to gear failure and the gear should not be replaced because of 
these marks. 

Hob marks are cutting marks or lines formed during the initial cutting 
of the gear teeth. Hob marks on the tooth face will be removed by the shaving 
process, but hob marks in the root of the tooth will most likely remain, and 
can be found even on gears with much wear on them.

[FIGURE: C95021A.gif]

Shaving marks are the distinct diagonal marks left on the face of the 
gear tooth during the shaving operation. These marks can be distinguished from 
scoring marks by the fact that they are diagonal, while scoring marks are more 
nearly vertical. Most shaving marks are removed during normal gear operation.

[FIGURE: C43691A.gif]

Lipping or shaving burrs are formed at the tip of the gear teeth during 
machining. These lips will not harm the gear.

[FIGURE: C95031A.gif]

 Shaft Twist and Failure 

Failure of transmission shafts through fracturing or twisting is caused 
when stresses are imposed on them which are greater than they were designed to 
withstand. The main causes for these failures are as follows: 

improper clutching techniques 

starting in too high gear (either front or auxiliary section) 

lugging 

attempting to start with brakes locked 

transmission used for application it was not designed to withstand 

bumping into dock when backing 

improper mounting of adjustable fifth wheel 

As with gear teeth, shafts may fracture as a result of fatigue or impact.

[FIGURE: C95041A.gif]

Loads not severe enough to cause shaft fractures may cause the shaft to 
twist.

[FIGURE: C94981A.gif]

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Transmission 

 Cleaning 

After the transmission has been disassembled, soak the parts, except 
the bearings, in a cleaning solvent until all the old lubricant is dissolved 
or loosened. Brush or scrape all foreign matter from the parts. Be careful not 
to damage any of the parts with the scraper. 

An excessive amount of foreign material usually results from a bearing 
failure, gear seizure, tooth breakage, extreme synchronizer wear or clashing 
gears. In such cases, the input and output shaft bearings, should be carefully 
inspected and replaced, if necessary. Since countershaft bearings, output 
shaft pilot bearings and reverse idler bearings are not as susceptible to 
damage from foreign material in the lubricant, they need not be replaced if 
satisfactory. 

Wipe the parts or blow compressed air on them until they are thoroughly 
dry. 

To clean the bearings, rotate them in clean solvent until all lubricant 
is removed. Hold the bearing assembly to prevent it from rotating and dry it 
with compressed air. 

When the bearings are dry, lubricate them thoroughly with transmission 
lubricant and cover them with a clean, lint-free cloth until ready for use. 

 Inspection 

Inspect all transmission parts before assembly to determine if they 
should be replaced. 

 Transmission Case Service 

 NOTE: Steam clean the transmission or transfer unit case to remove grease, 
oil or road dirt. Clean the service area thoroughly. Epoxy resin will not 
stick to a dirty or oily surface.

Inspect the case for cracks, worn or damaged bearing bores, damaged 
threads or similar damage. If such is found, replace the case. However, if the 
cracks do not extend into bearing bores or bolt holes in the machined surface, 
the case may be welded or brazed . 

Holes smaller than 6.35 mm (1/4-inch) diameter, such as sand holes or 
casting porosity, can be serviced using an epoxy resin material meeting 
manufacturing standard M3D35-A (E).

Holes larger than 6.35 mm (1/4 inch) can be serviced by drilling, 
tapping and plugging. 

The recommended procedure for using the epoxy resin is as follows:

 NOTE: Steam clean the transmission case to remove grease, oil or road dirt. 
Clean the service area thoroughly. Epoxy resin will not stick to a dirty or 
oily surface. 

Prepare surface to be serviced by grinding or rotary filing to a clean, 
bright metal surface. Chamfer or undercut the hole or porous area to a depth 
greater than that in the surrounding cleaned surface. Solid metal must 
surround the hole. 

Apply service mixture with suitable clean tool (putty knife, wood 
spoon, etc.), forcing mixture into hole or porosity. 

Allow mixture to harden by either of two methods: heat cure with a 
250-watt lamp placed 254 mm (10 inches) from serviced surface or air dry for 
10 to 12 hours at temperatures above 10°C (50°
F). 

Sand or grind serviced area, blending it with general contour of 
surrounding surface. Do not use this method to service casing cracks. 

Inspect front face of the case, and file or grind off any minor nicks 
or burrs that could cause misalignment of transmission with clutch housing. 

 Shift Housing 

Check the operation and condition of the cross-shaft, forks and shift 
rails. If binding occurs when the shaft is operated, disassemble the housing 
assembly, and replace the worn or damaged parts. Lubricate the shift lever 
ball seat and trunnion with Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B. Replace cover if it is bent 
or distorted. Make sure the vent hole in the case is open.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Seals and Gaskets 

When disassembling a later-design, twin-countershaft Eaton 
transmission, you may notice a small rubber lip seal on the input shaft under 
the front cover. This shipping seal was added for the sole purpose of 
eliminating oil leakage during shipment. 

When this seal is found during service on a twin-countershaft 
transmission, it should be removed. There is no need to install a replacement 
as this is a nonserviceable item. The transmission continues to be sealed 
during operation by the spiral cut grooves on the input shaft.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Synchronizer Blocking Rings 

Check synchronizer cones and clutching teeth. 

Replace synchronizer if cone wear is excessive or clutching teeth are 
chipped. 

Inspect the synchronizer blocking rings for widened index slots,

grooves). With the blocker ring on the cone, the distance between the face of 
the gear must not be less than 0.254 mm (0.010 inch).

Check the synchronizer sleeves for free movement on the hubs. Make sure 
the alignment marks (etched marks) are properly indexed.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Bearings 

Inspect the bearing assemblies. If any of the following conditions are 
present, replace the bearings. 

 Bearing Raceways 

Examine the races for discoloration, pitting, flaking, fretting, 
scoring, scratches, cracks or other damage.

 Bearing External Surfaces 

Examine the bearings for looseness, discoloration, pitting, scoring, 
scratches or other damage.

 Spin Test 

 CAUTION: Do not spin bearings with compressed air as this will damage bearing. 

Spin bearings by hand. Bearing should spin freely without roughness.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Gear Inspection

Some forms of grind marks and tooth wear contact patterns are 
acceptable and should not be considered as a source of gear noise. Grind marks 
are different from damaged areas such as local swells (polished raised 
projections), nicks and chips. All gears have possible factory service grind 
marks. Phosphate-coated gears are especially easy to recognize since the grind 
operation removes a patch of phosphate and base metal, exposing the lighter 
metallic color. 

 Countershaft Gear and Countershaft 

Replace the countershaft gear if the teeth are chipped or excessively 
worn. Replace the countershaft if the shaft is bent or grooved. 

 Reverse Idler Gear 

Replace the reverse idler gear if the gear or bushing is badly worn or 
if the teeth are chipped or burred. Replace the reverse idler gear shaft if it 
is excessively worn or scored.

================================================================================
PAGE 3323
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 07-03: Transmission, Manual, General

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Shaft Inspection

 Input Shaft 

Replace the input shaft if it is worn, bent, or twisted, if the gear 
has chipped, worn, or missing teeth, or if the cone surface is damaged. 
Replace the pilot bearing if scored, and inspect the input shaft for damage. 

 Output Shaft 

Replace all output shaft gears that are chipped, burred, or badly worn. 
Check the intermediate gear play. Replace the gear if the play is excessive. 
Replace the output shaft if it is out of round or worn, or if the bearing 
surface is scored. 

Replace the speedometer drive gear if the gear teeth are worn or 
broken. Be sure to install the correct replacement gear.

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Thrust Washer, Synchronizer Discs and Bearing Covers

Check the surfaces of all thrust washers. Replace washers that are 
scored or reduced in thickness. 

Replace synchronizer discs that are scored, burned, or warped. Also 
replace bearing covers that are grooved or showing wear from the thrust or 
adjacent bearings. Check the oil return threads in the bearing cover. If the 
sealing action of the threads has been destroyed by contact from the input 
shaft, replace the cover.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Identification

[FIGURE: C11744B.gif]

The FS-4205 series transmission is a five-speed synchronized unit which 
features a constant mesh low and reverse, and offers an efficient ratio of 
torque capacity to weight. The FS-4205 series is available in two models: 
FS-4205-A and FS-4205-B. Transmission features include split-pin synchronizers 
in second, third, fourth and fifth gears, tapered roller bearings, and needle 
roller bearings at main support locations. 

The shift forks have steel-backed bronze wear pads that can be 
replaced, if necessary. The shift pattern is the standard progression type 
with all shifts having the same throw at the shift lever. Transmissions are 
available with either standard ratio or the soft ratio which splits the step 
in a two-speed axle. The FS-4205-A is the standard ratio and the FS-4205-B is 
the soft-fourth ratio. 

The FS-4205 series transmissions have five forward speeds and one 
reverse speed with gear ratios as follows:

 Power Flow 

The transmission must efficiently transfer the engine's power (torque) 
to the vehicle's rear wheels. Knowledge of what takes place in the 
transmission during torque transfer is essential when troubleshooting and 
performing service.

 NOTE: The numbers in these steps correspond to the numbers in the following 
illustration.

Power (torque) from the engine is transferred to the transmission's 
input shaft.

Torque is transferred to the countershaft drive gear.

Torque is delivered along the countershaft to all countershaft gears.

Torque is transferred to engaged mainshaft gear. The cross section 
illustrates 1st speed gear position.

Engaged mainshaft gear external clutching teeth transfer torque to 
mainshaft through synchronizer assembly.

Mainshaft transfers torque directly to the driveshaft through the rear 
yoke.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission Oil Drain and Refill Procedure

 CAUTION: The use of mild EP gear oil or multi-purpose gear oil is not 
recommended, but if these gear oils are used, be sure to adhere to the 
following limitations. 

 CAUTION: Do not use mild EP gear oil or multi-purpose gear oil when operating 
temperatures are above 110°C (230°F). Many 
of these gear oils, particularly 85W140, break down above 110°
C (230°F) and coat seals, bearings, and gears with deposits 
that can cause premature failures. If these deposits are observed (especially 
a coating on seal areas causing oil leakage), change to Eaton Roadranger®
 CD50 transmission fluid, heavy-duty engine oil, or mineral 
gear oil to ensure maximum component life and to maintain your warranty with 
Eaton. Refer to Operating Temperatures in this section. 

 CAUTION: Additives and friction modifiers are not recommended for use in Eaton 
Fuller transmissions. 

Proper lubrication procedures are the key to a good all-around 
maintenance program. If the oil is not doing its job, or if the oil level is 
ignored, all the maintenance procedures in the world are not going to keep the 
transmission running or ensure long transmission life.

Eaton Fuller transmissions are designed so that the internal parts 
operate in an oil circulating bath by the motion of the gears and shafts.

All parts are amply lubricated if these procedures are closely followed:

Maintain oil level. Inspect regularly.

Change oil regularly.

Use the correct grade and type of oil.

Buy from a reputable dealer.

 LUBRICATION CHANGE AND INSPECTION

Eaton Roadranger® CD50 Transmission Fluid

HIGHWAY USE

Every 16 093 km (10,000 miles)

Check fluid level. Check for leaks.

Every 402 325 km (250,000 miles)

Change transmission fluid.

 OFF-HIGHWAY USE 

Every 40 hours

Inspect fluid level. Check for leaks.

Every 500 hours

Change transmission fluid where severe dirt conditions exist.

Every 1,000 hours

Change transmission fluid (normal off-highway use).

 HIGHWAY USE — Heavy-Duty Engine Lubricant or Mineral 
Gear Lubricant 

First 4 828 to 8 047 km (3,000 to 5,000 miles)

Factory fill initial drain.

Every 16 093 km (10,000 miles)

Inspect lubricant level. Check for leaks.

Every 80 465 km (50,000 miles)

Change transmission lubricant.

 OFF-HIGHWAY USE 

First 30 hours

Change transmission lubricant on new units.

Every 40 hours

Inspect lubricant level. Check for leaks.

Every 500 hours

Change transmission lubricant where severe dirt conditions exist.

Every 1,000 hours

Change transmission lubricant (normal off-highway use).

 Proper Oil Level 

Make sure oil is level with the filler opening. Because you can reach 
oil with your finger does not mean oil is at proper level. An oil level of 
25.4 mm (one inch) is about 3.7 liters (one gallon) of oil.

[FIGURE: C11745A.gif]

 Draining Oil 

Drain transmission while oil is warm. To drain oil, remove the drain 
plug at case bottom. Clean the drain plug before reinstalling.

 Refilling 

 CAUTION: When adding oil, do not mix types and brands of oil because of possible 
incompatibility. 

Clean case around filler plug and remove plug from case side. Fill the 
transmission to the level of the filler opening. If the transmission has two 
filler openings, fill to the level of both openings.

The exact amount of oil depends on the transmission inclination and 
model. Do not overfill — this causes oil to be forced out of 
the case through the front bearing cover.

 Proper Lubrication Levels As Related to Transmission Installation Angles 

If the transmission operating angle is more than 12 degrees, improper 
lubrication can occur. The operating angle is the transmission mounting angle 
in the chassis plus the percent of upgrade (expressed in degrees).

The chart below illustrates the safe percent of upgrade on which the 
transmission can be used with various chassis mounting angles. For example: if 
you have a four-degree transmission mounting angle, then eight degrees (or 14 
percent of grade) is equal to the limit of 12 degrees. If you have a 
zero-degree mounting angle, the transmission can be operated on a 12-degree 
(21 percent) grade.

Any time the transmission operating angle or 12 degrees is exceeded for 
an extended period of time, the transmission should be equipped with an oil 
pump or cooler kit to make sure transmission is properly lubricated.

Note on the chart the effect low oil levels can have on safe operating 
angles. Allowing the oil level to fall one-half inch below the filler plug 
hole reduces the degree of grade by approximately three degrees (5.5 percent). 
Proper lubrication levels are essential.

[FIGURE: C11746A.gif]

 Operating Temperatures 

 With Eaton Roadranger® CD50 Transmission Fluid, 
Heavy-Duty Engine Oil and Mineral Oil 

The transmission should not be operated consistently at temperatures 
above 120°C (250°F). However, intermittent 
operating temperatures to 149°C (300°F) will 
not harm the transmission. Operating temperatures above 120°C 
(250°F) increase the lubricant's rate of oxidation and 
shorten its effective life. When the average operating temperature is above 120°
C (250°F), the transmission may require 
more frequent oil changes or external cooling.

The following conditions in any combination can cause operating 
temperatures of over 120°C (250°F).

operating consistently at slow speeds

high ambient temperatures

restricted airflow around transmission

exhaust system too close to transmission

high horsepower, overdrive operation

External oil coolers are available to reduce operating temperatures 
when the above conditions are encountered.

Transmission oil coolers are recommended with the following engines:

350 HP and above with overdrive transmissions

Transmission oil coolers are required with the following engines:

399 HP and above with overdrive transmissions and GCW's over 40,824 kg 
(90,000 lbs.).

399 HP and above and 1898 Nm (1400 lb-ft) or greater 
torque

450 HP and above

 With EP or Multipurpose Gear Oil 

Mild EP gear oil and multipurpose gear oil are not recommended when 
lubricant operating temperatures are above 110°C (230°
F). In addition, transmission oil coolers are not 
recommended with these gear oils, since the oil cooler materials may be 
attacked by these gear oils. The lower temperature limit and oil cooler 
restriction with these gear oils generally limit their success to milder 
applications.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission 

 Removal 

Tilt cab. 

Disconnect battery(s).

Disconnect speedometer sensor and backup lamp switch.

[FIGURE: C5263D.gif]

Remove control rod ball joint-to-remote shift lever retaining nut and 
bolt. Remove rod bracket-to-remote shift lever control top retaining bolts. 
Remove lower ball joint and rod bracket.

[FIGURE: C5264C.gif]

Position a suitable drain pan under transmission. Remove drain plug and 
drain the transmission oil. Reinstall drain plug and tighten to 61-75 Nm
 (45-55 lb-ft).

Remove driveshaft. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Disconnect clutch linkage. Refer to Section 08-02 .

Disconnect and remove fuel lines and bracketry as required. Refer to 
 Section 10-01 .

Position Rotunda Heavy-Duty Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or 
equivalent under the transmission.

Fabricate two guide pins from standard bolts as shown.

[FIGURE: C52661A.gif]

Remove two lower screws and washers retaining the transmission to the 
clutch housing. Install the two fabricated guide pins into the lower holes. 
Remove the two upper screws and washers retaining the transmission to the 
clutch housing.

Remove transmission from the clutch housing. Refer to Section 08-01 . 

Lower transmission from vehicle.

 Installation 

If removed, reinstall the two fabricated guide pins into lower holes of 
clutch housing.

Using Rotunda Heavy-Duty Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or 
equivalent, raise and align transmission to the clutch housing. Install 
transmission to clutch housing. Refer to Section 08-01 .

Install two upper transmission-to-clutch housing retaining screws and 
washers and tighten to 122-136 Nm (90-100 lb-ft).

Remove fabricated guide pins. Install two lower transmission-to-clutch 
housing retaining screws and washers and tighten to 122-136 Nm
 (90-100 lb-ft).

Install and connect fuel lines and bracketry as required. Refer to 
 Section 10-01 .

Connect clutch linkage. Refer to Section 08-02 .

Install driveshaft. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Install lower ball joint and rod bracket to remote shift lever control 
top. Install and tighten retaining bolts to 27-39 Nm (20-29 
lb-ft).

Install control rod ball joint to remote shift lever. Install and 
tighten retaining bolt and nut to 9.6-13 Nm (85-115 lb-in).

Connect speedometer sensor and backup lamp switch.

Fill transmission with the appropriate type and quantity oil. Refer to Specifications 
.

Connect battery(s).

Lower cab.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Mainshaft Taper Bearing Adjustment

 NOTE: Each time a change is made, tighten nuts and roll mainshaft. 

Place transmission in vertical position with main drive gear pointing 
down. Install yoke and nut. Tighten mainshaft flange nut to 407-475 Nm
 (300-350 lb-ft). Roll main drive gear and mainshaft to 
seat front and rear taper bearings. Position Dial Indicator with Bracketry 
TOOL-4201-C or equivalent as shown. Pry on output flange to get mainshaft end 
play. End play must be between 0.203-0.305 mm (0.008-0.012 inch). Add shims 
for more end play or remove shims for less end play. 

[FIGURE: C66401B.gif]

Apply Gasket and Trim Adhesive D7AZ-19B508-B or equivalent meeting Ford 
specifications ESE-M2G52-A and ESR-M11P17-A to both sides of each shim during 
final assembly. Apply a band of Pipe Sealant with Teflon®, 
D8AZ-19554-A or equivalent meeting Ford specifications WSK-M2G350-A2 and 
ESR-M18P7-A to bearing cap retaining nuts. Install and tighten bearing cap 
retaining nuts to 81-95 Nm (60-70 lb-ft).

Position shift bar housing gasket on transmission case. With 
transmission in neutral, position shift bar housing over gears, aligning shift 
forks with gearshift hubs. If shift bar housing and transmission are in 
neutral, transmission drive gear should turn without output shaft turning.

[FIGURE: C5270D.gif]

Install two shift bar housing retaining capscrews in locations shown. 
These are special alignment holes. Tighten screws in alignment holes to 47-54 Nm
 (35-40 lb-ft). Install remaining capscrews and tighten to 
47-54 Nm (35-40 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: C66421A.gif]

Clean the remote shift lever control top gasket mating surfaces. Make 
sure the shift block and yoke notches are aligned in the neutral position. 
Install gasket and remote shift lever control top. Apply Threadlock®
 and Sealer EOAZ-19554-AA or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification WSK-M2G315-A5 to the retaining bolt threads. Then, install and 
tighten the retaining bolts to 42-57 Nm (31-42 lb-ft). 
Install the backup lamp switch.

[FIGURE: C12765A.gif]

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Countershaft 

 Disassembly 

If countershaft is to be disassembled for any reason, front bearing 
must be destroyed. Split front bearing cage. Remove cage and taper rollers.

[FIGURE: C66711A.gif]

 NOTE: Make sure snap ring is completely out of snap ring groove. 

Using snap ring pliers and screwdriver, remove drive gear retaining 
ring from ring groove.

[FIGURE: C66781B.gif]

With drive gear snap ring out of groove, press countershaft drive gear 
and front taper bearing inner race from shaft. Press 4th gear from shaft. 
Remove gear keys from countershaft. The 3rd and 2nd gears are splined on the 
countershaft and can be pressed from shaft if replacement is necessary.

[FIGURE: C6673B.gif]

If required, remove countershaft rear bearing.

 Assembly 

Press 2nd gear on countershaft with hub of gear as shown.

[FIGURE: C66741A.gif]

Press 3rd gear on countershaft with hub of gear as shown.

[FIGURE: C66751A.gif]

Install 4th gear key in countershaft key slot. With hub of gear as 
shown, align 4th gear keyway with key in countershaft. Press gear on shaft.

[FIGURE: C66761A.gif]

Install drive gear key in countershaft key slot. With hub of gear as 
shown, align drive gear keyway with key in countershaft. Press gear on shaft.

[FIGURE: C66771A.gif]

 NOTE: Make sure snap ring is in full position in ring groove. 

Install drive gear snap ring.

[FIGURE: C66721A.gif]

Install countershaft front and rear bearings.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Shift Bar Housing 

 Disassembly 

Do not disassemble the shift bar housing assembly to determine if parts 
are worn. Note the condition of the shift fork rails and forks by a visual 
inspection. If the forks are excessively worn, or if they bind when shifted 
into the various positions, disassemble the shift bar housing assembly to 
perform service. Check the interlocking system.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Identification

The transmission identification number indicates torque capacity, 
design level, number of forward speeds and ratio group.

[FIGURE: C11747B.gif]

The FS-5205 series transmissions are five-speed synchronized units that 
feature a constant mesh low and reverse, and offer an efficient ratio of 
torque capacity to weight. The series is available in two models, FS-5205A and 
FS-5205B. Transmission features include split-pin synchronizers in 2nd, 3rd, 
4th and 5th gears; two tapered roller bearings on the mainshaft and two on the 
countershaft. 

The shift forks have steel-backed bronze wear pads that can be 
replaced, if necessary. The shift pattern is of the standard progression type 
with all shifts having the same throw at the shift lever. Transmissions are 
available with either standard ratio or the soft-fourth ratio, which splits 
the step in a two-speed axle.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Power Flow

The transmission must efficiently transfer the engine's power (torque) 
to the vehicle's rear wheels. Knowledge of what takes place in the 
transmission during torque transfer is essential when troubleshooting and 
performing service.

 NOTE: The numbers in these steps correspond to the numbers in the Power Flow 
illustration below.

Power (torque) from the engine is transferred to the transmission's 
input shaft.

Torque is transferred to the countershaft drive gear.

Torque is delivered along the countershaft to all countershaft gears.

Torque is transferred to engaged mainshaft gear. The cross section 
illustrates 1st speed gear position.

Engaged mainshaft gear external clutching teeth transfer torque to 
mainshaft through synchronizer assembly.

Mainshaft transfers torque directly to the driveshaft through the rear 
yoke.

 Power Flow, FS-5205 Series 

[FIGURE: C11748B.gif]

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission Oil Drain and Refill Procedure

 CAUTION: The use of mild EP gear oil or multi-purpose gear oil is not 
recommended, but if these gear oils are used, be sure to adhere to the 
following limitations. 

 CAUTION: Do not use mild EP gear oil or multi-purpose gear oil when operating 
temperatures are above 110°C (230°F). Many 
of these gear oils, particularly 85W140, break down above 110°
C (230°F) and coat seals, bearings, and gears with deposits 
that can cause premature failures. If these deposits are observed (especially 
a coating on seal areas causing oil leakage), change to Eaton Roadranger®
 CD50 transmission fluid, heavy duty engine oil, or mineral 
gear oil to ensure maximum component life and to maintain your warranty with 
Eaton. Refer to Operating Temperatures in this section. 

 CAUTION: Additives and friction modifiers are not recommended for use in Eaton 
Fuller transmissions. 

Proper lubrication procedures are the key to a good all-around 
maintenance program. If the oil is not doing its job, or if the oil level is 
ignored, all the maintenance procedures in the world are not going to keep the 
transmission running or ensure long transmission life.

Eaton Fuller transmissions are designed so that the internal parts 
operate in an oil circulating bath by the motion of the gears and shafts.

All parts are amply lubricated if the following procedures are closely 
followed:

Maintain oil level. Inspect regularly.

Change oil regularly.

Use the correct grade and type of oil.

Buy from a reputable dealer.

 LUBRICATION CHANGE AND INSPECTION

Eaton Roadranger® CD50 Transmission Fluid

 HIGHWAY USE 

Every 16 093 km (10,000 miles)

Check fluid level. Check for leaks.

Every 402 325 km (250,000 miles)

Change transmission fluid.

 OFF-HIGHWAY USE 

Every 40 hours

Inspect fluid level. Check for leaks.

Every 500 hours

Change transmission fluid where severe dirt conditions exist.

Every 1,000 hours

Change transmission fluid. (Normal off-highway use.)

 HIGHWAY USE — Heavy-Duty Engine Lubricant or Mineral 
Gear Lubricant 

First 4 828 to 8 047 km (3,000 to 5,000 miles)

Factory fill initial.

Every 16 093 km (10,000 miles)

Inspect lubricant level. Check for leaks.

Every 80 465 km (50,000 miles)

Change transmission lubricant.

 OFF-HIGHWAY USE 

First 30 hours

Change transmission lubricant on new units.

Every 40 hours

Inspect lubricant level. Check for leaks.

Every 500 hours

Change transmission lubricant where severe dirt conditions exist.

Every 1,000 hours

Change transmission lubricant. (Normal off-highway use.)

 Proper Oil Level 

Make sure oil is level with the filler opening. Because you can reach 
oil with your finger does not mean oil is at proper level. An oil level of 
25.4 mm (one inch) is equivalent to approximately 3.7 liters (one gallon) of 
oil.

[FIGURE: C11745A.gif]

 Draining Oil 

Drain transmission while oil is warm. To drain oil remove the drain 
plug at case bottom. Clean the drain plug before reinstalling.

 Refilling 

 CAUTION: When adding oil, do not mix types and brands of oil because of possible 
incompatibility. Do not overfill — this causes oil to be 
forced out of the case through the front bearing cover. 

Clean case around filler plug and remove plug from case side. Fill the 
transmission to the level of the filler opening. If the transmission has two 
filler openings, fill to the level of both openings.

The exact amount of oil depends on the transmission inclination and 
model.

 Proper Lubrication Levels As Related to Transmission Installation Angles 

If the transmission operating angle is more than 12 degrees, improper 
lubrication can occur. The operating angle is the transmission mounting angle 
in the chassis plus the percent of upgrade (expressed in degrees).

The following chart illustrates the safe percent of upgrade on which 
the transmission can be used with various chassis mounting angles. For 
example: if you have a four-degree transmission mounting angle, then eight 
degrees (or 14 percent of grade) is equal to the limit of 12 degrees. If you 
have a zero-degree mounting angle, the transmission can be operated on a 
12-degree (21 percent) grade.

Anytime the transmission operating angle or 12 degrees is exceeded for 
an extended period of time, the transmission should be equipped with an oil 
pump or cooler kit to make sure transmission is properly lubricated.

Note on the chart the effect low oil levels can have on safe operating 
angles. Allowing the oil level to fall one-half inch below the filler plug 
hole reduces the degree of grade by approximately three degrees (5.5 percent). 
Proper lubrication levels are essential.

[FIGURE: C11746A.gif]

 Operating Temperatures 

 With Eaton Roadranger® CD50 Transmission Fluid, 
Heavy-Duty Engine Oil and Mineral Oil 

The transmission should not be operated consistently at temperatures 
above 120°C (250°F). However, intermittent 
operating temperatures to 149°C (300°F) will 
not harm the transmission. Operating temperatures above 120°C 
(250°F) increase the lubricant's rate of oxidation and 
shorten its effective life. When the average operating temperature is above 120°
C (250°F), the transmission may require 
more frequent oil changes or external cooling.

The following conditions in any combination can cause operating 
temperatures of over 120°C (250°F).

operating consistently at slow speeds

high ambient temperatures

restricted airflow around transmission

exhaust system too close to transmission

high horsepower, overdrive operation

External oil coolers are available to reduce operating temperatures 
when the above conditions are encountered.

Transmission Oil Coolers are recommended with the following engines:

350 HP and above with overdrive transmissions

Transmission Oil Coolers are required with the following engines:

399 HP and above with overdrive transmissions and GCW's over 40,824 kg 
(90,000 lb)

399 HP and above and 1898 Nm (1400 lb-ft) or greater 
torque

450 HP and above

 With EP or Multipurpose Gear Oil 

Mild EP gear oil and multipurpose gear oil are not recommended when 
lubricant operating temperatures are above 110°C (230°
F). In addition, transmission oil coolers are not 
recommended with these gear oils, since the oil cooler materials may be 
attacked by these gear oils. The lower temperature limit and oil cooler 
restriction with these gear oils generally limit their success to milder 
applications.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission

 Removal 

Tilt cab.

Disconnect battery(s).

Disconnect speedometer sensor and backup lamp switch.

[FIGURE: C5263D.gif]

Remove control rod ball joint-to-remote shift lever retaining nut and 
bolt. Remove rod bracket-to-remote shift lever control top retaining bolts. 
Remove lower ball joint and rod bracket.

[FIGURE: C5264C.gif]

Position a suitable drain pan under transmission. Remove drain plug and 
drain the transmission oil. Reinstall drain plug and tighten to 61-75 Nm
 (45-55 lb-ft).

Remove driveshaft. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Disconnect clutch linkage. Refer to Section 08-02 .

Disconnect and remove fuel lines and bracketry as required. Refer to 
 Section 10-01 .

Position Rotunda Heavy-Duty Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or 
equivalent under the transmission.

Fabricate two guide pins from standard bolts as shown.

[FIGURE: C52661A.gif]

Remove two lower screws and washers retaining the transmission to the 
clutch housing. Install the two fabricated guide pins into the lower holes. 
Remove the two upper screws and washers retaining the transmission to the 
clutch housing.

Remove transmission from the clutch housing. Refer to Section 08-01 . 

Lower transmission from vehicle.

 Installation 

If removed, reinstall the two fabricated guide pins into lower holes of 
clutch housing.

Using Rotunda Heavy-Duty Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or 
equivalent, raise and align transmission to the clutch housing. Install 
transmission to the clutch housing. Refer to Section 08-01 .

Install two upper transmission-to-clutch housing retaining screws and 
washers and tighten to 197-210 Nm (145-155 lb-ft).

Remove fabricated guide pins. Install two lower transmission-to-clutch 
housing retaining screws and washers and tighten to 197-210 Nm
 (145-155 lb-ft).

Install and connect fuel lines and bracketry as required. Refer to 
 Section 10-01 .

Connect clutch linkage. Refer to Section 08-02 .

Install driveshaft. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Install lower ball joint and rod bracket to remote shift lever control 
top. Install and tighten retaining bolts to 27-39 Nm (20-29 
lb-ft).

Install control rod ball joint to remote shift lever. Install and 
tighten retaining bolt and nut to 9.6-13 Nm (85-115 lb-in). 

Connect speedometer sensor and backup lamp switch.

Fill transmission with the appropriate type and quantity oil. Refer to Specifications 
.

Connect battery(s).

Lower cab.

[FIGURE: C5269C.gif]

Remove the shift bar housing retaining capscrews and lockwashers. Jar 
the housing lightly to break the gasket seal. Remove the shift bar housing and 
gasket from the transmission. 

Lock the transmission by engaging two mainshaft gears. Remove the yoke 
nut and the yoke or flange. Remove the mainshaft rear bearing cap retaining 
nuts and lockwashers. Remove the mainshaft rear bearing cap. Remove the 
speedometer rotor.

[FIGURE: C7415B.gif]

Using a soft hammer, tap the front end of the drive gear to move the 
mainshaft toward the rear approximately 6.35 mm (1/4 inch). Use pry bars to 
remove the rear bearing cup (and snap ring). 

[FIGURE: C64781B.gif]

Remove the main drive gear bearing cover capscrews. Using a soft 
hammer, tap on the threaded end of the mainshaft to move the mainshaft toward 
the front of the transmission housing. 

[FIGURE: C90421A.gif]

Working from front of transmission, remove main drive gear bearing 
cover and shims. Remove main drive gear and bearing assembly. 

Using a sling and Rotunda Hand Chain Hoist 164-R1713 or equivalent, 
lift the mainshaft assembly from the transmission housing. The mainshaft 
assembly can be removed by hand but is quite difficult to handle. 

[FIGURE: C71581A.gif]

Remove reverse idler lock and countershaft rear bearing cap capscrews. 
Remove countershaft rear bearing cap and shims. 

[FIGURE: C8896C.gif]

Remove countershaft rear taper bearing cup. 

[FIGURE: C88971A.gif]

Remove the reverse idler shaft with a suitable pry bar. 

[FIGURE: C64831A.gif]

 NOTE: Idler gear has loose needle rollers in it. Do not lose these rollers. 

Lift the reverse idler gear with roller bearings, spacers and thrust 
washers from the case. Remove needle rollers and spacers from inside reverse 
idler gear.

[FIGURE: C64841A.gif]

Move the countershaft assembly and lift it from transmission case. 

[FIGURE: C64871C.gif]

 Assembly 

If the transmission case or countershaft front taper bearing cup was 
replaced, install bearing cup location ring. From inside of case, install 
bearing cup. Coat outer diameter of bore plug with Gasket and Trim Adhesive 
D7AZ-19B508-B or equivalent meeting Ford specifications ESR-M11P17-A and 
ESE-M2G52-A, and install bore plug in case. 

[FIGURE: C66301A.gif]

Turn transmission case on end as shown. Position countershaft assembly 
into front bearing cup. Install rear bearing cup over rear taper bearing, and 
tap cup into place. 

[FIGURE: C66331A.gif]

Coat the reverse idler thrust washers with Premium Long-Life Grease 
XG-1-C or -K or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B and position 
them in the housing with tang of washer in housing groove, if so equipped. 

[FIGURE: C64921A.gif]

Coat inside diameter of reverse idler gear with Premium Long-Life 
Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B. This 
will hold needle rollers in position while assembling. Insert one roller 
spacer. 

[FIGURE: C64931A.gif]

Position first row of needle rollers on spacer. 

[FIGURE: C64941A.gif]

Place roller spacer on first row of rollers. 

Position second row of needle rollers. 

[FIGURE: C64951A.gif]

Place roller spacer on second row of rollers. Grease rollers to hold in 
place. 

 CAUTION: Do not disrupt needle rollers. 

 NOTE: Idler shaft lock groove must line up with the lock screw hole. 

Carefully position reverse idler gear in housing. Insert idler shaft 
through case and idler gear needle rollers. Drive shaft into position. Install 
capscrew and tighten to 27-34 Nm (20-25 lb-ft). 

Position the same shims that were removed at disassembly over 
countershaft rear bearing cup. Install countershaft rear bearing cap. Install 
and tighten capscrews to 47-54 Nm (35-40 lb-ft). 

[FIGURE: C6634B.gif]

 NOTE: Each time a change is made, tighten capscrews and roll countershaft. 

Roll countershaft to be sure bearings and bearing cups are seated. 
Position Dial Indicator with Bracketry TOOL-4201-C or equivalent as shown. Pry 
on countershaft to get countershaft end play. End play must be between 0.05 mm 
and 0.20 mm (0.002-0.008 inch). Add shims for more end play or remove shims 
for less end play. 

[FIGURE: C6635B.gif]

At final assembly, coat both sides of each shim with Gasket and Trim 
Adhesive D7AZ-19B508-B or equivalent meeting Ford specifications ESR-M11P17-A 
and ESE-M2G52-A. Position shims over countershaft rear bearing cup. Install 
countershaft rear bearing cap. Apply a band of Pipe Sealant with Teflon®
 D8AZ-19554-A or equivalent meeting Ford specifications 
WSK-M2G350-A2 and ESR-M18P7-A to bearing capscrews, 3 mm (.118 inch) from end 
of threads, 9 mm (.354 inch) long. Do not dip capscrews. Install and tighten 
capscrews to 47-54 Nm (35-40 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: C6496B.gif]

Tilt the rear of the mainshaft assembly downward and insert the end of 
the shaft through the output bore in the housing. Lower the front end of the 
mainshaft until it is in line with the pilot bearing opening of the main drive 
gear. 

[FIGURE: C71581A.gif]

Position mainshaft rear bearing cup in housing bore. Using soft hammer, 
tap rear bearing cup until cup snap ring is seated against housing. 

[FIGURE: C64971B.gif]

Install speedometer rotor on mainshaft. 

Shellac new gasket on mainshaft rear bearing cap and install the cap. 
Use care not to cover the oil return grooves. Install cap on housing with oil 
grooves aligned with oil hole in case. Apply Pipe Sealant with Teflon®
 D8AZ-19554-A or equivalent meeting Ford specifications 
WSK-M2G350-A2 and ESR-M18P7-A to the stud threads. Install bearing cap 
lockwashers and nuts. Tighten nuts to 81-95 Nm (60-70 lb-ft).

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Mainshaft Taper Bearing Adjustment

 NOTE: The mainshaft rear taper bearing and main drive gear taper bearing must 
have 0.20-0.30 mm (0.008-0.012 inch) end play after assembly of transmission 
is complete. The mainshaft rear taper bearing and bearing cup are not 
adjustable. The main drive gear taper bearing cup is located in the main drive 
gear bearing cover. The required taper bearing end play is achieved by 
inserting shims of different sizes between the bearing cover and transmission 
housing. 

Tighten four bearing cover capscrews to 3.39 Nm (30 
lb-in). Position two feeler gauges at the capscrew locations as shown, record 
gap between bearing cover and housing. Take an average of the two measurements 
and add 0.406 mm (0.016 inch). For example, if one measurement were 1.066 mm 
(0.042 inch) and the other 1.016 mm (0.040 inch), the average would be 1.041 
mm (0.041 inch). Adding the 0.406 mm (0.016 inch) and 1.041 mm (0.041 inch) 
produces a total of 1.447 mm (0.057 inch). This total represents the thickness 
of the shim pack required to start end play measurement. 

[FIGURE: C10931A.gif]

After determining the size of shim pack required, remove bearing cover 
from housing and install shim pack and bearing cover, making sure that oil 
grooves are up. Install and tighten capscrews to 20-34 Nm 
(15-25 lb-ft).

Place transmission in vertical position with main drive gear pointing 
down. Install companion flange or yoke. Tighten flange or yoke retaining nut 
to 407-475 Nm (300-350 lb-ft). 

 NOTE: Each time a change is made, retighten stud nuts and roll mainshaft. 

Rotate the input shaft six times in each direction to seat front and 
rear taper bearings. Position Dial Indicator with Bracketry TOOL-4201-C or 
equivalent, as shown. Pry on output flange to get mainshaft end play. End play 
must be between 0.20-0.30 mm (0.008-0.012 inch). Add shims for more end play 
or remove shims for less end play. 

[FIGURE: C6503C.gif]

At final assembly, remove bearing cover. Apply Gasket and Trim Adhesive 
D7AZ-19B508-B or equivalent meeting Ford specifications ESR-M11P17-A and 
ESE-M2G52-A to both sides of each shim. Install shims and bearing cover. Apply 
Pipe Sealant with Teflon® D8AZ-19554-A or equivalent meeting 
Ford specifications WSK-M2G350-A2 and ESR-M18P7-A to screw threads. Then, 
install and tighten capscrews to 20-34 Nm (15-25 lb-ft).

With the transmission and shift forks in neutral and a new shift bar 
housing gasket in place, position the shift bar housing over the gears, 
aligning the shift forks with the gearshift hubs. Install shift bar housing 
onto transmission case. If the shift bar housing is in neutral and the 
transmission is in neutral, the transmission main drive gear should turn 
without the output mainshaft turning. Install the center rear capscrew, then 
the center front capscrews and tighten to 47-54 Nm (35-40 
lb-ft). Install the remaining capscrews and tighten to 47-54 Nm
 (35-40 lb-ft).

Clean the remote shift lever control top gasket mating surfaces. Make 
sure the shift block and yoke notches are aligned in neutral position. Install 
gasket and remote shift lever control top. Apply Threadlock and Sealer 
EOAZ-19554-AA or equivalent meeting Ford specification WSK-M2G315-A5 to the 
retaining bolt threads. Then, install and tighten the retaining bolts to 42-57 Nm
 (31-42 lb-ft). Install the backup lamp switch.

Mainshaft 

 Disassembly 

Clamp the mainshaft, front end facing upward, in a soft-jawed vise. 

[FIGURE: C65041A.gif]

Remove the synchronizer cup and the 4th/5th speed synchronizer assembly. 

[FIGURE: C65051A.gif]

Remove the 4th/5th shift hub thrust bearing and race. 

[FIGURE: C65061A.gif]

Remove 4th/5th shift hub, synchronizer cup and 4th gear. 

[FIGURE: C6507C.gif]

[FIGURE: C66471B.gif]

[FIGURE: C65091A.gif]

 CAUTION: Do not lose locator ball when removing third gear thrust washer. 

Remove 3rd gear thrust washer and locator ball.

[FIGURE: C6510C.gif]

Remove 3rd gear and roller bearing.

Remove 2nd/3rd speed synchronizer assembly.

split washer.

Remove 1st gear and roller bearing.

Install retainer snap ring.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Main Drive Gear 

 Disassembly 

The main drive gear tapered roller bearing should not be removed unless 
it is intended to be replaced. To remove, use a clamp type puller behind the 
bearing retainer. Either an arbor press or a Bearing Pulling Attachment 
D79L-4621-A or equivalent can now be used to remove the bearing. 

[FIGURE: C3889E.gif]

Remove the roller bearing retainer ring and washer. Remove the 
mainshaft roller bearings. 

[FIGURE: C65411A.gif]

 Assembly 

Press new taper bearing on drive gear. Turn gear over. Coat the bore of 
the main drive gear with Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent 
meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B to retain the rollers. Position rollers 
in drive gear bore as shown. 

[FIGURE: C65421A.gif]

Install roller bearing washer and retainer ring. 

[FIGURE: C6670B.gif]

 Disassembly 

If countershaft is to be disassembled for any reason, front bearing

Place the countershaft assembly in a hydraulic press, and press the 
drive gear off the shaft. 

Press the fourth gear off the shaft. If necessary, remove the rear 
bearing. 

 Assembly

front. Press the fourth gear on the shaft.

Align countershaft drive gear to the shaft with the long hub facing 
toward the rear. Press the countershaft drive gear on the shaft.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Shift Bar Housing

 Disassembly 

Do not disassemble the shift bar housing assembly to determine if parts 
are worn. Note the condition of the shift fork rails and forks by a visual 
inspection. If the forks are excessively worn, or if they bind when shifted 
into the various positions, disassemble the shift bar housing assembly to 
perform service. Check the interlocking system.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Identification

[FIGURE: C7344F.gif]

The Eaton FS-6205 transmission has five forward speeds and one reverse 
speed with gear ratios as follows: 

1st 7.22:1 

2nd 3.89:1 

3rd 2.22:1 

4th 1.39:1 

5th 1.00:1 

Reverse 7.22:1 

Countershaft end play is controlled by shims located in the 
countershaft rear bearing cap. Mainshaft end play is controlled by shims 
located in the mainshaft rear bearing cover. The shift forks are single-piece 
forged and are equipped with bronze wear pads that can be replaced.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Power Flow

 NOTE: The numbers in these steps correspond to the numbers in the following 
Power Flow illustration.

The transmission transfers torque from the engine to the driveshaft 
through the following route: 

Power (torque) from the engine is transferred to the input shaft and 
drive gear. 

The input shaft drive gear transfers torque to the countershaft drive 
gear.

The countershaft drive gear turns the countershaft and all countershaft 
gears. 

Torque from the countershaft gear is transferred to the mainshaft gear 
that is currently engaged. 

The external clutching teeth of the engaged mainshaft gear transfer 
torque to the mainshaft through the synchronizer assembly. 

The mainshaft transfers torque directly to the driveshaft through the 
rear yoke.

 Power Flow, FS-6205 

[FIGURE: C7421C.gif]

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission Oil Drain and Refill Procedure

 CAUTION: The use of mild EP gear oil or multi-purpose gear oil is not 
recommended, but if these gear oils are used, be sure to adhere to the 
following limitations. 

 CAUTION: Do not use mild EP gear oil or multi-purpose gear oil when operating 
temperatures are above 110°C (230°F). Many 
of these gear oils, particularly 85W140, break down above 110°
C (230°F) and coat seals, bearings and gears with deposits 
that may cause premature failures. If these deposits are observed (especially 
a coating on seal areas causing oil leakage), change to Eaton Roadranger®
 CD50 transmission fluid, heavy-duty engine oil or mineral 
gear oil to ensure maximum component life and to maintain your warranty with 
Eaton. Refer to Operating Temperatures in this section. 

 CAUTION: Additives and friction modifiers are not recommended for use in Eaton 
Fuller transmissions. 

Proper lubrication procedures are the key to a good all-around 
maintenance program. If the oil is not doing its job, or if the oil level is 
ignored, all the maintenance procedures in the world are not going to keep the 
transmission running or ensure long transmission life.

Eaton Fuller transmissions are designed so that the internal parts 
operate in a bath of oil circulated by the motion of gears and shafts.

All parts will be amply lubricated if the following procedures are 
closely followed:

Maintain oil level. Inspect regularly.

Change oil regularly.

Use the correct grade and type of oil.

Buy from a reputable dealer.

 LUBRICATION CHANGE AND INSPECTION

 Eaton Roadranger® CD50 Transmission Fluid 

 HIGHWAY USE 

Every 16 093 km (10,000 miles)

Check fluid level. Check for leaks.

Every 402 325 km (250,000 miles)

Change transmission fluid.

 OFF-HIGHWAY USE 

Every 40 hours

Inspect fluid level. Check for leaks.

Every 500 hours

Change transmission fluid where severe dirt conditions exist.

Every 1,000 hours

Change transmission fluid (normal off-highway use).

 HIGHWAY USE — Heavy-Duty Engine Lubricant or Mineral 
Gear Lubricant 

First 4 828 to 8 047 km (3,000 to 5,000 miles)

Factory fill initial drain.

Every 16 093 km (10,000 miles)

Inspect lubricant level. Check for leaks.

Every 80 465 km (50,000 miles)

Change transmission lubricant.

 OFF-HIGHWAY USE 

First 30 hours

Change transmission lubricant on new units.

Every 40 hours

Inspect lubricant level. Check for leaks.

Every 500 hours

Change transmission lubricant where severe dirt conditions exist.

Every 1,000 hours

Change transmission lubricant (normal off-highway use).

 Proper Oil Level 

Make sure oil is level with the filler opening. Because you can reach 
oil with your finger does not mean oil is at proper level. An oil level of 
25.4 mm [one inch] is equal to approximately 3.7 liters [
one gallon] of oil.

[FIGURE: C11745A.gif]

 Draining Oil 

Drain transmission while oil is warm. To drain oil remove the drain 
plug at bottom of case. Clean the drain plug before reinstalling.

 Refilling 

 CAUTION: When adding oil, do not mix types and brands of oil because of possible 
incompatibility. Do not overfill — this will cause oil to be 
forced out of the transmission. 

Clean case around filler plug and remove plug from side of case. Fill 
transmission to the level of the filler opening. If transmission has two 
filler openings, fill to level of both openings. The exact amount of oil will 
depend on the transmission inclination and model.

 Proper Lubrication Levels As Related to Transmission Installation Angles 

If the transmission operating angle is more than 12 degrees, improper 
lubrication can occur. The operating angle is the transmission mounting angle 
in the chassis plus the percent of upgrade (expressed in degrees).

The following chart illustrates the safe percent of upgrade on which 
the transmission can be used with various chassis mounting angles. For 
example: if you have a four-degree transmission mounting angle, then eight 
degrees (or 14 percent of grade) is equal to the limit of 12 degrees. If you 
have a zero-degree mounting angle, the transmission can be operated on a 
12-degree (21 percent) grade.

Anytime the transmission operating angle of 12 degrees is exceeded for 
an extended period of time, the transmission should be equipped with an oil 
pump or cooler kit to make sure transmission is properly lubricated.

Note on the chart the effect low oil levels can have on safe operating 
angles. Allowing the oil level to fall one-half inch below the filler plug 
hole reduces the degree of grade by approximately three degrees (5.5 percent). 
Proper lubrication levels are essential.

[FIGURE: C11746A.gif]

 Operating Temperatures 

 With Eaton Roadranger® CD50 Transmission Fluid, 
Heavy-Duty Engine Oil and Mineral Oil 

The transmission should not be operated consistently at temperatures 
above 120°C (250°F). However, intermittent 
operating temperatures to 149°C (300°F) will 
not harm the transmission. Operating temperatures above 120°C 
(250°F) increase the lubricant's rate of oxidation and 
shorten its effective life. When the average operating temperature is above 120°
C (250°F), the transmission may require 
more frequent oil changes or external cooling.

The following conditions in any combination can cause operating 
temperatures of over 120°C (250°F).

operating consistently at slow speeds

high ambient temperatures

restricted airflow around transmission

exhaust system too close to transmission

high horsepower, overdrive operation

External oil coolers are available to reduce operating temperatures 
when the above conditions are encountered.

Transmission oil coolers are recommended with the following engines:

350 HP and above with overdrive transmissions

Transmission oil coolers are required with the following engines:

399 HP and above with overdrive transmissions and GCW's over 40,824 kg 
(90,000 lb).

399 HP and above and 1898 Nm (1400 lb-ft) or greater 
torque

450 HP and above

 With EP or Multipurpose Gear Oil 

Mild EP gear oil and multipurpose gear oil are not recommended when 
lubricant operating temperatures are above 110°C (230°
F). In addition, transmission oil coolers are not 
recommended with these gear oils, since the oil cooler materials may be 
attacked by these gear oils. The lower temperature limit and oil cooler 
restriction with these gear oils generally limit their success to milder 
applications.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission

 Removal 

Tilt cab.

Disconnect battery(s).

Disconnect speedometer sensor and backup lamp switch.

[FIGURE: C5263D.gif]

Remove control rod ball joint-to-remote shift lever retaining nut and 
bolt. Remove rod bracket-to-remote shift lever control top retaining bolts. 
Remove lower ball joint and rod bracket.

[FIGURE: C5264C.gif]

Position a suitable drain pan under transmission. Remove drain plug and 
drain the transmission oil. Reinstall drain plug and tighten to 61-75 Nm
 (45-55 lb-ft).

Remove driveshaft. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Disconnect clutch linkage. Refer to Section 08-02 .

Disconnect and remove fuel lines and bracketry as required. Refer to 
 Section 10-01 .

Position Rotunda Heavy-Duty Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or 
equivalent under the transmission.

Fabricate two guide pins from standard bolts as shown.

[FIGURE: C52661A.gif]

Remove two lower screws and washers retaining the transmission to the 
clutch housing. Install the two fabricated guide pins into the lower holes. 
Remove the two upper screws and washers retaining the transmission to the 
clutch housing.

Remove transmission from the clutch housing. Refer to Section 08-01 .

Lower transmission from vehicle.

 Installation 

If removed, reinstall the two fabricated guide pins into lower holes of 
clutch housing.

Using Rotunda Heavy-Duty Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or 
equivalent, raise and align transmission to the clutch housing. Install 
transmission to the clutch housing. Refer to Section 08-01 .

Install two upper transmission-to-clutch housing retaining screws and 
washers and tighten to 197-210 Nm (145-155 lb-ft).

Remove fabricated guide pins. Install two lower transmission-to-clutch 
housing retaining screws and washers and tighten to 197-210 Nm
 (145-155 lb-ft).

Install and connect fuel lines and bracketry as required. Refer to 
 Section 10-01 .

Connect clutch linkage. Refer to Section 08-02 .

Install driveshaft. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Install lower ball joint and rod bracket to remote shift lever control 
top. Install and tighten retaining bolts to 27-39 Nm (20-29 
lb-ft).

Install control rod ball joint to remote shift lever. Install and 
tighten retaining bolt and nut to 9.6-13 Nm (85-115 lb-in).

Connect speedometer sensor and backup lamp switch.

Fill transmission with the appropriate type and quantity oil. Refer to Specifications 
.

Connect battery(s).

Lower cab.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Transmission 

 Disassembly 

Position shift lever in neutral. Remove four capscrews retaining remote 
shift lever control top to shift bar housing. Jar housing lightly to break the 
gasket seal. Remove remote shift lever control top and gasket. Remove backup 
lamp switch.

Remove capscrews and separate shift bar housing and gasket from case. 

Lock the transmission by engaging two mainshaft gears with mainshaft 
sliding clutches.

Remove the yoke nut and the yoke or flange.

[FIGURE: C71361B.gif]

Remove six capscrews and tap the input shaft bearing cover with a 
rubber mallet to separate the cover from the case. Remove the cover. 

[FIGURE: C7138B.gif]

If necessary, remove the oil seal from the input shaft bearing cover. 
Refer to Input Shaft Bearing Cover in 
the Disassembly and Assembly portion of this section.

Remove the input shaft assembly from the transmission case. 

[FIGURE: C71591A.gif]

Remove the four nuts and lockwashers that hold the mainshaft rear 
bearing cover to the transmission case. Insert screwdrivers into the notches 
on either side of the mainshaft rear bearing cover and gently separate the 
cover from the transmission case.

[FIGURE: C71391A.gif]

Remove shims (if they did not come off when mainshaft rear bearing 
cover was removed) and speedometer rotor.

[FIGURE: C71401A.gif]

Wrap a sling around the 2nd-3rd synchronizer. Using Rotunda Hand Chain 
Hoist 164-R1713 or equivalent, remove mainshaft assembly from case. 

[FIGURE: C5274C.gif]

 NOTE: Countershaft may slide rearward and out of bearing bore. 

Remove the four capscrews and remove the countershaft rear bearing cap, 
shims and bearing cup from the transmission case.

[FIGURE: C7141B.gif]

Using Impact Slide Hammer D79P-100-A or equivalent, remove reverse 
idler gear shaft. Remove locating ball once it is exposed.

[FIGURE: C7143C.gif]

Remove reverse idler gear, bearings, spacer and thrust washers.

[FIGURE: C73471A.gif]

Move countershaft assembly to the rear and lift it from the case. 

[FIGURE: C73481A.gif]

If countershaft front bearing cup is to be replaced, use a suitable 
driver and bearing cup remover to drive the bore plug through the front of the 
transmission case and drive the bearing cup towards the rear of the 
transmission case.

[FIGURE: C71461A.gif]

 Assembly 

 NOTE: The snap ring should be installed with open end aligned with lube 
trough in the case. 

If removed, install snap ring, countershaft front bearing cup (from 
inside of case) and bore plug, using a suitable driver. Coat outer diameter of 
bore with Gasket and Trim Adhesive D7AZ-19B508-B or equivalent meeting Ford 
specifications ESE-M2G52-A and ESR-M11P17-A before installing.

[FIGURE: C71471A.gif]

Turn transmission case onto end with the rear of the transmission 
facing up. Stand countershaft assembly into front bearing cup.

[FIGURE: C73491A.gif]

Use Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent meeting Ford 
specifications ESA-M1C75-B on reverse idler thrust washers to hold them in 
place. Position tangs of washers in groove of housing.

[FIGURE: C7149B.gif]

Install bearings and spacer in reverse idler gear.

[FIGURE: C73501A.gif]

 NOTE: Gear can be installed either way. 

Position reverse idler gear in transmission case.

[FIGURE: C73511A.gif]

Insert reverse idler gear shaft through transmission case, bearings, 
spacer and thrust washers. Line up notch to shaft with notch in case. Install 
locating ball and drive the shaft into position.

[FIGURE: C7152B.gif]

Coat outer diameter of countershaft rear bearing cup with Gasket and 
Trim Adhesive D7AZ-19B508-B or equivalent meeting Ford specifications 
ESE-M2G52-A and ESR-M11P17-A. Install countershaft rear bearing cup into case.

[FIGURE: C71531A.gif]

Temporarily install new shims over countershaft rear bearing cup.

Install the countershaft rear bearing cap and capscrews. Tighten 
capscrews to 47-54 Nm (35-40 lb-ft).

Rotate countershaft to seat the bearings. Position Dial 
Indicator/Magnetic Base D78P-4201-B or equivalent on the shoulder of one of 
the countershaft gears. Lift countershaft to measure end play. End play must 
be between 0.15-0.25 mm (0.006-0.010 inch). Add shims for less end play or 
remove shims for more end play. Once end play is correct, remove rear bearing 
cap. Apply a light coat of Gasket and Trim Adhesive D7AZ-19B508-B or 
equivalent meeting Ford specifications ESR-M11P17-A and ESE-M2G52-A to both 
sides of shims and to the rear bearing cap and reinstall them. 

[FIGURE: C7155D.gif]

Coat threads of capscrews with Pipe Sealant with Teflon®
 D8AZ-19554-A or equivalent meeting Ford specifications 
WSK-M2G350-AZ and ESR-M18P7-A and tighten to 47-54 Nm (35-40 
lb-ft).

[FIGURE: C12970A.gif]

Place transmission in a horizontal position. Shift 2nd-3rd mainshaft 
synchronizer into 3rd gear.

Place a sling or rope around the 2nd-3rd synchronizer assembly. Using 
Rotunda Hand Chain Hoist 164-R1713 or equivalent, carefully lower the assembly 
into the transmission case.

[FIGURE: C5274C.gif]

Align clutching teeth on main drive gear with teeth in 5th speed 
synchronizer cup. Install input shaft into aligned teeth.

[FIGURE: C71591A.gif]

If removed, install input shaft oil seal and bearing cup into input 
shaft bearing cover. Refer to Input Shaft 
Bearing Cover in the Disassembly and Assembly portion of this section for procedure. 

 NOTE: Top of input shaft bearing cover is marked for proper installation. 

Install gasket input shaft bearing cover. Apply Pipe Sealant with Teflon®
 D8AZ-19554-A or equivalent meeting Ford specifications 
WSK-M2G350-AZ and ESR-M18P7-A to the threads of the capscrews and tighten to 
20-34 Nm (15-25 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: C7160B.gif]

Install speedometer rotor. 

[FIGURE: C71611A.gif]

 NOTE: Top of mainshaft rear bearing cover is marked for proper installation. 

If removed, install bearing cup and oil seal into mainshaft to rear 
bearing cover. Refer to Mainshaft Rear Bearing Cover in the Disassembly and 
Assembly portion of this section for procedure. Temporarily install shims and 
mainshaft rear bearing cover. Tighten nuts to 81-95 Nm (60-70 
lb-ft).

[FIGURE: C7162C.gif]

Place transmission in a vertical position (with the rear of the 
transmission facing up). Engage two mainshaft gears to lock transmission. 
Install yoke or flange and nut. Tighten nut to 407-475 Nm 
(300-350 lb-ft). 

 NOTE: Once end play is correct, remove yoke or flange and mainshaft rear 
bearing cover and apply a light coat of Gasket and Trim Adhesive D7AZ-19B508-B 
or equivalent meeting Ford specifications ESE-M2G52-A and ESR-M11P17-A to both 
sides of shims. 

Rotate input shaft and mainshaft to seat bearings and races. Position 
Dial Indicator/Magnetic Base D78P-4201-B or equivalent so it contacts the end 
of the output shaft as shown in the illustration. Pry up on output shaft to 
measure end play. End play must be between 0.15-0.25 mm (0.006-0.010 inch). 
Add shims for more end play. Remove shims for less end play.

[FIGURE: C7163F.gif]

 NOTE: Top of mainshaft rear bearing cover is marked for proper installation. 

Install mainshaft rear bearing cover. Apply Pipe Sealant with Teflon®
 D8AZ-19554-A or equivalent meeting Ford specifications 
WSK-M2G350-AZ and ESR-M18P7-A to studs and tighten nuts to 81-95 Nm
 (60-70 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: C71641B.gif]

Lock the transmission by engaging two mainshaft gears. Install yoke or 
flange and nut. Tighten nut to 407-475 Nm (300-350 lb-ft). 

With the transmission and shift yokes in neutral, and a new shift bar 
housing gasket in place, position the shift bar housing over the gears, 
aligning the shift yokes with corresponding synchronizers and sliding clutch. 
Install shift bar housing onto transmission case.

Apply Pipe Sealant with Teflon® D8AZ-19554-A or 
equivalent meeting Ford specifications WSK-M2G350-AZ and ESR-M18P7-A to the 
threads of the capscrews. Install two capscrews into alignment holes of shift 
bar housing and tighten to 47-54 Nm (35-40 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: C7354B.gif]

Install remaining capscrews and tighten to 47-54 Nm 
(35-40 lb-ft). 

With the shift bar housing in the neutral position, install the gasket 
and the remote shift lever control top on the shift bar housing. Fit the shift 
lever on the corresponding finger assembly in the shift bar housing as the 
lever is installed. 

[FIGURE: C12971A.gif]

Coat the threads of the retaining capscrews with Pipe Sealant with Teflon®
 D8AZ-19554-A or equivalent meeting Ford specifications 
WSK-M2G350-AZ and ESR-M18P7-A. Install capscrews and tighten to 42-57 Nm
 (31-42 lb-ft).
