REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Clutch Preassembly Procedures 

 WARNING: DO NOT INHALE THE DUST FROM BRAKES, CLUTCHES OR ASSOCIATED COMPONENTS. 
INHALATION OF DUST FROM THESE COMPONENTS COULD BE INJURIOUS TO YOUR HEALTH. 
COMPRESSED AIR OR BRUSHES MUST NOT BE USED TO CLEAN BRAKES, BRAKE DRUMS, 
CLUTCHES OR ASSOCIATED COMPONENTS. USE A VACUUM CLEANER SUCH AS ROTUNDA BRAKE, 
CLUTCH, SERVICE VACUUM 164-R3600 OR EQUIVALENT EQUIPPED FOR THIS PURPOSE 
CAREFULLY TO REMOVE ANY DUST. ADHERENT DUST SHOULD BE REMOVED WITH A DAMP RAG. 
ANY DUST SHOULD BE CONTAINED IN A SEALED AND LABELED BAG FOR DISPOSAL. WEAR AN 
APPROVED HIGH EFFICIENCY CARTRIDGE OR AIR LINE RESPIRATOR AND USE EXTRA 
CAUTION TO AVOID BREATHING THIS DUST. 

Clean the following components by scraping them and soaking them in a 
suitable solvent: 

flywheel housing face and bore

clutch housing face and input shaft

transmission input shaft 

front face 

Check for any damage or excessive wear and service as necessary. Clean 
the clutch housing interior with a suitable solvent. 

Clean the transmission input shaft with a wire brush, then polish the 
shaft and clean with a suitable solvent. Check condition of the transmission 
input shaft. Use a stone to dull sharp edges of the splines. If splines are 
worn excessively or notched, the clutch disc will not slide on the shaft. 
Replace the input shaft as required. 

Clean the flywheel face with a suitable solvent. 

Clean the clutch release lever with a wire brush. Smooth the release 
lever finger locating faces with a carborundum stone and then clean with a 
suitable solvent. Apply a light coating of Motorcraft Premium Long-Life Grease 
XG-1-C or -K or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B to the 
release lever finger tips and locating faces. If clutch release lever is worn 
excessively, replace it. 

Apply Motorcraft Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent 
meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B to the cross-shaft bushings until clean 
grease appears from all four bushings. Remove the excess grease. 

If reinstalling the old clutch, clean the pressure plate with a 
suitable solvent. 

If the shaft/fork assembly has not been dismantled, check that the 
shafts do not protrude into the fork locating space, and make sure that the 
non-operating shaft end is flush with the outside of the clutch housing. Make 
sure that the assembly turns freely.

 Removal 

Remove the driveshaft. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Remove the exhaust pipe.

Disconnect the gearshift linkage. Refer to Section 07-06B .

Disconnect reverse gear switch and speedometer cable.

Remove clutch housing cover to access clutch cover.

Remove the retainer spring and slave cylinder push rod from the clutch 
release lever. Remove clutch slave cylinder from transmission (it is not 
necessary to disconnect hydraulic tube). Refer to Section 08-02 .

Support the transmission on a suitable transmission jack, such as 
Rotunda Heavy Duty Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or equivalent.

Remove 12 bolts that retain clutch housing to flywheel housing.

Rotate clutch release lever counterclockwise as far as possible so it 
is in the horizontal position to allow clearance from clutch release bearing 
during removal of transmission and clutch housing assembly.

 CAUTION: Do not let the rear of the transmission drop and do not let the 
transmission hang unsupported in the splined hubs of the clutch discs. Taking 
these precautions will prevent bending and distortion of the clutch discs. 

Make sure that the transmission is approximately in line with the 
engine. Then, carefully withdraw the transmission until the transmission input 
shaft clears the clutch release bearing. 

Install the Truck Clutch Alignment Shaft D79T-7550-B or equivalent into 
the release bearing assembly and driven disc. An old transmission input shaft 
may be used for this purpose. 

 CAUTION: Before removing clutch cover assembly on an adjustment-free clutch, 
four shipping bolts must be installed in the clutch cover to prevent pressure 
plate from moving forward. Refer to illustration of adjustment-free clutch. 

Install four shipping bolts.

Because of the weight of a 14-inch clutch, install two guide studs (3/8 
x 16 x 2-inch) in the top mounting bolt holes to facilitate removal. 

[FIGURE: C11141A.gif]

 CAUTION: Do not remove the bolts at this time. 

Loosen the remaining mounting bolts around the flywheel in a 
criss-cross pattern to prevent cocking and bending of the clutch mounting bolts.

Remove the mounting bolts and carefully remove the clutch assembly. 

Remove the spline aligning tool and driven disc. 

Inspect the engine flywheel housing and flywheel. Refer to Section 08-00 . If flywheel is heat-checked or warped, refer to Section 03-00 for 
flywheel clutch surface machining. To replace flywheel or flywheel housing, 
refer to Section 03A-01 or Section 03B-01 .

Check condition of the transmission input shaft. Use a stone to dull 
sharp edges of the splines. If splines are worn excessively or notched, the 
clutch discs will not slide on the shaft. Replace the input shaft as required.

Inspect the pilot bearing. Refer to Section 08-00 . If required, remove 
the pilot bearing using a suitable puller.

Check wear on fingers of the clutch release lever, cross-shaft and 
cross-shaft bushings. Replace if any components are worn excessively.

 Installation 

Check pilot bearing and replace if necessary. Bearing must have press 
fit using Pilot Bearing Replacer T93T-7025-BH or T93T-7025-EH and Driver 
Handle T80T-4000-W and be installed flush for FD-1060 engine. 

Install two guide studs (3/8 x 16 x 2-inch) at the 11 and 1 o'clock 
positions. 

 CAUTION: Clutch will not function correctly if disc is installed backwards. Make 
sure the side marked pressure plate side faces the pressure plate, toward the 
rear of vehicle. 

Install the disc by inserting the aligning tool through the spline and 
into the pilot bearing. 

With the aligning tool still in place, carefully slide the clutch 
assembly over the aligning tool.

 CAUTION: Use only Ford approved mounting bolts. 

Install the clutch cover mounting bolts and lock washers hand-tight. 
Tighten in the following sequence to 48-61 Nm (35-45 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: DC0277A.gif]

Replace the guide studs with the two mounting bolts, and tighten to 
48-61 Nm (35-45 lb-ft).

 NOTE: Whenever an adjustment-free clutch assembly is removed, shipping bolts 
must be installed to prevent pressure plate from moving forward.

Remove four shipping bolts from clutch cover. Save shipping bolts.

[FIGURE: DC0028A.gif]

Check to make sure there is no visible gap between the spacer sleeve 
and the bolt head.

[FIGURE: C12985A.gif]

Remove the aligning tool. 

Apply a daub of Motorcraft Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B on both release bearing 
housing wear pad "ears."

Engage third gear. 

 NOTE: When the clutch housing is separated from the transmission assembly 
during a service procedure, the clutch housing must be reinstalled to the 
transmission assembly before the transmission assembly is installed into the 
vehicle. Refer to appropriate section in Group 07.

Lift the transmission to the vehicle with a suitable transmission jack 
such as Rotunda Heavy Duty Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or equivalent.

With the transmission input shaft aligned approximately with the 
flywheel pilot bearing, carefully guide the transmission input shaft into the 
release bearing sleeve bushing. Make sure the clutch release lever is in the 
horizontal position to clear release bearing, as shown. Slide the transmission 
forward to engage the guidepins and then further forward until the shaft 
touches the clutch disc hub. While applying a light forward pressure, rotate 
the transmission output shaft flange (or yoke) very slowly to engage the 
transmission input shaft into the clutch disc hub. Slide the transmission 
further, engaging the clutch housing top studs and then carefully locate the 
shaft into the flywheel pilot bearing. Make sure that the transmission input 
shaft has fully entered the clutch housing bore. 

 Clutch Release Lever 

[FIGURE: C9445B.gif]

Install clutch housing to flywheel housing bolts. Tighten to 48-61 Nm
 (35-45 lb-ft).

Connect the gearshift linkage. Refer to Section 07-06B .

Connect reverse gear switch and speedometer cable.

Set gear selector to NEUTRAL position. Grease the fork end, lever hole, 
washers and pin with Motorcraft Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K, or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B.

Install clutch slave cylinder. Refer to Section 08-02 .

Align the push rod and lever holes and install the retainer spring.

[FIGURE: C8187B.gif]

 NOTE: Adjustment-free clutch must be reset for clutch to self-adjust properly.

Depress clutch pedal in order to disengage the clutch assembly.

While the clutch assembly is disengaged, slide the indicator to the no 
wear position. This will allow the CAMs to reset themselves after installing 
the new disc. This step will require two technicians.

Connect the driveshaft. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Install the exhaust pipe.

Install clutch housing cover.

Check the adjust clutch.

For adjustment-free clutch, actuate the clutch assembly by depressing 
the clutch pedal five to ten times, releasing the clutch. Check release 
bearing travel. Release travel must be 11.9-12.5 mm (0.472-0.492 inch). Adjust 
clutch pedal free play with linkage. Refer to Section 08-02 .

 CAUTION: Clutch will not function correctly if disc is installed backwards. Make

Install the front disc in the engine housing.

Check the condition of the clutch intermediate plate and adapter ring.

 CAUTION: Make sure the side marked PRESSURE PLATE SIDE faces the clutch cover. 

 CAUTION: The drive straps must face the pressure plate. 

 NOTE: The four holes at the drive straps are the pilot holes for the adapter 
ring.

Install the intermediate plate and adapter ring over the guide studs.

 CAUTION: Clutch will not function correctly if disc is installed backwards. Make

ADJUSTMENTS

Clutch

 Internal Adjustment 

Because of the self-adjusting feature of the hydraulically actuated 
clutch assembly, no adjustments are required to compensate for clutch disc wear.

Clutch pedal and slave cylinder push rod adjustments may be required if 
part of the clutch or control system is replaced. Refer to Section 08-02 for 
procedure.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Clutch Control System

 Hydraulic 

The hydraulic clutch control system is comprised of the clutch pedal, 
the clutch master cylinder, a hydraulic line and the clutch slave cylinder.

================================================================================
PAGE 3518
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 08-02: Clutch Linkage, Hydraulic

1997 CF8000 and CFT8000 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Clutch Pedal 

The clutch is actuated (disengaged) by pressing the clutch pedal which 
is connected to the clutch master cylinder by means of a push rod. The clutch 
pedal range of motion is controlled by stop bolts installed in the cab 
bulkhead. These bolts are factory installed and should require no adjustment.

================================================================================
PAGE 3519
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 08-02: Clutch Linkage, Hydraulic

1997 CF8000 and CFT8000 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Clutch Master Cylinder 

The clutch master cylinder is located behind the hood adjacent to the 
foot brake control valve. 

The clutch master cylinder reservoir supplies the hydraulic fluid for 
the system. The fluid from the reservoir is fed to the area in front of the 
piston in the cylinder housing through the supply orifice. At rest (clutch 
engaged) position there is no pressure in the clutch master cylinder. 

When the clutch pedal is depressed, the piston is forced forward by the 
push rod that is attached to the clutch pedal. As the piston moves forward, 
the seal blocks the supply orifice and the hydraulic force is transmitted 
through the fluid line to actuate the slave cylinder and turn the clutch 
release shaft. 

When the clutch pedal is released, the clutch spring forces the piston 
back to the rest position. Because fluid return is slower than piston return, 
a mild vacuum is formed which forces the fluid that is behind the piston to 
bend the lip of the seal away from the cylinder wall and enter the chamber in 
front of the piston. This flow of liquid prevents the possible entry of air. 
The supply orifice from the reservoir keeps the cylinder filled at all times. 

The fluid reservoir is mounted to the clutch master cylinder housing. 
It is made of translucent plastic that permits instant fluid level checking 
without removing the filler cap.

================================================================================
PAGE 3520
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 08-02: Clutch Linkage, Hydraulic

1997 CF8000 and CFT8000 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Clutch Slave Cylinder

The clutch slave cylinder is installed on the transmission housing with 
a mounting bracket. 

The clutch slave cylinder is actuated by hydraulic force transmitted 
from the clutch master cylinder through the fluid lines. The hydraulic 
pressure drives the piston and push rod forward, actuating the clutch release 
mechanism. 

The clutch spring returns the piston to the rest position after the 
clutch pedal is released. The springs inside the clutch slave cylinder preload 
the release bearing, making sure the clutch slave cylinder adjusts 
automatically.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Clutch Pedal and Support

 Removal 

Remove the two nuts that retain the clutch master cylinder to the 
passenger compartment bulkhead. Secure the cylinder so that the hydraulic line 
remains attached and the cylinder cannot empty. 

Remove the spring clip and clevis pins from the brake and clutch pedal 
push rods and the two shaft spring clips from either end of the pedal shaft. 

Push the D-shaped end of the shaft out of the pedal box and remove the 
four flat and two wavy washers, both return springs, spring sleeves and the 
clutch and brake pedals. 

Thoroughly clean all components and discard the spring clips. Inspect 
the shaft for deep pits or grooves, and replace if required. 

 Installation 

Apply a light film of Motorcraft Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K 
or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B to the clutch and brake 
pedal bushings. 

Enter the D-shaped end of the shaft through the brake pedal side of the 
pedal box and fit a flat, a wavy, and a second flat washer on the shaft. 

Fit the brake pedal return spring in the locating slot above the pedal 
box center support shaft hole and insert the sleeve inside the spring. 

Align the brake pedal and push the shaft through its bushings, spring 
sleeve and the center support. 

Fit the clutch pedal return spring in the locating slot below the pedal 
box center support shaft hole and insert the sleeve inside the spring. Push 
the shaft through the sleeve. 

Align the clutch pedal making sure that the push rod seats in the 
recessed area of the piston and push the shaft through its bushings. 

Fit a flat, a wavy and a second flat washer on the shaft. Align and 
insert the D shape of the shaft in the corresponding D slot in the pedal box. 

Fit a new spring clip on either end of the shaft adjacent to the outer 
flatwashers making sure that the clips are positioned in their locating 
grooves in the shaft. 

Align the brake pedal push rod and the pedal. Fit the clevis pin and 
secure with a new spring clip. 

Align the clutch master cylinder with its push rod. Fit two new 
retaining nuts and tighten to 11-15 Nm (8-11 lb-ft).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Clutch Master Cylinder and Reservoir

 WARNING: BRAKE FLUID CONTAINS POLYGLYCOL ETHERS AND POLYGLYCOLS. AVOID CONTACT 
WITH EYES. WASH HANDS THOROUGHLY AFTER HANDLING. IF BRAKE FLUID CONTACTS EYES, 
FLUSH EYES WITH RUNNING WATER FOR 15 MINUTES. GET MEDICAL ATTENTION IF 
IRRITATION PERSISTS. IF TAKEN INTERNALLY, DRINK WATER AND INDUCE VOMITING. GET 
MEDICAL ATTENTION IMMEDIATELY. 

 CAUTION: Brake fluid is harmful to painted and plastic surfaces. If brake fluid 
is spilled onto a painted or plastic surface, immediately wash it with water. 

 Removal 

 CAUTION: Cap the fluid line to avoid possible fluid contamination. 

Disconnect the fluid line.

Drain fluid into a suitable container. Pump clutch pedal until all 
fluid is drained from the clutch master cylinder. 

Remove the two nuts that retain the clutch master cylinder to the 
bulkhead.

 CAUTION: Use care not to spill any fluid that may remain in the cylinder or 
reservoir. 

Withdraw the clutch master cylinder from the vehicle. To remove the 
reservoir from the master cylinder, refer to Clutch Master Cylinder in the 
Disassembly and Assembly portion of this section.

 Installation 

Position the clutch master cylinder on the bulkhead studs. Make sure 
that the clutch pedal push rod seats in the recessed portion of the cylinder 
piston. Install nuts and tighten to 11-15 Nm (8-11 lb-ft).

Install fluid line in clutch master cylinder and tighten to 17-19 Nm
 (12-14 lb-ft). 

Bleed the system. Refer to Clutch Hydraulic System Bleeding in the 
Adjustments portion of this section.

[FIGURE: C6621D.gif]

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Clutch Hydraulic Lines 

 WARNING: BRAKE FLUID CONTAINS POLYGLYCOL ETHERS AND POLYGLYCOLS. AVOID CONTACT 
WITH EYES. WASH HANDS THOROUGHLY AFTER HANDLING. IF BRAKE FLUID CONTACTS EYES, 
FLUSH EYES WITH RUNNING WATER FOR 15 MINUTES. GET MEDICAL ATTENTION IF 
IRRITATION PERSISTS. IF TAKEN INTERNALLY, DRINK WATER AND INDUCE VOMITING. GET 
MEDICAL ATTENTION IMMEDIATELY. 

 CAUTION: Brake fluid is harmful to painted and plastic surfaces. If brake fluid 
is spilled onto a painted or plastic surface, immediately wash it with water. 

 CAUTION: Hydraulic lines should always be replaced if inspection reveals cracks 
or other damage. 

 Removal 

 CAUTION: Plug the fluid ports to avoid possible contamination and fluid loss. 

Disconnect the line at the clutch master cylinder and slave cylinder. 

 CAUTION: Use care not to kink, bend or break any other lines or harnesses. 

Remove side rail tie straps and hydraulic line.

 Installation 

 CAUTION: Use care not to kink, break or bend any of the lines or harnesses. 

Position and secure the new fluid line to the side rail with tie straps. 

Install fluid line ends into their respective fluid ports and tighten 
to 17-19 Nm (12-14 lb-ft).

Bleed the system. Refer to Clutch Hydraulic System Bleeding in the 
Adjustments portion of this section.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Clutch Slave Cylinder

 WARNING: BRAKE FLUID CONTAINS POLYGLYCOL ETHERS AND POLYGLYCOLS. AVOID CONTACT 
WITH EYES. WASH HANDS THOROUGHLY AFTER HANDLING. IF BRAKE FLUID CONTACTS EYES,

IRRITATION PERSISTS. IF TAKEN INTERNALLY, DRINK WATER AND INDUCE VOMITING. GET

 CAUTION: Brake fluid is harmful to painted and plastic surfaces. If brake fluid 
is spilled onto a painted or plastic surface, immediately wash it with water. 

 Removal 

Remove retainer spring from push rod and the clutch release arm. 

Remove push rod from clutch release arm. 

Disconnect and plug fluid line. For non-synchronized transmission, 
remove return spring.

Remove cylinder to bracket retaining bolts. 

Remove cylinder from transmission bracket. 

Pump push rod several times to drain fluid from cylinder into a 
suitable container.

Plug cylinder port. 

 Installation 

Position cylinder on transmission mounting bracket, install spacers, 
lockwashers and bolts and tighten to 25-28 Nm (18-21 lb-ft). 
For non-synchronized transmission, install return spring and spacer.

Position cylinder push rod in slave cylinder and clutch release arm.

Install the retainer spring in push rod. 

Install fluid line connection to cylinder and tighten to 17-19 Nm
 (12-14 lb-ft).

Bleed system. Refer to Clutch Hydraulic System Bleeding in the 
Adjustments portion of this section.

For non-synchronized transmission, readjust clutch slave cylinder. 
Refer to Clutch Slave Cylinder, Non-Synchronized Transmission in the

ADJUSTMENTS

Clutch Pedal 

 Height 

Thread the upper stop to a distance of 8 mm (.314 inch) from bracket to 
pedal stop screw shoulder. This will produce 2-10 mm (.0787-.394 inch) of 
clutch pedal free play at the clutch pedal pad.

Thread the lower pedal stop to a distance of 3.1 mm (.122 inch) from 
nut to pedal stop screw shoulder.

Install pedal stop pad.

 Total Travel 

Total travel of the clutch pedal is limited by the upper and lower 
stops that are installed at the factory and should not need adjustment. When 
the pedal is fully depressed, it should not reach the engine compartment 
bulkhead. 

 Free Play 

 NOTE: The practice of using a ruler to measure free play from the pedal 
straight down to the floor board is not acceptable. This method does not take 
the arc of pedal travel into account and measures only the straight line 
distance and will always read less than the actual free play distance.

Using a suitable measuring tape, hook the end of the tape to the middle 
of the clutch pedal as shown in the following illustration. Pull the tape case 
back to the middle of the driver's seat so that it can be easily held in one 
hand and read for the initial measurement.

[FIGURE: DC0036A.gif]

Use the other hand to push on the clutch pedal (following the pedal 
arc), using no more than three pounds of force, and read the distance of free 
play travel on the measuring tape. The difference between initial and final 
measurement readings is free play travel which should be between 2-10 mm 
(0.0787-0.394 inch).

Adjust the upper clutch pedal stop if free play is not within 
specification.

[FIGURE: C10919D.gif]

 Non-Synchronized Transmission 

 NOTE: Refer to the following illustration for component identification.

Adjust the clutch free play at clutch slave cylinder rod as follows: 

Disconnect spring and loosen the smaller nut A. 

Manually unscrew the long nut B to remove the free play from the system 
(between the rod end and piston, and the release lever and bearing). 

Keeping nut B locked, turn nut A only to achieve a clearance between 
nut A and nut B of 2.7 mm (0.106-inch). A 2.7-mm (0.106 inch) gauge block is 
recommended for setting this clearance. 

Remove gauge block. Keeping nut A locked, tighten nut B until it 
contacts nut A. Tighten to 42-57 Nm (31-42 lb-ft). 

Install spring. Check free play clearance between the fork and release 
bearing for 1.19-1.70 mm (0.047-0.067-inch).

ADJUSTMENTS

Clutch Hydraulic System Bleeding 

System bleeding is performed to purge any air that may be in the 
hydraulic system and also to flush the system as it eliminates old fluid. 

System bleeding should be carried out as described below whenever 
service is are performed which require disconnecting any hydraulic system part 
or if the clutch pedal feels spongy.

 WARNING: BRAKE FLUID CONTAINS POLYGLYCOL ETHERS AND POLYGLYCOLS. AVOID CONTACT 
WITH EYES. WASH HANDS THOROUGHLY AFTER HANDLING. IF BRAKE FLUID CONTACTS EYES, 
FLUSH EYES WITH RUNNING WATER FOR 15 MINUTES. GET MEDICAL ATTENTION IF 
IRRITATION PERSISTS. IF TAKEN INTERNALLY, DRINK WATER AND INDUCE VOMITING. GET 
MEDICAL ATTENTION IMMEDIATELY. 

 CAUTION: Brake fluid is harmful to painted and plastic surfaces. If brake fluid 
is spilled onto a painted or plastic surface, immediately wash it with water. 

Remove clutch master cylinder reservoir filler cap. 

Fill fluid reservoir to specified level. 

Remove slave cylinder bleeder dust cover and install a hose over the 
bleeder nipple. Place the other end of the hose in an appropriate container. 
Position the container above the bleeder valve level. 

Slowly depress the clutch pedal five times. On the fifth pump, hold the 
pedal to the floor. 

With the pedal applied, loosen the bleeder valve to let the fluid flow 
into the container. 

 NOTE: Check if fluid flowing into container contains air bubbles (aeration). 
If fluid does show signs of aeration, repeat Steps 4 and 5 until fluid runs 
clear with no signs of bubbles. 

Close bleeder valve and then release clutch pedal.

 CAUTION: Do not overtighten. 

Tighten bleeder valve to 10-15 Nm (7-11 lb-ft). Remove 
hose and install bleeder dust cover. 

Check reservoir fluid level. Fill to specified level with Ford High 
Performance DOT 3 Brake Fluid C6AZ-19542-AA or DOT-3 equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESA-M6C25-A. Do not overfill.

================================================================================
PAGE 3535
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 08-02: Clutch Linkage, Hydraulic

1997 CF8000 and CFT8000 Workshop Manual

ADJUSTMENTS

Fluid Level

The clutch (reservoir) system works in reverse to a brake system. As 
the clutch wears, the master cylinder reservoir fills up rather than goes 
down. The master cylinder needs to be filled to the MIN. level for a new 
clutch or maintained between the MIN. and MAX. levels. This will make sure 
that when the cab is tilted, fluid will not leak out the air vent hole in the 
reservoir cap. 

For a new clutch it is recommended that the fluid level be filled to 
the top of the MIN. mark using Ford High Performance DOT 3 Brake Fluid 
C6AZ-19542-AA or DOT 3 equivalent meeting Ford Specification ESA-M6C25-A. Do 
not overfill.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Exhaust Brake 

An exhaust brake is an auxiliary braking system that attaches to the 
engine exhaust system. The effect of the exhaust brake is to make the engine 
act as a compressor. The exhaust brake functions by partially closing off the 
exhaust system from the engine exhaust manifolds, creating an increase in 
exhaust back pressure.

During vehicle deceleration, the engine must turn against the back 
pressure and this creates a braking effect on the driving wheels. 

The exhaust brake system is composed of the following components: 

dash-mounted control switch 

dash-mounted indicator light 

accelerator switch 

clutch switch 

pneumatic solenoid control valve 

actuating cylinder 

exhaust brake body 

The following guidelines must be followed when installing an exhaust 
brake on Ford diesel engines or the warranty will be voided. 

Maximum allowable exhaust back pressure is 310 kPa (45 psi) at 10 
percent above engine rated speed. 

Maximum allowable exhaust back pressure while exhaust brake is engaged 
is as follows:

 MAXIMUM ALLOWABLE EXHAUST BACK PRESSURE 

Engine

RPM

Maximum

Pressure

FD-1060

2750

240 kPa

(35 psi)

FD-1460

2530

240 kPa

(35 psi)

The effect of an exhaust brake is not felt as a normal braking force as 
with service brakes, but is more of a gradual decelerating effect, as if the 
service brakes were lightly applied. 

The exhaust brake is used to aid the engine and the service brakes in 
slowing the vehicle, reducing service brake wear. 

 Exhaust Brake 

[FIGURE: U2412C.gif]

With the dash-mounted switch on, accelerator pedal released and the 
clutch pedal in the UP (clutch engaged) position, the exhaust brake will be 
activated. The accelerator and clutch switches are closed and current is 
applied to the control valve. The control valve allows system air pressure to 
be applied to the actuating cylinder, which shifts the brake body butterfly 
valve to the closed position.

When the accelerator pedal or clutch pedal is pressed, the switch will 
open and interrupt current to the control valve. The control valve will stop 
air pressure from going to the actuating cylinder, and will exhaust existing 
air from the cylinder. The return spring in the actuating cylinder will then 
open the exhaust brake butterfly valve. 

When the exhaust brake switch is in the ON position, the exhaust brake 
unit will operate whenever the following conditions are met: 

The clutch pedal must be in the UP (clutch engaged) position. 

The accelerator pedal must be in the idle position. 

The vehicle air supply system must be up to operating pressure.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Exhaust System

 Inspection and Verification 

Exhaust system performance complaints such as excessive back pressure 
are usually noticeable by their effect on engine performance. 

Other malfunctioning components may have similar effects on engine 
performance and be characterized by the same symptoms or complaints. It is 
necessary to refer to the Powertrain Control/Emissions Diagnosis Manual
 when attempting to diagnose this type of problem. 

For general exhaust system complaints, refer to the symptom chart in 
this section. 

 Exhaust Leakage or Noise 

Exhaust fumes in the cab or excessive exhaust noise may be due to 
exhaust system leakage. Inspect the exhaust system and refer to the symptom 
chart and the appropriate pinpoint tests in this section.

 Exhaust Brake, Preliminary Inspection 

 CAUTION: Never operate the exhaust brake if engine condition is in doubt. Do not 
operate the vehicle if the exhaust brake is stuck in the ON position or engine 
damage may result. 

Before testing the operation of the exhaust brake:

Inspect the exhaust system for leaks. 

The engine must be fully warmed up. 

The vehicle air system must be up to full operating pressure.

Follow standard back pressure test procedures if a chassis dynamometer 
is available. A chassis dynamometer is the preferred and most accurate method 
of achieving rated speed and load. If a chassis dynamometer is NOT available, 
use the following procedure:

Install a pressure gauge to the back pressure test port found on either 
the muffler-catalytic converter inlet pipe near the turbocharger outlet or the 
inlet side of the muffler-catalytic converter assembly. Use a gauge that has 
at least 3 percent of full scale accuracy between 0 and 10 in-Hg (140 in-H 2 
O).

If the vehicle does not have a tachometer, install a temporary one on 
the engine.

Run engine until it is warmed up and at normal operating temperatures.

Select a location and gear where an acceleration to wide-open throttle 
(WOT) can be accomplished safely.

Drive vehicle at wide-open throttle and peak engine power. If possible, 
drive vehicle up a long hill or load vehicle to the maximum gross vehicle 
weight to attain maximum engine load and speed. Record the maximum exhaust 
back pressure when engine is at maximum RPM and load.

Exhaust Brake Assembly 

 Removal

 Installation 

 CAUTION: The exhaust brake body must be installed in a specific direction. Make

Connect the air line to the cylinder.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Actuating Cylinder 

 Removal 

Disconnect the air line from the actuating cylinder. 

Using a suitable drift, tap the roll pin from the actuating cylinder 
pivot pin bushing. Remove the bushing from the pivot pin. 

[FIGURE: U21651A.gif]

Tap the roll pin from the bushing on the end of the exhaust valve lever 
pin. Remove the bushing from the pin. 

 CAUTION: Actuating cylinder is under spring pressure. Use care when removing. 

Remove the actuating cylinder from the mounting bracket. 

 Installation 

Position the actuating cylinder on the mounting bracket pivot pin and 
on the exhaust valve lever pin. 

Position the bushings on the two pins, lining up the roll pin holes. 

Tap the roll pins through the bushings and the pins. 

Connect the air line.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Actuating Cylinder 

 Disassembly 

Mount the air supply end of the cylinder in a vise, using care to 
prevent cylinder damage. 

Measure and record the assembled length of the cylinder. 

Loosen the jam nut and remove the nut and clevis from the end of the 
cylinder push rod. 

Using a pair of Channel Lock® pliers, loosen the 
center portion of the cylinder from the air supply end of the cylinder. 

Remove the cylinder from the vise and remove the air supply end of the 
cylinder from the end of the cylinder. 

Remove the push rod, springs, spring retainer and push rod locator from 
the cylinder. Remove the O-ring from the air supply end of the cylinder. 

 Assembly 

Lubricate seals and O-rings with Silicone Lubricant COAZ-19553-AA or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESR-M13P4-A. 

Install the push rod, springs, spring retainer and push rod locator in 
the cylinder. Install the O-ring in the air supply end of the cylinder. 

Install the air supply end of the cylinder on the cylinder and push rod 
assembly.

 CAUTION: Use care not to overtighten the cylinder and compress to O-ring. 

Position the cylinder in a vise, and tighten the cylinder to the 
cylinder air supply end until it contacts the O-ring. Then tighten the 
cylinder slightly more.

Install the jam nut on the push rod and install the clevis on the push 
rod. Position the clevis and push rod so that the length of the assembled 
actuating cylinder and push rod equals the dimension recorded in Step 2 of the 
disassembly procedure. Tighten the jam nut against the clevis.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel System Service

The fuel system supply components are the most important components in 
the fuel system. The fuel charging components cannot operate efficiently 
unless each component in the fuel system functions correctly.

Section 03A-04A and Section 10-01 cover testing and adjustment 
procedures relating directly to specific vehicle fuel supply problem 
resolutions.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Engine Air Cleaner

 WARNING: DO NOT SMOKE OR CARRY LIGHTED TOBACCO OR OPEN FLAME OF ANY TYPE WHEN

Cleaning the air cleaner or crankcase ventilation filter elements is 
not recommended. They should be replaced at the specified mileage intervals.

air. Wipe the air cleaner body and cover dry if a solvent is used. Inspect the 
air cleaner body and cover for distortion or damage at the gasket mating 
surfaces. Replace cover or air cleaner element body if they are damaged beyond 
service.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel Injected Engines

Fuel from the tank (under suction) is routed to the fuel block located 
on the engine. From the fuel block the fuel goes through a sediment bowl and 
lift pump which is mounted on the side of the fuel injection pump. After going 
through the lift pump the fuel is pumped under pressure through the fuel 
filter/water separator, and past the primer pump assembly mounted on the side 
of the intake manifold. Once the fuel is filtered it goes to the fuel gallery 
of the fuel injection pump.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel Tank Filler Cap

 WARNING: USE OF AN AFTERMARKET FUEL FILLER CAP OTHER THAN A SPECIFIED SERVICE 
PART OR THE EQUIVALENT IS NOT RECOMMENDED AND CAN RESULT IN DAMAGE TO THE FUEL 
SYSTEM. IT CAN ALSO CAUSE IMPROPER SYSTEM OPERATION DUE TO PRESSURE OR VACUUM 
BUILDUP, WHICH CAN COMPROMISE THE PERFORMANCE OF THE FUEL SYSTEM IN THE EVENT 
OF A COLLISION. 

The fuel tank filler cap is sealed and of the threaded screw-on, 
screw-off type.

 NOTE: Use of an aftermarket fuel tank filler cap other than an authorized 
Ford service part can result in damage to the fuel tank if not properly 
designed and manufactured.

PAGE 3557
================================================================================

Section 10-01: Fuel Tank, Filters, Tubes and Fuel Pump, Diesel Engine

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel Selector Valve — Vehicles with Dual Tanks Only

Some vehicles are equipped with dual fuel tanks. The fuel crossover 
tube which extends from tank to tank is a balance tube for the dual tanks and 
has a fuel selector valve on each end. These valves must always be in the ON 
(open) position during vehicle operation. The fuel is drawn from the left tank 
(normally) and returned to the right tank. If the valves on one or both ends 
are closed, the return fuel will pressurize the right-hand tank. In extreme 
cases, the fuel tank ends can expand or appear to bulge.

================================================================================
PAGE 3558
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 10-01: Fuel Tank, Filters, Tubes and Fuel Pump, Diesel Engine

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel Filter, In-Line

The in-line fuel filter provides filtration to protect the small 
metering orifices of the fuel injector nozzles. The fuel filter assembly is 
located on the left frame rail.

 NOTE: The fuel filter should be changed at 24,000 km (15,000 miles) or 
15-month intervals, and each time a fuel tank sending unit and pump is replaced.

If the fuel tank is replaced, or the fuel system is contaminated with 
particles, replace the fuel filter. If contamination of fuel is suspected, 
refill tank with clean fuel, not fuel from fuel tanks.

================================================================================
PAGE 3559
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 10-01: Fuel Tank, Filters, Tubes and Fuel Pump, Diesel Engine

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel/Water Separator

Filtration and separation of water from the fuel is important for 
trouble-free operation and long life of the fuel system. Some of the 
clearances between the fuel and injection pump parts are very close. For this 
reason, the parts can easily be damaged by corrosion, contaminants, or loss of 
the lubricating film of fuel. 

Be sure to use the correct element. The element has a valve that must 
be opened daily to drain the collected water.

 Fuel/Water Separator, Typical 

[FIGURE: V10280A.gif]

A dual fuel/water separator-filter adapter provides additional 
filtering capacity. The fuel flows through the adapter to a larger combination 
fuel/water separator-filter, and back to the fuel filter for final filtering.

Regular maintenance, including draining moisture from the fuel/water 
separator-filter and supply tanks, is essential to keep water out of the fuel.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel Tubes

 WARNING: DISCONNECT THE BATTERY GROUND CABLES FROM BOTH BATTERIES PRIOR TO 
SERVICING THE FUEL SYSTEM, OR BODILY INJURY AND VEHICLE DAMAGE DUE TO POSSIBLE 
ELECTRICAL SPARKING AND POSSIBLE FIRE HAZARD MAY OCCUR. 

 WARNING: DO NOT SMOKE, CARRY LIGHTED TOBACCO OR AN OPEN FLAME OF ANY TYPE WHEN 
WORKING ON OR NEAR ANY FUEL-RELATED COMPONENT. HIGHLY FLAMMABLE MIXTURES ARE 
ALWAYS PRESENT AND CAN BE IGNITED, RESULTING IN POSSIBLE PERSONAL INJURY. 

 CAUTION: Use only Ford Motor Company approved fuel tubes and O-rings for service 
or replacement because substitute materials can leak or deteriorate rapidly 
from contact with fuel. Never substitute hose clamps for approved fittings on 
nylon fuel tubes as they can pull loose because of the fuel pressure. 

The fuel tubes used on the diesel engine are mostly of stainless steel 
tubing and flexible composite tubing or shielded with steel braid.

Keep the front end of the vehicle higher than the rear when servicing 
fuel tubes. If the fuel tubes are disconnected with the front of the vehicle 
lower than the rear, fuel can syphon out through the tubes.

 Organizer Assembly 

Fuel tubes on some vehicles are part of an organizer assembly.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel Tank Sending Unit, Diesel

The fuel tank level sending unit consists of a variable resistor 
(potentiometer) which is attached to a float in the fuel tank and varies 
according to fuel level in the tank. When the fuel level is low, resistance in 
the sending unit is high and allows only a low current to flow through the 
indicator gauge windings, causing the pointer to move a short distance. When 
the fuel level is high, the resistance in the sending unit is low and allows a 
higher current flow, causing the pointer to move a greater distance.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Fuel Filling

 WARNING: FUEL MAY BE UNDER PRESSURE. ALWAYS REMOVE THE FUEL CAP CAREFULLY AND 
SLOWLY. IF THE CAP IS VENTING FUEL OR A HISSING SOUND IS HEARD, WAIT UNTIL THE

 CAUTION: The fuel crossover tube (tank to tank) is a balance tube for the dual 
tanks and has a shutoff valve on both ends. 

You can prevent excessive condensation in the fuel tank by keeping it 
over half full.

 Installation 

 CAUTION: Use a suitable jack to support tank during installation. 

If fuel tank has been replaced, install fuel tank sending unit, a new 
gasket, rollover vent and vent tube on tank. Install shutoff valve assembly, 
if so equipped. Position new insulating strips on fuel tank mounting bracket. 
Install drain plug in fuel tank. 

Install fuel tank on mounting brackets. 

Install retaining straps, but do not tighten mounting bolts. Align 
tank. Make sure insulators are properly centered under straps and brackets. 
Tighten retaining strap mounting bolts carefully to avoid crushing fuel tank. 

Connect fuel crossover tube to tank. Connect fuel gauge sending unit 
wire. 

Connect fuel supply and return tubes. 

On a vehicle with dual fuel tanks, connect crossover tube connecting 
tanks. 

Fill tank with fuel and install filler cap.

Connect battery ground cable. Start engine and check for leaks.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Fuel Tank Support Straps

 Removal 

Support the fuel tank using a suitable jack before removing one or both 
fuel tank straps.

Remove the lower fuel tank retaining strap nut(s).

 NOTE: When removing upper fuel tank strap, use caution not to let holding 
bolt fall out of frame hole. If fuel tank strap bolt falls out of frame hole, 
use a length of wire to pull strap bolt back into position.

Remove the upper fuel tank retaining strap nut(s).

Remove the strap(s) from the fuel tank.

If a new strap(s) is being installed, the rubber insulator must be 
removed from the tank strap(s) for installation of the new strap(s).

 Installation 

If a new strap(s) is being installed, position rubber insulator(s) to 
strap.

Position fuel tank strap(s) to fuel tank.

Install upper strap(s) stud retaining nut and hand-tighten.

Install lower strap(s) stud retaining nut and hand-tighten.

Make sure strap(s) is properly positioned and tighten upper and lower 
strap(s) stud nuts to specification.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Sending Unit, Fuel Tank

 Removal 

Apply parking brake and disconnect battery ground cable.

Disconnect wiring from fuel gauge sending unit.

Remove five bolts that hold sending unit. Lift assembly out of fuel 
tank, maneuvering float assembly to avoid damage. Remove and discard gasket.

 Installation 

To install the sending unit, insert float assembly and position by 
lining up holes. Use new gasket.

Install five bolts and wiring.

Connect battery ground cable.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Fuel Tube Organizer

 Removal 

Either single tubes and hoses can be removed from the organizer 
assemblies or the entire assembly can be removed.

Disconnect the battery ground cable.

To remove a single tube or hose, snap open the organizer-to-frame clips.

Disconnect tube or hose ends, if necessary.

Snap tube or hose out of organizer core and remove. It may be necessary 
to remove some other tubes to remove one.

To remove the entire assembly, use the following procedure.

Disconnect all tubes, hoses and electrical connections going through 
the organizer, if necessary.

Remove nuts retaining the organizer assembly to the frame.

Remove the fuel tube organizer assembly.

 Installation 

Position fuel tube organizer assembly for installation on frame.

Install organizer clip nuts and tighten to 8-10 Nm 
(71-89 lb-in).

Connect all hoses, tubes and wires.

Connect the battery ground cable.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Fuel Tubes, Flexible Hose 

Flexible fuel tubes must be serviced with bulk hose and reusable swivel 
sockets. The appropriate bulk hose and socket replacements must satisfy SAE 
J1402 requirements. Ford trucks use Aeroquip hose and sockets. Use the 
conversion chart. 

 BULK HOSE CONVERSION CHART

Hose Assembly Base

Bulk Hose No. (Aeroquip Part Numbers)

Socket Part No. (Aeroquip Part Numbers)

2C037

FC350-06

401-6S

2C038

FC350-08

401-8S

2C039

FC350-10

401-10S

 Removal 

Disconnect fuel tubes at both ends. If removing crossover tube, shut 
off valves. Remove units from holding clips and remove from truck. 

Slide looms, if used, off tubes. Replace all worn or damaged parts. 

 Installation 

Use bulk hose, according to above chart, as determined from hose 
assembly base numbers shown in service manual. 

 NOTE: For long hose lengths, it may be preferable to place the hose in the 
vise and screw socket until tight. Then back off one-quarter turn. 

Cut hose square with either a cut-off wheel or fine-toothed hacksaw. 

Put socket in vise. Screw hose counterclockwise into socket until tight 
and back off one-quarter turn. 

Thoroughly lubricate nipple threads and inside of hose with heavy oil 
or hose assembly lubrication. 

Screw nipple clockwise into socket and hose, leaving 1/32-inch to 
1/16-inch clearance between nipple hex and socket. 

Clean hose assembly by blowing out with clean compressed air. Then 
rinse inside of hose assembly with diesel fuel. 

Install connecting hoses and clamps, if required, on fuel tubes. 
Position lines in clips on vehicle. Tighten connecting hose clamps, if so 
equipped.

Fuel Return System

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Fuel Tubes, Filter and Water Separator 

With the engine stopped, examine the fuel tube connections for wetness, 
washed or stained areas that might indicate a fuel leak. Start the engine and 
observe all the connections for fuel seepage. Tighten or replace fuel tubes as 
necessary. 

Drain the water reservoir by turning valve to open drain. The 
filter/water separator is located on the LH side of the engine. After water 
has been drained, close valve. Refer to Section 03A-04A for service 
procedures.

PAGE 3573
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 10-01: Fuel Tank, Filters, Tubes and Fuel Pump, Diesel Engine

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Fuel Sediment Bowl and Filter

On tanks equipped with check ball, check drain valves. Remove 1/8 NPT 
plug and dislodge check ball with small Allen-head wrench. Contents of tank 
will slowly drain, allowing water and sediment to escape. On tanks equipped 
with 1/2 NPT drain plugs, first reduce fuel level by using Rotunda Fuel 
Storage Tanker (Diesel) 164-R3203 or equivalent on the fuel hose, or by 
siphoning fuel. After fuel is reduced to a residual amount, the drain plug can 
be removed to allow water or sediment to escape. 

Check drainage for sediment. If sediment is very obvious, remove tank 
and thoroughly clean using an approved steam cleaner.

tube is required to replace the damaged section.

Section 10-02: Accelerator Pedal and Linkage

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Accelerator Pedal and Linkage

The throttle is controlled by accelerator cables, rods, and a pedal 
assembly. The accelerator pedal must travel smoothly from the idle to the 
wide-open throttle positions. Hesitation on return and/or prevention of return 
to the idle position must not occur. Surrounding components, such as wiring, 
hoses, sound insulator and floor covering, must not contact any moving member 
of the accelerator linkage or the accelerator pedal assembly.

================================================================================
PAGE 3579
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 10-02: Accelerator Pedal and Linkage

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Accelerator Pedal and Linkage

 Inspection and Verification 

 WARNING: SURROUNDING ENGINE COMPARTMENT COMPONENTS, SUCH AS WIRING OR HOSES, 
MUST NOT CONTACT ANY MOVING MEMBER OF THE ACCELERATOR CONTROLS. CHECK ALL 
VEHICLES FOR RETURN TO IDLE. PERCEPTIBLE HESITATION OR PREVENTION OF RETURN TO 
IDLE POSITION MUST NOT OCCUR DURING SLOW REMOVAL OF THE FOOT FROM THE 
ACCELERATOR PEDAL AND SHAFT, STARTING AT THE FULLY DEPRESSED, WIDE-OPEN 
THROTTLE (WOT) POSITION. 

Verify the customer's concerns by inspecting the condition. Check for 
any resistance in accelerator pedal action. Inspect the accelerator pedal and 
linkage if a high engine idle speed condition exists. After inspection and 
verification, refer to the symptom chart for the condition, and perform the 
appropriate action to correct the condition.

Operate the accelerator pedal and linkage by hand, observing and 
feeling that the full range of travel is not restricted by wiring, hoses, dash 
panel insulation, carpet, mat, padding or any other components.

 Symptom Chart — Accelerator Pedal To Throttle Body 

 ACCELERATOR PEDAL TO THROTTLE BODY 

Condition

Possible Source

Action

Accelerator Pedal Is Hard to Push Down or Has a Rough/Raspy or Sticky 
Feel

Accelerator cable and spring contacting surrounding parts.

DISCONNECT the accelerator cable from the throttle body lever. If 
vehicle is equipped with hand throttle, DISCONNECT the hand throttle cable 
from the accelerator cable. VERIFY that the disconnected end of the 
accelerator cable or its spring does not come into contact with any of the 
surrounding parts.

Insulation or trim interferes with pedal travel.

OPERATE the accelerator pedal and shaft by hand, observing and feeling 
that the full pedal range of travel is not restricted by the dash panel 
insulator or carpet/mat/padding. If full pedal travel to wide-open throttle is 
restricted, ADJUST insulator and/or trim items as required.

Internal components other than cable not working properly.

OPERATE the accelerator pedal and shaft by foot.

Cable is worn.

If the condition reoccurs (making sure disconnected end of accelerator 
cable has not come into contact with anything), CHECK the accelerator pedal 
and shaft for free operation. If the pedal operation is free, REPLACE the 
accelerator cable.

High Engine Idle Speed

Internal components interacting improperly.

If the accelerator cable ball socket extends beyond the throttle lever 
ball stud, REFER to the throttle body diagnosis procedures in the appropriate 
section in the Powertrain Control/Emissions Diagnosis Manual. 

Component, trim or insulation interference.

If the socket does not extend beyond the stud, CHECK the accelerator 
pedal and shaft for free operation (free from carpet, mats, wiring, etc., 
contact). If the pedal operation is free, REPLACE the accelerator cable.

ADJUSTMENTS

Accelerator Cable 

 WARNING: SURROUNDING ENGINE COMPARTMENT COMPONENTS, SUCH AS WIRING OR HOSES, 
MUST NOT CONTACT ANY MOVING MEMBER OF THE ACCELERATOR CONTROLS. CHECK ALL 
VEHICLES FOR RETURN TO IDLE. PERCEPTIBLE HESITATION OR PREVENTION OF RETURN TO 
THE IDLE POSITION MUST NOT OCCUR DURING SLOW REMOVAL OF THE FOOT FROM THE 
ACCELERATOR PEDAL AND SHAFT, STARTING AT THE FULLY DEPRESSED, WIDE-OPEN 
THROTTLE (WOT) POSITION. 

Install throttle control cable assembly as shown in main views of 
illustrations under Removal and Installation . 

After inserting threaded cable end through throttle control cable 
bracket, install adjusting nut but do not tighten. 

At the engine, hold pump lever against wide-open throttle stop-bolt, 
while an assistant holds pedal lightly against the floor. 

Adjust turnbuckle on rod assembly until rod extends 0-2 mm (0-3/32 inch).

Tighten jam nut to 9-11 Nm (80-97 lb-in).

With engine running, depress accelerator pedal to its fullest travel 
and verify that wide-open throttle (WOT) can be achieved. From wide-open 
throttle, slowly release pedal to idle. The pedal must return completely from 
wide-open throttle position to idle position without any indication of drag or 
binding. A "slow release" means movement no faster than approximately two 
seconds per inch at a point 25.4 mm (1 inch) from top of pedal.

Accelerator Cable, Hand

 WARNING: SURROUNDING ENGINE COMPARTMENT COMPONENTS, SUCH AS WIRING OR HOSES,

1997 Cargo

Section 11-00: Steering System, Service

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Steering System

 Inspection and Verification 

The procedure used to diagnose a steering system condition must be 
systematic and thorough. Short cuts or a hit-or-miss approach will result in a 
misdiagnosis and can cause unnecessary repairs and customer comebacks.

The data sheet included in this section ensures a thorough and 
systematic procedure. The sheet must be completely filled in and the results 
evaluated before any repair is made.

The data sheet begins with a description of the customer concern. 
Interview the driver whenever possible. Use the Description of Common Steering 
System Conditions in this section to properly label the condition and then 
enter the driver's description of what, when, where and how on the data sheet.

The Vehicle Information portion of the data sheet includes items that 
must be noted during a vehicle inspection and road test. Entries in the test 
results are specifically for the power steering system tests. As each test is 
performed, the test data is entered on the sheet. A procedure for this test 
sequence is included in this section.

With a completed data sheet, a complete evaluation of the steering 
system can be made. If a test result is not within the acceptance standards, 
the pinpoint tests can be used to determine the correct service. Items listed 
under Vehicle Information can be used in the symptom charts to isolate a 
concern and make the necessary service. After service, the final step in a 
systematic approach to diagnosis is a road test to verify that the customer 
concern has been resolved.

 Description of Common Steering System Conditions 

A customer will use a wide variety of terms to describe a steering 
condition. The following description of common steering system conditions is 
intended to establish a common terminology between a customer's description of 
a condition and the terms used in the symptom charts and test procedures.

Wander is described as the vehicle not tracking properly on the road 
surface. The vehicle tends to drift from side to side. Continual correction is 
required to keep the vehicle on the road.

The customer may describe wander in the following ways:

squirrelly

continually correcting

constantly fighting the wheel

can't hold it on the road

all over the road

loose steering

hard to steer

To determine if wander is present, drive the vehicle on a flat, 
straight road with no traffic and carefully release the steering wheel. If the 
vehicle has a wander condition, the vehicle will tend to drift from 
side-to-side. Refer to Wander in the Symptom Chart for possible causes.

Pulling is a term used to describe a constant movement of the vehicle 
in one direction.

The driver may describe pulling in the following ways:

won't track

pushes to one side

wanders

drives one way

To determine if a pull condition exists, drive the vehicle on a 
straight, flat road with no traffic. Carefully release the steering wheel. If 
the vehicle tracks to one side, a pull condition exists. Refer to Pulls in the 
symptom chart for possible causes.

Binding is an increase in steering wheel effort that is momentary or 
intermittent.

The driver may describe binding in the following ways:

high spot

hangs up

locks up

catches when turning

seizes

intermittent loss of power steering or power assist

Binding can be the result of either a mechanical or hydraulic system 
problem with steering components. A mechanical bind will occur at the same 
position on the steering wheel while turning. A bind caused by a hydraulic 
system problem will occur randomly. Refer to Binding, Uneven or Intermittently 
Hard Steering in Symptom Chart for possible causes.

No return or poor returnability is used to describe the poor return of 
the steering wheel to center after a turn or steering correction is completed.

The driver may describe poor returnability in the following ways:

the wheel won't come back

hangs up in turns

wheel sticks

steering does not return

Refer to Poor Returnability in Symptom Chart for possible causes.

Excessive steering effort/hard steering is experienced when steering 
wheel effort exceeds 18-22 pounds measured at the steering wheel rim. Hard 
steering can remain constant through the full turn or occur near the end of a 
turn. Do not confuse hard steering with binding.

The driver may describe hard steering in the following ways:

no power assist

steers like a manual gear

won't turn all the way

hard steering

Hard steering can result from either hydraulic or mechanical problems. 
A complete mechanical and power steering diagnosis is necessary to determine 
the cause. It is extremely important to know if the driver complaint occurs 
during driving or during very slow or static park maneuvers. Refer to 
Excessive Steering Effort in Symptom Chart for possible causes.

Excessive free play or unresponsive motion is a condition in which 
there is too much steering wheel movement before the tires move. A small 
amount of free play is considered normal.

The driver may describe free play in the following ways:

too much slop in the wheel

too much backlash

slack in the wheel

Free play is normally a function of looseness in the steering linkage. 
Refer to Excessive Free Play or Unresponsive Motion in Symptom 
Chart for possible causes.

Shimmy is a shake or vibration of the front tires that is transmitted 
through the steering wheel.

The driver may describe shimmy in the following ways:

steering wheel shake

cab shakes

steering wheel chatter

Typically, once something triggers a shimmy condition, it is sustained 
until the driver does something (such as slow down) to dampen out the 
condition. Refer to Shimmy in Symptom Chart for possible causes.

Steering wheel kick is felt when the road wheels hit a bump that the 
steering wheel reacts to. The kick is usually dampened out quickly.

Some level of steering wheel kick is normal when operating the vehicle 
on poor roads. Excessive wheel kick on normal roads is generally caused by 
out-of-balance tires, excessive wheel runout or worn shock absorbers. Refer to 
 Section 00-04 for tire and wheel inspection procedures or to Section 04-00 for 
suspension component inspection procedures.

The driver may describe steering wheel kick in the following ways:

kickback

backlash

bump steer

Refer to Steering Wheel Kick in Symptom Chart ssible causes.

 NOTE: A power steering system should not generate excessive noise in normal 
highway driving and typical maneuvering of a moving vehicle. Noise is normally 
accompanied by poor steering performance if caused by the steering system. In 
some cases, the noise heard by the driver is not caused by the steering 
system. 

Noise in the steering system can come from any number of components. 
Hydraulic system noise can be caused by fluid flow. Metallic or grinding 
noises come from component parts.

The driver may describe noise in the following ways:

growls

swishes

pops when steering

moans/drums

Some noise of an acceptable level is common in all systems, and should 
not be interpreted as a system failure or near failure. High-pressure and 
high-efficiency systems are prone to some noise due to severe operating 
conditions. 

Increased noise may occur during such operating conditions as 
stationary vehicle steering at abnormally high or low engine speed with 
maximum axle loads, or during a rapid steering maneuver, and are considered 
normal for the additional system work requirements.

When noise is present, it must first be determined if it is a 
mechanical or hydraulic noise. Most mechanical noises are a result of 
looseness or wear in components. Hydraulic noise will normally be associated 
with problems in pump flow, such as cavitation or low fluid levels. Refer to 
the Steering System Noise Symptom Chart ssible causes.

External leakage — The actual source of external 
leakage may be difficult to locate because of visual obstruction by other 
components, fan blast, road grime and the fact that fluid tends to run and 
drip from the lowest point, which may not be close to the leakage source. Some 
leakage may only occur with the engine off while other leakage may require 
pressure. The system may have to be cleaned and dried to find the source. The 
source of the leak needs to be found before removing or changing parts.

The driver may describe external leakage in the following ways:

loss of steering fluid

addition of fluid to reservoir continually required

oil on components

oil puddle under vehicle after being parked

leaks at gear box

Refer to External Oil Leakage — Steering Gear or 
External Oil Leakage — Power Steering Pump in Symptom Chart 
for possible causes.

 Steering System Test Cycle 

If a standard road test does not verify a steering system condition, 
the following road test can be used to diagnose and resolve customer concerns 
about binds, hard steering or intermittent loss of power assist.

 NOTE: The best place to drive is a large asphalt or concrete parking lot that 
has sufficient space to conduct the maneuvers.

Move vehicle to test drive site. Place wheels straight ahead, place 
transmission in neutral and engage parking brake. Do not test with foot on the 
service brake.

Check fluid level and note level on dipstick.

Start engine and run at idle speed for 3-5 minutes. 

Shut down engine and note fluid level. If oil level increases, there is 
an air pocket trapped in the steering gear. Air can be sucked into the system 
through cracks in the hoses, loose clamps or loose fittings on the inlet side 
of the pump.

Start engine. With engine at idle speed, slowly rotate steering wheel 
to right and left between the axle stops. Increase speed of steering wheel 
rotation as rapidly as possible and repeat.

Increase engine rpm to 2000 and repeat. Note any differences.

Disengage parking brake and put vehicle into gear. With engine at as 
low a speed as possible, move vehicle in a tight figure eight.

Repeat test if space permits with engine at 1100-1500 rpm. Depending on 
the gear ratio and type of transmission, the figure eight may become larger.

Note anything unusual felt in the steering wheel and compare with the 
information provided by the driver. This test cycle will detect many of the 
different types of steering concerns.

If air in the system is suspected, bleed system, add fluid and drive 
vehicle again. Determine if steering performance feels different. Concern may 
have been air in the system. Whatever the results, the total Power Steering 
System Test Sequence should be run to ensure that the system is working 
properly.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

System Diagnostic Tips

 Importance of Proper Fan Clutch Operation 

On a vehicle equipped with an on-off fan clutch, a duty cycle used by 
the customer that has many slow-speed steering maneuvers at low ambient 
temperatures can cause excessive system temperatures. Fan clutch operation is 
controlled by coolant water temperature. When ambient temperature is cool, and 
vehicle speed is slow, the fan clutch does not engage and air is not 
circulated around the reservoir, plumbing and steering gear. If the vehicle is 
run at these conditions for an extended time period, the power steering system 
can overheat, reducing pump output flow, damaging the seals in the pump and 
steering gear, and causing excessive internal leakage. Continued operation at 
elevated temperatures can damage the steering gear relief valve spring, 
causing a reduction in output pressure. The fluid temperatures can be reduced 
by addition of a power steering cooler. Check fan clutch performance before 
adding a cooler. If the fan clutch is not working properly, this is the cause 
of the high temperatures and no cooler is required.

 Effects of Vehicle Loads 

Although a vehicle can be at a rated axle load, there are at least two 
events in a duty cycle that can cause the front axle to be overloaded. 
Understanding the duty cycle will help with the diagnosis.

When backing up a ramp, weight is transferred to the front axle. If the 
customer has the concern during this mode, high efforts can be expected.

A vehicle in city delivery operation that is equipped with a long body 
with a high amount of rear overhang can have an overloaded front axle near the 
end of its duty cycle. When fully loaded, the load on the front axle does not 
exceed the front axle rating. As the vehicle is partially unloaded from the 
rear at each stop, more weight can be transferred to the front axle. The 
amount of weight transferred is dependent on the commodity. Steering efforts 
will increase as weight is added to the front axle.

 Tires and Their Relation to Steering Efforts 

Low inflation pressures will increase steering efforts because of a 
larger footprint and higher friction on the ground. Inflation pressures should 
be set to vehicle load.

Oversized tires will increase steering efforts. The high effort will be 
noted during maneuvers at one mile per hour or less, or when wheels are turned 
with brakes applied. After determining that system is operating normally by 
performing Test Sequence Procedures, high efforts under these conditions are 
normal.

 Turning the Steering Wheel with Brakes Applied 

Depending on front axle weight, turning the steering wheel with brakes 
applied will produce high efforts. This is because the front tires cannot 
rotate as they are turned. With front brakes applied, the efforts can be even 
higher. After determining that the system is operating normally by conducting 
Test Sequence Procedures Test A1, turn steering wheel with brakes applied. 
Note effort level. Release brake and turn steering wheel. If efforts are 
reduced, system is operating normally.

The data taken during this test can be helpful in determining not only 
if the end-of-travel valves are operating correctly, but can be used as a 
guide to help solve other steering-related concerns.

The test starts with the steering wheel in the vehicle straight-ahead 
position. The pressure buildup should be rapid during the first turn of the 
steering wheel and begin to level off as the amount of turning is increased. 
Effort should be constant. As the road wheels near full turn capability, a 
large effort increase will be felt as the end-of-travel dump valves are 
activated.

The pressure as it levels off should be in the 55-96 bars (800-1400 
psi) range. The actual pressure will vary from vehicle to vehicle depending on 
front end weight and tires.

If an extreme increase in effort is felt and no increase in pressure 
occurs, look for a mechanical fault between the steering gear control valve 
and steering wheel. If pressure spike or large pressure increase and effort 
increase is observed, look for a mechanical fault in the steering gear or 
between the steering gear and road wheel.

 High Efforts Near End of Steering Wheel Travel 

Vehicles equipped with a steering gear with end-of-travel unloader 
valves will experience higher steering effort when the valves are activated. 
When the valve is actuated, it permits fluid to flow from the high-pressure 
side of the steering gear piston to the low-pressure side. This reduces the 
amount of available power assist. Additional effort is required to steer the 
vehicle to overcome the reduced level of power assist. Condition is normal if 
all requirements of Test Sequence Procedures test have been met. Unloader 
valves should operate just before the wheel stop contacts the axle beam. 
Always check that correct wheel stop is installed before adjusting unloader 
valves.

 Air Bleeding 

If bubbles are visible in the power steering fluid, bleed air from the 
system as follows:

Check the power steering reservoir fluid level. Add fluid if necessary. 

Run the engine until the fluid reaches normal operating temperature. 

 WARNING: DO NOT HOLD THE STEERING WHEEL IN THE FAR LEFT OR FAR RIGHT POSITION 
FOR MORE THAN FIVE SECONDS TO AVOID HIGH TEMPERATURE AND POSSIBLE DAMAGE TO 
COMPONENTS. 

Turn the steering wheel all the way to the left and right several times 
and return to center.

Recheck fluid level and add Motorcraft MERCON® ATF 
XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent if necessary. 

 Fluid Level 

Check the fluid level in the power steering reservoir with the engine 
off. Use the HOT or COLD markings on the dipstick, depending upon the fluid 
temperature. 

Use COLD for checking at room temperature, 20°C (70°
F). 

Use HOT for normal operating temperatures, 80°C (175°
F). 

The fluid level must show between the ADD and FULL markings on the 
dipstick. If the fluid is below the ADD mark, add Motorcraft MERCON®
 ATF XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent.

 NOTE: After any major power steering system or component overhaul, the system 
should be purged of old fluid and the oil filter discarded, and new fluid and 
a new filter installed.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Fluid Leak

With the engine off, wipe the power steering hoses, steering gear and 
reservoir to aid in leak detection. 

If the power steering fluid does not already include dye, mix one 
teaspoonful of oil-soluble aniline dye into power steering fluid and fill the 
reservoir to specification if necessary. 

 CAUTION: Do not hold the wheels against the far right or left position for more 
than 5 seconds to prevent damage to pump. 

With the engine running at 1000-1500 rpm, turn the steering wheel all 
the way to the left and right several times.

Shut off the engine and check for leaks. 

Determine the exact source of leakage. Since most fluid leaks occur at 
fittings and connections in a power steering hydraulic system, the following 
areas should be checked before any other part is replaced. 

 CAUTION: Adjustable hose clamps at oil cooler should not exceed 1.35 Nm
 (12 lb-in). 
Return line hose clamps — tighten or reposition 
adjustable hose clamps to eliminate leakage.

Adapters at gear/assist cylinder ports — if leakage is 
evident at a straight adapter, tighten adapter to 48 Nm (35 
lb-ft). If leakage persists, remove adapter and replace O-ring on the adapter. 
If adapter cannot be tightened one full turn or if leak persists, remove 
adapter, replace O-ring on adapter, and reinstall directional adapter as 
follows: 

Be sure jam nut is in loose position on adapter, and metal backup 
washer is positioned against threads for jam nut with O-ring against backup 
washer. 

Install adapter and tighten until metal backup washer contacts pump or 
gear boss. 

Position adapter by loosening adapter no more than one turn. 

Holding adapter in desired direction, tighten jam nut and washer 
against pump or gear boss. 

Thread damage — if leakage is due to damaged threads 
(cross-threaded), replace the connector, the hose fitting end or replace the 
hose assembly where required. If housing threads on the gear, pump or cylinder 
are badly stripped and cannot be re-dressed with a proper sized tap, replace 
the gear housing, pump body or cylinder.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Start-Up Procedure After Power Steering Pump or Gear Overhaul

Upon initial engine start-up, there is frequently noise and aeration. 
This is due to air trapped in the overhauled unit which mixes with the surging 
fluid and causes aeration. The problem can be minimized if the following 
procedure is used. 

 Fill Process 

Whenever a steering gear, pump or cooler is replaced, follow Steps 1-5.

Place front wheels in straight-ahead position and engage parking brake. 
Do not turn steering wheel during initial fill procedure. 

Fill reservoir with fluid and allow the fluid to gravity feed the 
system. Crack the pressure line fittings at the pump and steering gear. 
Tighten fittings when fluid is visible. Keep adding fluid to reservoir as 
required.

When fluid level in reservoir no longer goes down, start engine. 
Continue to add fluid to reservoir as required. Do not exceed full mark.

After fluid level in reservoir no longer goes down, rotate steering 
wheel to full right and left turns, stop to stop. Add fluid as required.

Continue process until fluid level no longer changes. Fluid level is 
correct when it is in the full range on the dipstick.

Whenever a minor leak is corrected, follow Steps 6-8.

Place front wheels in straight-ahead position and engage parking brake.

Fill reservoir to full mark on dipstick. Start engine and let idle for 
several minutes. Check fluid level and add as required.

Rotate steering wheel to full right and left turn, stop to stop, 
several times. Stop engine and check fluid level. Fill reservoir to full range 
indicated on dipstick.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Steering System, Power

TAS power steering gears are the latest design in the Ross family of 
integral hydraulic power steering gears. Integral hydraulic power steering 
means that the gear contains a manual steering mechanism, a hydraulic control 
valve, and a hydraulic power cylinder, all in a single, compact package.
