1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Cooling System 

 Rust or Dirt Contamination 

If the cooling system is contaminated by residual solids such as rust 
or dirt, the system must be cleaned by using Ford Premium Cooling System Flush 
F1AZ-19A503-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESR-M14P7-A. Heavy rust 
or scale may require additional radiator cleaning service. 

 Oil Contamination 

If the cooling system is contaminated by oil: 

Determine the source or cause of the contamination and eliminate it. 

Drain the cooling system and fill with clean water containing two 
ounces per gallon of non-foaming automatic dishwasher detergent. 

Run the engine for 30 minutes at 1000-1200 rpm. 

Drain the cooling system. Allow engine to cool. 

Refill with Ford Heavy Duty Diesel Engine Cooling System Fluid 
E6HZ-19549-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESE-M97B18-C.

================================================================================
PAGE 4166
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 03A-01: Engine, FD-1060 Diesel

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Lubrication System 

 NOTE: Also observe condition of coolant. If there is evidence of oil 
contamination in coolant, the cooling system must be cleaned following the 
directions outlined. 

If the engine oil has been contaminated by coolant, the engine 
lubrication system must be cleaned. Determine the level/severity of 
contamination and proceed with the appropriate cleaning procedure.

 Contamination Slight to Moderate with No Sludging 

Defined as showing evidence of coolant in oil. 

Sludging is defined as gelled, slimy deposits attached to engine parts. 

 Contamination Heavy with Sludging 

Defined as showing heavy concentration of coolant in oil with sludging. 
Sludging is evidence of gelled, slimy deposits on parts under rocker cover and 
bottom end — oil pan area. 

Determine the source or cause of the contamination and eliminate it. 

 Cleaning — Slight to Moderate Contamination, No Sludge 

Drain all oil from the engine. Also remove the oil cooler drain plug 
and drain oil. Replace drain plug. 

Remove and discard the oil filter and fit new oil filter. Remove 
crankcase breather element.

 WARNING: READ AND FOLLOW ALL STATEMENTS ON CLEANING SOLVENT CONTAINER TO ENSURE 
SAFE OPERATION. 

Mix 9.5 liters (10.0 quarts) of kerosene with 9.5 liters (10.0 quarts) 
of recommended engine oil and refill crankcase. 

Run engine for 30 minutes at 1000-1200 rpm with no load.

 CAUTION: When performing this procedure, check oil pressure frequently. Make 
sure oil pressure does not fall below 103 kPa (15 psi). 

Drain all oil from the engine. Also remove the oil cooler drain plug 
and drain oil. Replace drain plug. 

Remove and discard the oil filter and fit new oil filter. 

Repeat Steps 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 one time. 

Fill crankcase with recommended engine oil. 

Replace crankcase breather element. 

 Cleaning — Heavy Contamination with Sludge 

Drain all oil from the engine. Also remove the oil cooler drain plug 
and drain oil. Replace drain plug. 

If sludge is heavy and built up, remove as much sludge deposit as 
possible from exposed engine parts, i.e., under rocker cover and lower end 
(oil pan removed) before proceeding further. 

Remove and discard the oil filter and fit new oil filter. Remove 
crankcase breather element.

 WARNING: READ AND FOLLOW ALL STATEMENTS ON CLEANING SOLVENT CONTAINER TO ENSURE 
SAFE OPERATION. 

Mix 9.5 liters (10.0 quarts) of commercially available cleaning solvent 
such as Butyl Cellosolve (Union Carbide) or Downol E-B (Dow Chemical) or 
Glycol Ether E-13 (Chem Central) or equivalent with 9.5 liters (10.0 quarts) 
recommended engine oil and refill crankcase. 

Run engine for 30 minutes at 1000-1200 rpm with no load.

 CAUTION: When performing this procedure, check oil pressure frequently. Make 
sure oil pressure does not fall below 103 kPa (15 psi). 

Drain all oil from the engine. Also remove the oil cooler drain plug 
and drain oil. Replace drain plug. 

Remove and discard the oil filter and fit new oil filter.

 WARNING: READ AND FOLLOW ALL STATEMENTS ON CLEANING SOLVENT CONTAINER TO ENSURE 
SAFE OPERATION. 

Mix 9.5 liters (10.0 quarts) of commercially available cleaning solvent 
such as Butyl Cellosolve (Union Carbide) or Downol E-B (Dow Chemical) or 
Glycol Ether E-13 (Chem Central) or equivalent with 9.5 liters (10.0 quarts) 
recommended engine oil and refill crankcase. 

Run engine for 30 minutes at 1000-1200 rpm with no load.

 CAUTION: When performing this procedure, check oil pressure frequently. Make 
sure oil pressure does not fall below 103 kPa (15 psi). 

Drain all oil from the engine. Also remove the oil cooler drain plug 
and drain oil. Replace drain plug. 

Remove and discard the oil filter and fit new oil filter. Fill the 
crankcase with the recommended engine oil. 

Run engine for 30 minutes at 1000-1200 rpm with no load.

 CAUTION: When performing this procedure, check oil pressure frequently. Make 
sure oil pressure does not fall below 103 kPa (15 psi). 

Drain all oil from the engine. Also remove the oil cooler drain plug 
and drain oil. Replace drain plug. 

Remove oil pan and inspect main and rod bearings for signs of distress. 
Replace bearings if necessary and replace oil pan. 

Remove and discard the oil filter and fit new oil filter. Fill the 
crankcase with the recommended engine oil. Install new crankcase breather 
element.

ADJUSTMENTS

Valve Adjustment, Cold 

 CAUTION: Adjust the valves when the engine is cold — below 60°
C (140°F). 

 CAUTION: Make sure to disengage the pin after locating top dead center. 

 NOTE: Valve lash should be checked and adjusted at the first 32,000 km 
(20,000 miles) and thereafter at 64,000 km (40,000 miles) intervals. 

Use the timing pin to locate top dead center (TDC) for cylinder No. 1, 
and then remove the valve covers.

[FIGURE: A17171A.gif]

 NOTE: The clearance is correct when some resistance is felt when the feeler 
gauge is slipped between the valve stem and the rocker lever. 

Valve lash is checked by inserting a feeler gauge between the rocker 
arm pad and the valve stem tip. Adjust the valves by loosening the lock nut 
and turning the adjusting screw.

[FIGURE: A17172A.gif]

Adjust the clearance for the valves shown in the illustration. 

Intake: 0.25 mm (0.010 inch) 

Exhaust: 0.51 mm (0.020 inch)

[FIGURE: A17173A.gif]

Tighten the lock nut to 24 Nm (18 lb-ft) and check the 
valve lash. 

 CAUTION: Make sure timing pin is disengaged before rotating the crankshaft. 

Mark the pulley and rotate the crankshaft 360 degrees.

[FIGURE: A17174A.gif]

Adjust the clearance for the valves shown in the illustration. 

Intake: 0.25 mm (0.010 inch) 

Exhaust: 0.51 mm (0.020 inch)

[FIGURE: A17175A.gif]

Tighten the lock nut to 24 Nm (18 lb-ft) and check the 
valve lash. 

Install the valve covers and gaskets. Tighten valve cover retaining 
bolts to 24 Nm (18 lb-ft).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Cooling System

 WARNING: NEVER REMOVE THE RADIATOR CAP UNDER ANY CONDITIONS WHILE THE ENGINE IS 
OPERATING. FAILURE TO FOLLOW THESE INSTRUCTIONS CAN RESULT IN PERSONAL INJURY 
AND DAMAGE TO THE COOLING SYSTEM AND ENGINE. 

TO AVOID HAVING SCALDING HOT COOLANT OR STEAM BLOW OUT OF THE RADIATOR, 
USE EXTREME CARE WHEN REMOVING THE CAP FROM A HOT RADIATOR. IF POSSIBLE, WAIT 
UNTIL THE ENGINE HAS COOLED, THEN WRAP A THICK CLOTH AROUND THE RADIATOR CAP 
AND TURN IT SLOWLY TO THE FIRST STOP. STEP BACK WHILE THE PRESSURE IS RELEASED 
FROM THE COOLING SYSTEM. WHEN YOU ARE SURE ALL THE PRESSURE HAS BEEN RELEASED, 
PRESS DOWN ON THE CAP (STILL USING A CLOTH), TURN AND REMOVE IT. 

Refer to Section 03-03 .

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Thermostat, Water 

 CAUTION: Do not attempt to service the thermostat. It should be replaced if it 
is not operating properly. 

 NOTE: When changing the thermostat to a higher or lower temperature range on 
vehicles equipped with automatic shutters, always change the shutterstat to a 
corresponding higher or lower range.

The poppet-type thermostat used in production is a high-temperature 
thermostat for use with a mixture of water and permanent-type coolant. Install 
a low temperature thermostat if a nonpermanent type coolant and water solution 
is used (except on vehicles with automatic radiator shutters). 

 Removal 

Disconnect the battery negative cables.

Drain the engine coolant. Refer to Section 03-03 .

Remove the air cleaner assembly.

Disconnect the air duct assembly at the turbocharger inlet.

Remove the accessory drive belt. Refer to Section 03A-05 .

Remove the bolts retaining the generator support strap (upper bracket) 
to the generator and the cylinder head, then remove the generator support strap.

Remove the generator pivot bolt, washers and nut, then reposition the 
generator away from the thermostat housing.

Remove retaining bolts, generator mounting bracket and water inlet 
support bracket.

Disconnect the upper radiator hose from the thermostat housing.

Remove the water outlet connection retaining bolts.

 Thermostat and Thermostat Housing 

[FIGURE: A24895A.gif]

Item

Part Number

Thermostat

Remove the thermostat housing and thermostat, and lift bracket from the 
cylinder head.

Remove the gasket and any residue from the thermostat housing.

 Installation 

 NOTE: Check the thermostat before installing it. Refer to test procedures in 
 Section 03-03 . 

Place the thermostat and a new gasket in the thermostat housing.

Position the thermostat housing and lift bracket on the cylinder head 
and install the retaining bolts. Tighten the water outlet connection retaining 
bolts to 21-27 Nm (15-20 lb-ft).

Connect the upper radiator hose to the thermostat housing.

Position the water inlet support bracket and generator mounting bracket 
and install the retaining bolts. Tighten the bolt retaining both brackets to 
55-65 Nm (41-48 lb-ft). Tighten the bolt retaining the water 
inlet support bracket to the thermostat housing to 30-40 Nm 
(22-30 lb-ft). Tighten the remaining bolt to 40-50 Nm (30-37 
lb-ft).

Position the generator to the generator mounting bracket and install 
the generator pivot bolt, washers and nut. Do not tighten the pivot bolt at 
this time.

Install the generator support strap (upper bracket) and retaining 
bolts. Tighten the retaining bolts to 30-40 Nm (22-30 lb-ft).

Tighten the generator pivot bolt to 55-67 Nm (41-49 
lb-ft).

Install the accessory drive belt. Refer to Section 03A-05 .

Connect the air duct assembly to the turbocharger inlet.

Install the air cleaner assembly.

Fill the cooling system. Refer to Section 03-03 .

Connect the battery negative cables.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Radiator Hoses

Replace the cooling system hoses whenever they become cracked or 
deteriorated, or have a tendency to collapse.

 Removal 

Partially drain the cooling system to replace cooling system upper 
hose(s). Drain the cooling system completely to replace the lower radiator 
outlet hose.

Loosen the clamps on each end of the hose(s) to be removed. Slide the 
hose(s) off the connections.

 Installation 

 NOTE: If the connections have a single bead around the edges, make sure the 
clamps are located beyond the beads. If the connections have a double bead, 
make sure the clamp is located between the beads after assembly.

Position the clamps on each end of the new hose. Slide the hose onto 
the connections, then tighten the clamps.

Fill the cooling system with coolant and bleed the system. Refer to 
 Section 03-03 .

Operate the engine for several minutes, then check the hose(s) and 
connections for leaks.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Radiator Lower Hose Tube 

 Removal 

Drain the cooling system. 

Loosen the clamps on each end of the hoses. Slide the lower hose tube 
off the connections. 

 Installation 

 NOTE: If the connections have a single bead around the edges, make sure the 
clamps are located beyond the beads. If the connections have a double bead, 
make sure the clamp is located between the beads after assembly.

Position the clamps on each end of the hose connectors. Slide the lower 
hose tube into the connections, then tighten the clamps. 

Fill the cooling system with coolant and bleed the system. Refer to 
 Section 03-03 . 

Operate the engine for several minutes, then check the hose(s) and 
connections for leaks.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Radiator

 Removal 

Tilt the cab and lock in position. 

Remove the A/C condenser-to-radiator bolts (if so equipped) and 
position condenser out of the way. 

Remove the fan shroud-to-radiator bolts and hang shroud on fan. 

Remove charge air cooler duct and disconnect upper radiator hose. 

Disconnect coolant recovery reservoir hose at the radiator. 

Remove the throttle cable bracket-to-radiator retaining bolt. 

Remove the charge air cooler to engine duct.

Remove the lower radiator hose. 

Remove the radiator and charge air cooler support bolts from both sides. 

With the aid of an assistant, lift the radiator and charge air cooler, 
and remove from the vehicle. 

Lift the shroud off the fan. 

 Installation 

Hang shroud on the fan. 

With the aid of an assistant, lift the radiator and charge air cooler, 
and position it in the vehicle. 

Install the radiator and charge air cooler support bolts on both sides. 

Connect the lower radiator hose and tighten hose clamp. 

Connect the charge air cooler to engine duct and position clamp as 
shown. Tighten clamp to 10-14 Nm (7-11 lb-ft). 

Install the throttle cable bracket-to-radiator retaining bolt. 

Connect the coolant recovery reservoir hose. Tighten clamp. 

Connect the upper radiator hose and tighten clamp. 

Position fan shroud and install retaining bolts. 

Install charge air cooler duct and position clamp as shown. Tighten 
clamps to 10-14 Nm (7-11 lb-ft). 

Position condenser (if equipped) and install retaining bolts. 

Fill cooling system. 

Lower the cab. Operate and check system for leaks.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Charge Air Cooler and Heat Exchanger

 Removal 

Remove radiator. 

Disassemble the module by removing the nuts and bolts that hold the 
charge air cooler to the radiator support frame.

Remove the charge air cooler from the radiator assembly.

Remove the drain cock and de-aeration fitting as required.

Service heat exchangers as required. Refer to Section 03-03 .

 Installation 

If removed, install the drain cock and de-aeration fitting.

Install the charge air cooler to the radiator assembly.

 NOTE: Threadlock® 242 E2FZ-19554-B or equivalent meeting 
Ford specification WSK-M2G351-A6 is recommended on all threads.

Assemble the module by installing the bolts and nuts that hold the 
charge air cooler to the radiator assembly. Tighten 3/8-inch shoulder bolts to 
47 Nm (35 lb-ft). Tighten 3/8-inch nuts to 20 Nm
 (15 lb-ft).

Install radiator.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel System Flow

Fuel from the tank (under suction) is routed to the prefilter and then 
to the transfer pump that is mounted on the left side of the engine. After 
going through the transfer pump, the fuel is pumped under pressure through the 
fuel filter and water separator. Once the fuel is filtered, it goes to the 
fuel gallery of the fuel injection pump.

The FD-1060 and FD-1460 diesel engines use a fuel prefilter and a 
secondary filter/water separator assembly to ensure that only clean fuel gets 
to the fuel injection pump. The use of properly filtered fuel cannot be 
overemphasized because of the tight clearances in the fuel injection pump and 
fuel injection nozzles. Never bypass the fuel filters.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel Injection Pump

When the key is turned to run, the rack inside the injection pump moves 
to the START position and allows fuel entering the injection pump to fill the 
pumping elements.

Fuel is distributed through individual pumping elements and on to each 
cylinder through high pressure fuel tubes. Fuel pressure and quantity is 
controlled by the action of the camshaft opening and closing the plungers and 
the control rack position of the individual pumping elements. Refer to 
Delivery Valve in the Description and Operation portion of this section for 
further information.

A shutoff lever is used for engine shutdown. When the lever is moved in 
the direction to shut down the engine, the control rack is pulled to the stop 
position. At this time, no fuel is delivered to the engine.

Surplus fuel is provided to the fuel injection pump and injection 
nozzles for cooling and lubrication.

The fuel injection pump is mounted at the front left side of the 
engine. It is driven by a gear timed to the camshaft gear. The fuel injection 
pump is not a serviceable component and should not be tampered with. Do not 
attempt to service the fuel injection pump; service is to be performed only by 
authorized service centers. Tampering with the injection pump can void the 
warranty.

The fuel injection pump is of the constant stroke, in-line type, driven 
at half engine speed by the timing gears. There is one pumping element per 
cylinder actuated through roller tappets by a fully enclosed camshaft. The 
pumping elements are responsible for accurately metering and delivering fuel 
to the fuel injectors.

Each of the pumping elements includes a barrel and plunger closely 
toleranced to give an accurate fit. Fuel is admitted to each pumping element 
by two bores on either side of the barrel. The barrel is splined, with a 
master spline for correct location within the pump body.

================================================================================
PAGE 4188
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 03A-04A: Fuel Injection, FD-1060 and FD-1460 Diesel Engines

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Delivery Valve

A delivery valve is located above each plunger on the Bosch P-7100 
In-Line Pump inside each high-pressure outlet fitting. The delivery valve 
allows fuel under injection pressure to move into the high-pressure tubes and 
also allows some drainback to occur. The delivery valve also serves to rapidly 
reduce pressure in the injection tube once pressure from the plunger has 
ceased. Rapid pressure reduction is required to make certain the injector 
needle valve snaps shut to prevent fuel "dribble," a condition which can cause 
carbon formation on the injector tip and abnormal exhaust smoke.

Pumping element operation is detailed in the following steps and 
illustration.

With the plunger at the bottom of the stroke (A), fuel flows into the 
barrel through the spill port and fills the space above the plunger.

As the plunger (B) rises, the spill port in the barrel is covered and 
the fuel is trapped. This is the point of port closure. The continued upward 
movement of the plunger pressurizes the trapped fuel until the delivery valve 
(at the base of each high pressure injection tube) is lifted from its seat. 
High pressure fuel is transmitted through the tube to the injector and 
injection takes place through the injector nozzle.

Injection stops (C) when the upper edge of the helix uncovers the lower 
edge of the spill port. Pressure escapes to the fuel gallery. The drop in 
pressure causes the injector to close and injection to stop. After fuel 
delivery, the plunger continues to the top of the stroke and is returned by a 
spring for the next cycle.

Because the end of delivery is reached when the helix on the plunger 
uncovers the spill port (D), the amount of fuel delivered is varied by turning 
the pump plunger. If the plunger is turned until the vertical groove 
completely uncovers the spill port during the entire lift of the plunger, 
there will be no fuel delivered to the engine (E). This is because injection 
pressure cannot be reached, thereby shutting off the engine.

The plungers are rotated by a control rack splined to each plunger. 
Rack movement is determined by the control rod, actuated by the throttle and 
governor.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Governor

An all-speed mechanical governor is used on the pump to regulate fuel 
at all engine speeds and loads. The governor also contains the boost control 
device (for starting) and the fuel shutoff solenoid. The governor is to be 
serviced only at authorized service centers. Tampering with the governor can 
void the warranty.

[FIGURE: A17764A.gif]

All engines are equipped with a boost control. This device limits the 
fuel during periods of low turbocharger boost. Smoke is kept to a minimum 
because the engine is provided with a fuel charge closely matched to the 
amount of air available in the combustion chamber. Operation of the device is 
quite simple. A diaphragm (which is connected via linkage to the control rack) 
inside the housing is exposed to boost pressure via a tube from the intake 
manifold. The other side of this diaphragm is exposed to reference spring 
pressure. When boost pressure drops, the spring forces the diaphragm back, 
pulling the control rack in a fuel decrease direction. This limits the amount 
of fuel available to the engine, which helps prevent excess smoke. This device 
is not to be adjusted or serviced except at authorized service centers.

[FIGURE: A17875A.gif]

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Injector Nozzle Assemblies

The injector nozzles used in the six-cylinder diesel are of the 
inwardly opening, hydraulically operated, hole type. The injector nozzle 
assembly consists of two subassemblies: the nozzle body and nozzle holder. A 
section view of the injection nozzle assembly is shown.

[FIGURE: V43231A.gif]

================================================================================

================================================================================
1997 Cargo

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Nozzle Holder

The nozzle holder is used to hold the nozzle in its correct position in 
the cylinder head and to provide channels for conducting diesel fuel to the 
nozzle valve.

================================================================================
PAGE 4192
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 03A-04A: Fuel Injection, FD-1060 and FD-1460 Diesel Engines

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Nozzle

The nozzle valve consists of two parts: needle valve and nozzle. These 
parts are precision machined and lapped to form an extremely close-fitting 
matched set. The nozzle has a cone-shaped area on which the needle valve 
seats. There are holes in the nozzle through which fuel is injected into the 
engine combustion chamber. The use of multihole injectors is necessary in 
direct injection diesel engines because they provide a uniform distribution of 
fuel throughout the combustion chamber.

 CAUTION: The pressure of the fuel in the high pressure tube is sufficient to 
penetrate the skin and cause serious bodily harm. 

 NOTE: Fuel pressure generated by the fuel injection pump must overcome the 
counterforce of the pressure spring before the needle valve lifts off its seat.

The injector is operated by fuel pressure generated by the fuel 
injection pump. Fuel under high pressure acts on the exposed annular (ring 
shaped) area of the needle valve and lifts it from its seat.

The fuel is then injected through the nozzle orifices into the 
combustion chamber.

 NOTE: Opening pressure is adjustable by changing the initial tension on the 
pressure spring in the nozzle holder. This is accomplished by changing the 
shim thickness on the spring seat.

The opening pressure is determined by the initial tension of the 
pressure spring.

The needle valve lift is limited by the annular face at the base of the 
valve stem.

During injection, fuel takes the following path: fuel injection tubing 
to the fuel inlet passage of the nozzle holder, onto the inlet passages, 
pressure chamber and spray orifices of the nozzle, and then into the 
combustion chamber. Fuel leaking past the valve stem is returned to the fuel 
tank via the leak-off connection on the nozzle holder which is attached to the 
fuel return tube.

After injection of the fuel delivered by the injection pump, the 
pressure spring forces the needle valve back on its seat via the spindle and 
needle valve stem. The injection is then closed for the next pressure stroke. 
Fuel dribble should not occur, as might happen if the nozzle showed excessive 
wear.

[FIGURE: V4324E.gif]

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fuel Shutoff Solenoid

When the key is switched off, the fuel shutoff solenoid shuts off fuel 
by forcing the fuel pump control lever to the fuel OFF position. When the key 
is switched to RUN, power applied to the solenoid pulls the fuel pump control 
lever to the fuel-open position, allowing fuel delivery and engine combustion. 
While the engine is running, power is continuously applied to the solenoid and 
continues to hold the control lever to the fuel-open position.

 NOTE: In instances of a no-start condition where the engine turns over 
normally and all correct starting procedures are being followed, inspect the 
fuel shutoff solenoid to make sure it is moving the fuel pump control lever 
when the key is turned to run and off. In some cases it may be necessary to 
adjust the length of the fuel shutoff solenoid rod. Refer to Fuel Shutoff 
Solenoid Adjustment in the Adjustments portion of this section.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Fuel Injection Pump

 CAUTION: Do not wash or steam clean the engine while it is running or still hot 
from running. Serious damage to the engine can occur. 

 NOTE: Before removing any fuel tubes, clean the exterior of the fuel 
injection pump with clean fuel oil or solvent to help prevent the entry of 
dirt or other contamination. The area can be steam cleaned but it can only be 
done when the engine is cold and shut off.

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

Steering Wheel Puller

T67L-3600-A

 Removal 

Disconnect all fuel tubes (supply tube, high pressure tubes and 
pressure relief valve) at injection pump.

Disconnect throttle control linkage.

Disconnect air fuel control tube from pump.

Disconnect wastegate control tube from pump.

For FD-1060, disconnect the external oil feed tube at the inboard side 
of the fuel injection pump and the main oil rifle.

 NOTE: Once top dead center (TDC) is located, make sure TDC timing pin is 
completely disengaged from camshaft sprocket.

Using Rotunda Engine Barring Tool Kit D92T-6000-A or equivalent, locate 
top dead center (TDC) for cylinder No. 1. Slowly turn the engine while pushing 
on the TDC timing pin until timing pin drops into the hole in the camshaft 
sprocket.

Remove the fuel injection pump mounting bracket.

Remove the gear housing access cap. Remove the nut and washer from the 
fuel injection pump shaft.

Attach Steering Wheel Puller T67L-3600-A to the fuel injection pump 
drive gear and turn forcing screw until fuel injection pump drive gear comes 
loose from fuel injection pump shaft.

[FIGURE: A17780A.gif]

Remove the four mounting nuts. Remove the fuel injection pump.

[FIGURE: A17789A.gif]

 Installation 

Make sure the engine has cylinder No. 1 at TDC.

 NOTE: The fuel injection pump timing pin is located inside the access plug at 
the governor housing. To set fuel injection pump timing, the timing pin must 
be turned backwards inside the plug so the slot will fit into timing tooth of 
the pump. Refer to the following steps.

The fuel injection pump also has a timing pin, located in the governor 
housing. This pin is used to position the fuel injection pump shaft to 
correspond with top dead center for cylinder No. 1.

Remove the access plug from fuel injection pump governor housing.

[FIGURE: A17790A.gif]

Remove the timing pin from access plug.

[FIGURE: A17791A.gif]

If the timing tooth is not aligned with the timing pin hole, rotate the 
fuel injection pump shaft until the timing tooth aligns as shown.

[FIGURE: A17792A.gif]

Reverse the position of the timing pin so the slot of the timing pin 
will fit over the timing tooth in the fuel injection pump. Install and secure 
the timing pin with the access plug.

[FIGURE: A17793A.gif]

Use a 50/50 mixture of clean engine oil and STP® or 
equivalent to lubricate the gear housing bore to ensure the fuel injection 
pump will slide easily into the gear housing.

[FIGURE: A17794A.gif]

Lubricate the O-ring and mounting flange of the fuel injection pump.

[FIGURE: A17795A.gif]

 NOTE: The fuel injection pump shaft has a provision for a Woodruff key; 
however, it is not required. Timing mark alignment is not required for the 
fuel injection pump drive gear.

 NOTE: Make sure fuel injection pump shaft and gear taper is clean of oil and 
dry.

Slide the fuel injection pump shaft through the fuel injection pump 
drive gear and position the fuel injection pump flange onto the mounting studs.

[FIGURE: A17796A.gif]

 CAUTION: Do not attempt to pull the fuel injection pump flange into the gear 
housing with the mounting nuts. Damage to gear housing will occur. 

 NOTE: Push the fuel injection pump forward until the mounting flange and 
O-ring are properly fitted into the gear housing bore.

Install the mounting nuts. Tighten to 43 Nm (32 lb-ft).

 CAUTION: To prevent damage to the timing pin, do not exceed the torque value 
given. This is not the final torque value for the fuel injection pump shaft nut. 

Install the fuel injection pump shaft nut and washer. Tighten to 10-15 Nm
 (7-11 lb-ft).

Disengage the engine timing pin.

Remove the fuel injection pump timing pin access plug. Reverse the 
position of the timing pin and reinstall the timing pin, access plug and 
sealing washer. Tighten access plug to 40 Nm (30 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: A17797A.gif]

Tighten the fuel injection pump shaft nut to a final torque value of 165 Nm
 (122 lb-ft). Install the gear housing access cap hand-tight.

Install the fuel injection pump mounting bracket capscrews.

[FIGURE: A17798A.gif]

Connect all fuel tubes (supply tube, high pressure tubes and pressure 
relief valve) to injection pump. Tighten low-pressure supply tube to 15 Nm
 (11 lb-ft). Tighten high-pressure tubes to 30 Nm
 (22 lb-ft).

Connect wastegate control tube.

On the FD-1060, install the external oil feed tube at the inboard side 
of the fuel injection pump and the main oil rifle. Connect wastegate tube to 
turbocharger.

Connect throttle control linkage. Check for stop-to-stop throttle 
travel and proper operation of breakover mechanism.

 CAUTION: The governor housing must be prelubricated before engine operates. 
Failure to do so will result in premature governor wear. 

Add 750 ml (0.71 qt) of clean engine oil to the governor housing.

 WARNING: WEAR SAFETY GLASSES OR A PROTECTIVE FACE SHIELD WHEN WORKING WITH 
HIGH-PRESSURE FUEL. KEEP EYES AND HANDS AWAY FROM NOZZLE SPRAY. FUEL SPRAYING 
FROM THE NOZZLE UNDER HIGH PRESSURE CAN PENETRATE THE SKIN AND CAUSE BLOOD 
POISONING. MEDICAL ATTENTION SHOULD BE PROVIDED IMMEDIATELY IN THE EVENT OF 
SKIN PENETRATION. 

Vent the high-pressure fuel tubes. Loosen the fitting at the No. 1 
injector. Place the fuel injection pump control lever in the run position. 
Crank the engine so air can bleed from the fuel tubes. Then, tighten the 
fitting to 30 Nm (22 lb-ft).

Vent each high-pressure tube separately until the engine runs smoothly.

 Low-Pressure Fuel Injection Tube

 Injection Pump Supply Tube

[FIGURE: A17806A.gif]

[FIGURE: A17807A.gif]

 CAUTION: When replacing fuel tubes, replace sealing washers each time they are

 High-Pressure Fuel Tubes 

 Removal 

Fuel injection high-pressure tubes may be replaced one at a time, 
without having to remove the entire set from the engine. If all tubes are to 
be replaced, go to Step 4.

Remove clamping devices holding tubes together, then remove connections 
at delivery valves and injector nozzles.

Replace damaged tubes, making connections at injector nozzles and 
delivery valves first, then reinstall clamping devices.

If all high-pressure tubes are to be removed, refer to the following 
procedure.

 WARNING: DO NOT BLEED A HOT ENGINE. THIS CAN CAUSE FUEL TO SPILL ONTO A HOT 
EXHAUST MANIFOLD CREATING A DANGER OF FIRE. 

 WARNING: WEAR SAFETY GLASSES OR A PROTECTIVE FACE SHIELD WHEN WORKING WITH 
HIGH-PRESSURE FUEL. KEEP EYES AND HANDS AWAY FROM NOZZLE SPRAY. FUEL SPRAYING 
FROM THE NOZZLE UNDER PRESSURE CAN PENETRATE THE SKIN AND CAUSE BLOOD 
POISONING. MEDICAL ATTENTION SHOULD BE PROVIDED IMMEDIATELY IN THE EVENT OF 
SKIN PENETRATION. 

Clean area around fuel tubes at injection pump and nozzles.

Disconnect high-pressure tubes from injectors. Cap each tube and 
injector to prevent the entry of dirt into the system.

[FIGURE: A17808A.gif]

 NOTE: Use two wrenches to prevent delivery valve holder from turning.

Remove tube clamp capscrews from intake manifold.

[FIGURE: A17809A.gif]

Remove tubes from injection pump.

[FIGURE: A17811A.gif]

 Installation 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order.

Tighten fuel tube connections to 30 Nm (22 lb-ft). 
Start engine and vent one tube at a time until the engine runs smoothly.

 Injector Leak-Off Tube 

 Removal 

Clean area around injector leak-off tube.

Remove capscrews from hold-down clamps, where applicable.

Remove banjo fittings and washers from nozzle bodies.

[FIGURE: A17813A.gif]

Disconnect injector leak-off tube connections.

[FIGURE: A17814A.gif]

Remove injector leak-off tube.

 Installation 

 CAUTION: Use new washers for fittings. 

 CAUTION: Be very careful to avoid cross-threading the banjo bolts into the 
nozzle body. 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order.

Tighten banjo fittings to 9 Nm (80 lb-in) and 
connections to 13 Nm (10 lb-ft). 

Once all connections are secure, start engine and check connections for 
fuel leaks.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Fuel Filter/Water Separator

 Removal 

The fuel filter is a spin-on type filter mounted to a manifold located 
on the left side of the engine. The prefilter (sedimentor) is also mounted to 
the manifold. The filter/water separator is replaced as part of the scheduled 
maintenance unless it becomes plugged and must be replaced sooner. The fuel 
prefilter is unscrewed from the manifold and the filter screen is cleaned or 
replaced during scheduled maintenance or when it becomes plugged with sediment.

 Installation 

When installing a new filter, fill with clean, fresh diesel fuel and 
coat the seal with diesel fuel. Hand-tighten filter until it seats firmly 
against the mount, then hand-tighten an additional one-half to three-quarters 
turn. Start engine and check for leaks.

It may be necessary to bleed the system after installing fuel filters. 
Refer to Bleeding Fuel System or Restarting 
After Running Out of Fuel in the Adjustments portion of this section.

[FIGURE: A17815A.gif]

Injector Nozzle

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

 Removal 

Before removing nozzle assemblies, clean the exterior of each nozzle 
assembly and the surrounding area with clean fuel oil or solvent to prevent 
the entry of dirt into the engine when the nozzle assemblies are removed. 
Also, clean the fuel inlet and fuel drain manifold connections. Blow dry with 
compressed air.

Loosen the high pressure fuel tube going into the injection nozzle. It 
will pull off to the side enough to get the injector out. Place a cap on the 
high pressure fuel tube opening to prevent the entry of dirt.

Remove the fuel drain manifold banjo bolt from the injection nozzle. 
There is an "ear-muff" type copper washer sealing both sides of banjo fitting. 
This washer must be discarded and replaced.

 CAUTION: When rust has formed on the hold-down nut, the injector can turn in the 
bore when the nut is loosened. This will cause the injector locating ball to 
cut a groove in the bore, resulting in severe damage to the head. 

Soak the hold-down nut with Penetrating Lubricant E8AZ-19A501-B or 
equivalent for a minimum of 3 minutes.

[FIGURE: A17819A.gif]

Hit the injector body with the brass drift to loosen any rust.

[FIGURE: A17820A.gif]

 CAUTION: Damage to the cylinder head will result if the injector is allowed to 
turn while hold-down nut is loosened. 

Hold the injector body with an adjustable wrench while you loosen the 
hold-down nut with a 24-mm box wrench.

[FIGURE: A17821A.gif]

 NOTE: Rotunda Injector Remover Adapter D92T-9000-A or equivalent can be used 
to remove injector nozzles from cylinders 2, 3 and 4. Use Rotunda Injector 
Removal Tool Kit D92T-9000-B or equivalent to remove other injector nozzles.

Remove injector from bore. If injector is tight and will not come out 
by hand, attach Rotunda Injector Remover Adapter D92T-9000-A or equivalent and 
Impact Slide Hammer T50T-100-A to the injector. Pull up on the slide hammer 
with enough force to free the injector. Remove copper washer from bore if it 
doesn't come out with injector.

[FIGURE: A17822A.gif]

Cover the nozzle tip with Fuel System Protector Cap Set T86T-9395-A to 
prevent the entry of dirt.

 Installation 

To install, refer to Stuck Fuel Injectors, Installation in this section.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Stuck Fuel Injectors

 Removal 

If the injectors in cylinders 1, 5 and 6 are stuck and will not come 
out even after soaking, they can be removed using Rotunda Injector Removal 
Tool Kit 014-00269 or equivalent. Refer to the following instructions.

Attach adapter to the threaded end of the forcing screw.

 CAUTION: Once all slack is taken up, do not turn the forcing screw. The injector 
can turn in its bore, resulting in damage to the cylinder head. 

Position bridge over the stuck injector and thread the adapter onto the 
injector and take up all slack by turning the hex nut.

Using a 1/2-inch open end wrench to hold the forcing screw, turn the 
hex nut using a 1-1/8-inch open end wrench until the injector is removed from 
the head.

 Installation 

 NOTE: Test all used nozzle assemblies for opening pressure, tip leakage and 
spray pattern before installation. Refer to the Powertrain Control/Emissions Diagnosis Manual
for the appropriate procedure.

Thoroughly clean the nozzle bore in the cylinder head before 
reinserting the nozzle assembly. Use Rotunda Nozzle Cleaning Kit D83T-9000-G 
or equivalent to perform this job. Pay particular attention to seating 
surface, in order that no small particles of metal or carbon will cause the 
assembly to be cocked or permit blow-by of combustion gases. Blow out the 
particles with compressed air.

Remove the protective cap from the nozzle tip and install a new copper 
gasket. Use a small daub of Multi-Purpose Grease DOAZ-19584-AA or equivalent 
meeting Ford specifications ESB-M1C93-B to hold the washer in place during 
installation.

Apply a light coat of anti-seize compound to the threads of the 
injector hold-down nut and between the top of the nut and injector body.

[FIGURE: A17823A.gif]

 CAUTION: Align the injector's protrusion with the notch in the bore. 

Install the injector into the cylinder head injector bore. Tighten to 60 Nm
 (44 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: A17824A.gif]

Position the O-ring into the groove at the top of the hold-down nut.

 CAUTION: Do not overtighten banjo bolts. They are hollow and can break if 
overtightened. 

Install fuel drain manifold with banjo bolts and washers.

Remove the protective cap from the high-pressure fuel injection tube. 
Install the tube on the injector. Tighten the connecting nut to 30 Nm
 (22 lb-ft).

Start the engine.

If necessary, purge the high-pressure fuel tubes of air. Loosen the 
connectors of the serviced injectors one at a time, one-half to one turn while 
cranking the engine. Crank the engine until solid fuel, free from bubbles, 
flows from the connection.

 WARNING: WEAR SAFETY GLASSES OR A PROTECTIVE FACE SHIELD WHEN WORKING WITH 
HIGH-PRESSURE FUEL. KEEP EYES AND HANDS AWAY FROM NOZZLE SPRAY. FUEL SPRAYING 
FROM THE NOZZLE UNDER HIGH PRESSURE CAN PENETRATE THE SKIN AND CAUSE BLOOD 
POISONING. MEDICAL ATTENTION SHOULD BE PROVIDED IMMEDIATELY IN THE EVENT OF 
SKIN PENETRATION. 

Check for fuel leakage at the high pressure connections.

ADJUSTMENTS

Bleeding Fuel System or Restarting After Running Out of Fuel

Restarting an engine that has run out of fuel is made difficult by the 
fact that, after fuel is exhausted from the fuel tank, air enters the sediment 
bowl, fuel filter/water separator and the fuel supply becomes insufficient to 
sustain engine firing. These assemblies must be refilled with fuel and the 
fuel tubes purged of air before the system can provide adequate fuel to the 
injectors to start the engine.

Follow these steps in restarting a fuel-depleted engine.

Fill the fuel tank with clean fuel. If only partial filling of the tank 
is possible, add a minimum of 5 gallons of fuel to make sure priming can be 
achieved and the engine can run for a short time.

Purge the air from the fuel system as follows:

 NOTE: If the primer will not pump fuel, either there is an air leak in the 
system, the primer is malfunctioning, or the plunger or arm is on the top of a 
cam lobe. Rotate engine 180 degrees and try to prime pump.

Depress primer button until effort to stroke primer increases, then 
stroke an additional 15 strokes (approximately 60 strokes total).

[FIGURE: V9976A.gif]

Open fuel filter vent screw until fuel and air bubbles appear. Allow 
1-1/2 to 2 minutes bleed time until air bubbles and fuel flow cease and the 
fuel system has lost its pressure. During this period, air is "back flowing" 
from the injection pump.

[FIGURE: A17827A.gif]

Close filter vent screw.

Stroke primer 10 times.

 CAUTION: Check filter vent screw after engine starts to ensure there are no fuel 
leaks. 

Start engine as follows:

Crank engine and while cranking, depress accelerator pedal to floor.

Engine should start in 3-8 seconds of cranking, run rough for 5-10 
seconds, and will either smooth out or stall. (Note: Keep accelerator to floor 
during rough running until clear and running smooth, then throttle back.)

If stall occurs, up to 15 seconds of additional cranking may be 
required to restart engine without additional priming.

If engine does not start, repeat Steps 2 and 3 to clear additional air 
from fuel system, and start engine.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Turbocharger System

A turbocharger system uses the energy in the flow of exhaust gases to 
increase engine power and efficiency. These increases occur when the 
turbocharger converts the exhaust flow into a pressurized airflow on the 
intake side of the engine. Because more air is available to support 
combustion, additional fuel can be injected into the cylinders. It is the 
combination of additional fuel and a more complete scavenging of exhaust gases 
from the cylinders that produces the increased engine horsepower.

 Turbocharger Flow Diagram 

[FIGURE: A24459A.gif]

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Turbine

The turbocharger consists of two operating elements, a turbine and a 
compressor, which are installed on opposite ends of a common shaft. The 
turbine is enclosed in a housing connected to the exhaust manifold. Exhaust 
gases entering the housing are directed against the turbine wheel blades, 
causing it to spin at more than 100,000 rpm (engine under load).

================================================================================
PAGE 4214
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 03A-04B: Turbocharger and Charge Air Cooler, FD-1060 and FD-1460 Diesel Engines

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Compressor

Spinning at turbine speed, the compressor draws air through the intake 
filter and delivers it, under pressure, to the engine intake. The air is 
pressurized by the centrifugal force and the internal shape of the compressor 
housing. As air enters and is thrown outward against the housing, it flows 
through passages that narrow and compress the air as it approaches the 
turbocharger outlet. Air leaving the outlet is routed through a duct to the 
charge air cooler and then through another duct to the engine intake.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Wastegate Actuator

The wastegate regulates the amount of boost pressure developed by the 
turbocharger. When the boost pressure reaches a predetermined value, the 
wastegate opens and bypasses some of the exhaust gases directly into the 
exhaust manifold. Turbine speed is reduced, thereby reducing the speed of the 
compressor. This limits the amount of boost.

[FIGURE: A24460A.gif]

As pressure is reduced, the wastegate begins to close again. If boost 
is not controlled, engine components will be damaged from the excessive 
pressure.

[FIGURE: A24461A.gif]

The wastegate is a poppet-type valve operated by a turbocharger-mounted 
actuator. Air pressure from the compressor housing is applied to the actuator 
diaphragm. As pressure increases, the diaphragm moves against the spring 
pressure, holding the valve in the closed position. Movement of the actuator 
diaphragm is transferred to the poppet valve through an external rod and lever.

 CAUTION: The wastegate bracket is an integral part of the turbocharger. The 
turbocharger is a performance part and must not be tampered with after it is 
adjusted at the factory. Tampering with the wastegate components can reduce 
durability by increasing cylinder pressure and thermal loading due to 
incorrect inlet and exhaust manifold pressure, with a potential for poor fuel 
economy and failure to meet regulatory emission laws.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Charge Air Cooler

As air in the turbocharger is compressed, it is also heated. To remove 
the heat, the air is routed through the charge air cooler. The charge air 
cooler is an air-to-air heat exchanger similar in construction and function to 
a radiator. By lowering the temperature of the air, it is made denser. The 
increased density of the air delivered to the engine cylinders permits a 
corresponding increase in the weight of fuel that can be injected into the 
cylinders, while maintaining the air/fuel ratio required for proper 
combustion. Since engine power output is a function of the weight of fuel 
burned, the increase in the weight of fuel introduced as a result of 
turbocharger operation results in an increase in engine power output.

[FIGURE: A24462A.gif]

In addition to power increases, cooler air tends to lower stress on the 
engine by reducing detonation. It also reduces NOx emissions by lowering 
combustion chamber temperature.

================================================================================

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Intake Manifold

The air intake manifold directs compressed air from the charge air 
cooler to the engine cylinders, where it is used for combustion.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air-Fuel/Exhaust Gas Flow

During operation of a turbocharged engine, exhaust gas from the engine 
exhaust manifold flows into the turbine. The exhaust gas pressure and the heat 
energy extracted from the gas cause the turbine wheel to rotate which, in 
turn, causes the compressor wheel to rotate.

The cooled and expanded exhaust gas leaving the turbine wheel is 
directed by the turbine housing to engine exhaust system, which expels it to 
atmosphere.

Rotation of the compressor wheel causes ambient air from the engine air 
cleaner to be drawn into the compressor housing, where it is compressed and 
delivered to appropriate ducting which delivers it to the engine intake 
manifold.

================================================================================
PAGE 4220
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 03A-04B: Turbocharger and Charge Air Cooler, FD-1060 and FD-1460 Diesel Engines

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Lubrication

Engine oil is used to lubricate the turbocharger bearings. The oil is 
routed to the turbocharger center housing through a pressure hose connected to 
the filter head located on the engine.

[FIGURE: A24463A.gif]

The center housing supports the compressor and turbine wheel shaft in a 
pair of identical bearings which contain oil holes for directing oil to the 
bearing bores and shaft journals. Split ring seals are installed at each end 
of the shaft between the bearing and the adjacent turbine or compressor wheel 
to prevent lubricating oil from entering the turbine and the compressor area. 
Passages drilled in the center housing provide for directing oil from the 
inlet port to oil grooves machined in the bearing bores, which align with 
holes in the bearings. Due to the high rotation speeds, the bearings are the 
full-floating type that have an oil film on both the inside diameter and 
outside diameter. The pumping action of the oil flow and the shaft rotation 
cause the bearings to rotate at approximately one-third of the shaft speed.

From the center housing, the oil drains to the engine crankcase through 
an oil return tube.

It is important that maximum oil flow is maintained whenever the engine 
is operating. Without lubrication, turbocharger failure can occur within 30 
seconds during operation. To prevent turbocharger damage, observe the 
following service guidelines.

Use only high-quality, recommended engine oil.

Allow engine to idle for one minute upon start-up. This allows for 
lubrication to reach the turbocharger bearings.

Do not switch off the engine while it is running at high speed. The 
turbocharger will continue to spin for a long time without oil pressure. 
Always allow the engine to idle and run for approximately 3 to 5 minutes to 
ensure that bearings have time to cool off before shutting off the engine.

Do not run the engine without an air cleaner; even minute particles of 
dirt can cause severe turbocharger damage.

If the turbocharger has been replaced, fill the center housing rotating 
assembly through the oil supply hole with clean engine oil. As the oil is 
poured into the housing, rotate the compressor wheel to distribute the oil 
onto the bearings. This will give the bearing the initial lubrication until 
normal engine oil flow is received.

 Symptom Chart — Turbocharger 

 TURBOCHARGER 

Condition

Possible Source

Action

Excessive Black Smoke Under Load/Low Power 

 NOTE: Other engine systems can cause this condition. Refer to thePowertrain Control/Emissions Diagnosis Manual
. 

Air leak. Excess smoke and low power from a turbocharged engine can be 
caused by pressurized air leaking from loose connections or cracks in the 
crossover tube or intake manifold. This can also cause a noise problem.

CHECK entire system for leaks. PERFORM turbocharger system leak checks. 
REFER to Component Tests in this section.

Exhaust leak or restriction. Leaks or restrictions will cause the 
turbine and impeller to operate at a lower speed and reduce the amount of air 
being forced into the cylinders. Again, the symptom will be excess smoke, low 
manifold pressure and low power.

CHECK for leaks and/or restriction in exhaust system. SERVICE as 
required.

Air flow restriction. A restriction on the pressure side of the system 
will change the air-to-fuel ratio, reducing power and increasing smoke from 
the engine.

CHECK for restricted or leaking charge air cooler. PERFORM charge air 
cooler leak checks. REFER to Component Tests in this section.

Wastegate. Malfunctioning turbocharger wastegate, failure or 
miscalibration of the turbocharger wastegate can result in excessively high or 
low boost pressures. Low boost pressures can cause excessive smoke and low 
power.

CHECK wastegate function and calibration. PERFORM turbocharger 
wastegate function check. REFER to Component Tests in this section.

Turbocharger. Failure of the internal components of the turbocharger 
can reduce its effectiveness and also cause excessive smoke and low power. A 
bearing failure can produce friction, which will slow the speed of the rotor 
assembly. Failed bearings can also allow the blades of the rotor assembly to 
rub the housings, thus reducing the rotor assembly speed.

REPLACE turbocharger.

Air filter. Restriction increases as the filter removes contaminants 
from the intake air. Restricted airflow changes the air-to-fuel ratio, 
reducing power and increasing smoke from the engine.

REPLACE air filter.

High Oil Consumption

 NOTE: Other engine systems can cause this condition. Refer to thePowertrain Control/Emissions Diagnosis Manual
.

Restricted oil return line. Engine lubricating oil is used to lubricate 
the bearings and provide some cooling for the turbocharger. The oil supplied 
to the turbocharger through the supply line is at engine operating pressure. A 
return line connected to the bottom of the turbocharger routes the oil back to 
the engine oil pan. A restricted or damaged oil return line will cause the 
turbocharger housing to be pressurized, causing oil to migrate past the seals.

CLEAN or REPLACE oil return line.

Seal rings. Seal rings are used on each end of the rotor assembly. The 
primary function of the seals is to prevent exhaust gases and compressed air 
from entering the turbocharger housing. Oil leakage from the seals is rare, 
but it can occur. Do not consider a small amount of oil inside of the turbo 
housing a problem; this is normal. Since the turbo is increasing the amount of 
air into the cylinders, there will be an increase of blow-by. Blow-by carries 
oil vapors from the crankcase into the turbo housing where they condense. 
Suspect the carbon seal only if there is an excessive amount of oil in the 
turbo housing, and no other defects are found for excessive oil consumption.

REPLACE turbocharger.

Excessive blow-by.

 NOTE: Excessive crankcase pressure will not allow the oil to drain from the 
turbocharger. This will load the bearing housing and allow oil to leak past 
the compressor seals and into the engine.

REFER to Section 03B-01 for causes of excessive blow-by.

Boost Pressure High/Low

Wastegate. Turbocharger wastegate failure or miscalibration of the 
turbocharger wastegate can result in excessively high or low boost pressures. 
Low boost pressures can cause excessive smoke and low power. High boost 
pressures can cause major engine damage.

CHECK wastegate function and calibration. PERFORM turbocharger 
wastegate function check. REFER to Component Tests in this section.

Air leakage/restrictions.

REFER to Excessive Black Smoke Under Load/Low Power in this symptom 
chart.

Noise/Vibration

Air leaks. It is normal for the turbocharger to emit a whine sound that 
varies in intensity depending on engine speed and load. The sound is caused by 
the very high rotational speed of the rotor assembly. The sound will be more 
audible as engine speed increases. If possible, operate the engine at full 
speed to verify the maximum noise level. Leaks in the air system intake and/or 
exhaust components can produce additional noises.

CHECK system for leaks. PERFORM turbocharger system leak checks. REFER 
to Component Tests in this section.

Debris in system or rotor assembly contacting housing. Lower pitch 
sounds or rattles at slower engine speeds can indicate debris in the system or 
worn bearings are allowing the rotor assembly to touch the housings.

DISCONNECT exhaust pipe and outlet duct. INSPECT for debris, damage and 
signs of rotor contacting housing.

Rotor assembly imbalance. Because the rotor assembly speed is 100,000 
rpm or more, minor dents or nicks in the turbine or compressor wheel can 
result in an imbalance condition and vibration.

REPLACE turbocharger.

 Component Tests 

 Turbocharger Wastegate Functional Check 

Inspect wastegate lever pin. Replace turbocharger if excessively worn.

[FIGURE: A17632A.gif]

Check for excessive movement between shaft and bushing. Replace the 
turbocharger if shaft and bushing are damaged or seized.

[FIGURE: A17633B.gif]

Actuate lever by hand to make sure shaft rotates freely and is not 
seized.

[FIGURE: A17634A.gif]

Visually inspect wastegate actuator hose for cracks or holes. Replace 
hose if damaged.

[FIGURE: A17635A.gif]

Visually inspect wastegate mounting bracket, actuator rod and lever for 
damage. A bent wastegate actuator mounting bracket, actuator rod or lever can 
cause improper turbocharger operation.

If wastegate actuator mounting bracket is damaged, it must be replaced. 
If actuator rod is bent, replace wastegate actuator. If wastegate lever is 
bent, replace turbocharger.

[FIGURE: A17636A.gif]

Attach a dial indicator so its shaft is in line with the wastegate 
actuator rod. Set the indicator to zero, with no air pressure applied to the 
wastegate actuator.

Loosen clamp and disconnect hose at wastegate actuator.

Connect clean, regulated air pressure supply and an accurate pressure 
gauge to the actuator.

Adjust pressure to actuator until axial travel of rod is 5 mm (0.200 
inch). Pressure reading at this point should be approximately 190-204 kPa 
(27.5-29.5 psi). The rod should not begin to move until air pressure reaches 
155-162 kPa (22.5-23.5 psi). Air must not leak through actuator. An air leak 
can be determined by listening for escaping air. Replace the actuator if it 
leaks or no movement/improper movement of the actuator rod and lever is 
detected.

[FIGURE: A17637A.gif]

 Turbocharger System Leak Checks 

 Air Pressure Leaks 

Air leaks on pressure side could cause excessive smoke and a loss of 
engine power, as well as a noise problem.

Visually inspect components for loose connections or damage. Apply 
liquid soap to duct connectors, air intake adapter and air intake manifold 
cover sealing surfaces to assist in detecting any air leakage. Any bubbles 
created will indicate the leak source.

 Exhaust Leaks 

Inspect for exhaust leaks at the exhaust manifold and turbocharger, 
gasket leaks or exhaust pipe restrictions. Exhaust leaks can usually be 
detected audibly or visually by a discoloration caused by the escaping hot 
gases.

Leaks or restrictions will cause the turbine and impeller to operate at 
a lower speed and reduce the amount of air being forced into the cylinders. 
The symptoms will be excessive smoke, low manifold pressure and low power.

 Charge Air Cooler Leak Checks 

Loss of engine power, low turbocharger boost pressure and higher than 
normal exhaust temperature can be caused by a leaking charge air cooler.

Look for two types of cracks: tube cracks and/or tank weld cracks. Tube 
cracks will usually occur first in the corners of the core and will be seen 
where the tube goes into the tank. Visual inspection will usually suffice to 
find most tube cracks. A better way to locate cracks is to pressurize the 
cooler to 276 kPa (40 psi). Apply a liquid soap film to all the tank joints. 
If bubbles form, there is a tube crack present.

If tube cracks are found, replace the cooler. Refer to the Master Parts 
Catalog for proper application.

[FIGURE: Q1810C.gif]

If there are no tube cracks, check for tank weld cracks. Tank weld 
cracks can usually be seen.

Refer to Service Procedures in this section to determine appropriate 
repair for leaking or damaged charge air cooler.

 Bearing Clearance Check 

When there is reason to suspect that the turbocharger bearings are worn 
to the extent that the compressor or turbine wheel rubs the housing, perform 
the following procedures.

Loosen clamps and remove air inlet elbow.

Disconnect exhaust pipe.

With a bright light, visually inspect entire inlet and outlet surfaces 
for signs of wheel-to-housing rub. If scratching has occurred, replace 
turbocharger.

If there is no sign of wheel-to-housing rubbing/interference, proceed 
to Step 4.

Measure the shaft end play using Dial Indicator/Magnetic Base 
D78P-4201-B or equivalent. End play is represented by dimension A in 
illustration.

 Installation 

 NOTE: Service replacement turbocharger compressor outlet orientation may not 
be the same as the replaced turbocharger. If the compressor outlet orientation 
is the same, omit Steps 2, 5 and 6.

Clean turbocharger, exhaust manifold and oil drain tube gasket surfaces.

Loosen band clamp so compressor housing may be rotated.

Coat the turbocharger mounting studs with a high-temperature anti-seize 
compound and install new turbocharger-to-exhaust manifold gasket onto exhaust 
manifold mounting flange.

Install turbocharger onto exhaust manifold and install retaining nuts. 
Tighten nuts to 45 Nm (33 lb-ft).

Rotate compressor housing until outlet port aligns with air charge 
cooler inlet duct.

Tighten compressor housing band clamp to 8 Nm (71 
lb-in). Tap around the clamp with a plastic-tipped hammer and tighten again.

Using new gasket, install oil return line to turbocharger. Tighten 
return line retaining bolts to 24 Nm (18 lb-ft).

Fill turbocharger oil feed port with 50-60 cc (2-3 oz.) of recommended 
engine oil. Rotate compressor wheel by hand to lubricate bearings.

[FIGURE: A17639A.gif]

Install the oil feed line to the turbocharger. Tighten fitting to 35 Nm
 (26 lb-ft).

If removed, install O-ring, outlet adapter and clamp.

Install air charge cooler inlet duct and exhaust outlet tube.

Install inside splash shield. Connect batteries.

Disconnect fuel shutoff solenoid. Crank engine to prime turbocharger 
lubrication system.

Reconnect fuel shutoff solenoid and start engine. Check for air and oil 
leaks.

 Disassembly 

Clamp the turbocharger in a bench vise.

[FIGURE: A17647A.gif]

Scribe marks onto turbine-to-bearing housing, bearing 
housing-to-diffuser and diffuser-to-compressor housing so turbocharger can be 
reassembled with all parts in their original positions.

[FIGURE: A17648A.gif]

Loosen band clamp enough to remove from bearing housing-to-compressor 
flange.

[FIGURE: A17649A.gif]

Remove the compressor housing and inspect for impeller contact. Remove 
band clamp.

[FIGURE: A17650A.gif]

 NOTE: Turn the nut to the right to loosen; nut and shaft have left-hand 
threads.

Remove the impeller nut.

[FIGURE: A17651A.gif]

 WARNING: IMPELLER BLADES ARE VERY SHARP. WEAR GLOVES OR USE SHOP RAG WHEN 
HANDLING IMPELLER TO AVOID PERSONAL INJURY. 

 NOTE: The wheel and shaft assembly is balanced as a unit. If the impeller is 
damaged, the complete assembly must be replaced.

Remove the impeller and inspect the blades for damage.

[FIGURE: A17652A.gif]

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Charge Air Cooler, Aluminum

Listed in the following chart are the components of the air cooler 
system and the types of damage that occur. Some types of damage can be 
repaired while other types cannot. The corrective action is shown for each 
type of damage. In some cases, the cooler should be replaced not repaired.

 CHARGE AIR COOLER, ALUMINUM

Condition

Action to Take

 · Tubes torn or cracked.

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

 · Tubes dented, kinked or bent resulting in a round edge (radius less than 1
mm [1/32 in.]).

 · Weld or epoxy. Refer to Welding Repairs or Epoxy Repairs in the Service
Procedures portion of this section.

 · Tubes dented, kinked or bent resulting in a round edge (radius greater
than 1 mm [1/32 in.]).

 · No repair required.

 · Holes in tubes less than 1 mm (1/32 in.) in all directions on tube surface.

 · Weld or epoxy to fill. Refer to Welding Repairs or Epoxy Repairs in the
Service Procedures portion of this section.

 · External fins crushed or bent; no more than 1 mm (1/32 in.) height
reduction per fin row and the sidemember-to-sidemember dimension is within
specification (687 mm [26-3/4 in.]).

 · No repair required.

 · External fins pushed in with no tearing.

 · Straighten fins. Refer to Straightening in the Service Procedures portion
of this section.

 · External fins pushed in with tearing less than 10mm (3/8 in.) deep from
core face. Also tearing is less than 20% of a given fin row and less than 5%
of the total fin rows.

 · Remove loose fin material and straighten. Refer to Straightening in the
Service Procedures portion of this section.

 · External fins pushed in with tearing of more than 10mm (3/8 in.) from face
core or more than 20% of a given row or more than 5% of the total fin row.

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

 · Sidemembers bent or dented.

 · Straighten sidemember to original form. If tubes are dented or fins
crushed, refer to appropriate repair procedure in this section.

 · Sidemembers surface cracked or broken through.

 · Weld sidemember. Refer to Welding Repairs in the Service Procedures
portion of this section.

 · Headers bent or dented resulting in three or fewer tube or tube-to-header
leaks, and cracks are less than 2 mm (1/16 in.).

 · Weld header. Refer to Welding Repairs in the Service Procedures portion of
this section.

 Note: If crack is less than 1 mm (1/32 in.) repair can be
made with epoxy.

 · Headers bent or dented with more than three tube or tube-to-header leaks
or a crack width greater than 2 mm (1/16 in.).

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

 · Headers cracked.

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

 · Tank walls dented but not cracked or broken through and fit and function
of cooler is not affected.

 · No repair required.

 · Tanks cracked. Crack is no more than 2 mm (1/16 in.) wide and 20mm (3/4
in.) long.

 · Weld tanks. Refer to Welding Repairs in the Service Procedures portion of
this section.

 · Tanks cracked. Crack is more than 2 mm (1/16 in.) wide or 20mm (3/4 in.)
long.

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

 · Tanks punctured. Hole is no more than 5 mm (3/16 in.) in all directions on
tank surface.

 · Weld tanks. Refer to Welding Repairs in the Service Procedures portion of
this section.

 · Tanks punctured. Hole is more than 5 mm (3/16 in.) in any direction on
tank surface.

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

 · Tank-to-header welds cracked or porous.

 · Weld. Refer to Welding Repairs in the Service Procedures portion of this
section.

 Caution: Repair welds must not start or stop where a 
production weld ends. 

 · Threads stripped in tapped holes.

 · Drill out stripped threads and tap to accept proper helicoil insert of
same diameter and thread pitch of original hole.

 · Bosses and mounting brackets cracked or broken off, but crack or fractured
surface does not go into tank wall.

 · Weld. Refer to Welding Repairs in the Service Procedures portion of this
section.

 · Bosses or mounting brackets cracked or broken off, and crack goes into
tank wall.

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

 · Mounting pins or other hardware cracked, broken or otherwise damaged, and
repair will not affect fit, function or durability.

 · Repair to original condition.

 · Mounting pins or other hardware cracked, broken or otherwise damaged, and
repairs will affect fit, function or durability.

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Straightening

 Straightening Fins 

Use a pointed object no more than 0.5 mm in diameter at the tip that 
will allow access to the apex of the fin. Straighten fins, taking care not to 
damage louvers or distort louver angle.

 Straightening Sidemembers 

Using pliers, vise-grips or similar tool, straighten side-member from 
sides only. Never pry against tubes or header. Care must be taken not to 
damage fins, tubes or headers when straightening sidemembers.

================================================================================
PAGE 4233
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 03A-04B: Turbocharger and Charge Air Cooler, FD-1060 and FD-1460 Diesel Engines

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Welding Repairs

 Surface Preparation 

All surfaces to be welded must be free of all paint, oil, grease, water 
and other foreign matter in the area so the weld repair will adhere to the 
bare aluminum and will not be contaminated.

 Welding Tanks 

Prepare surfaces. Heat crack to chase ends until they stop. MIG weld to 
fill crack and continue bead past ends of crack approximately 25 mm (1 in.). 
Wire brush and grind excess weld material to blend with tank surface.

 Welding Sidemembers 

Prepare surface. Cut a V-shaped groove along the length of the crack to 
a depth equal to the member thickness. MIG weld to fill the groove grind 
excess material away to provide a flat surface.

 Welding Mounting Brackets 

 CAUTION: Take care not to melt fins of tube-to-header braze joint. If welding 
near core, shield core with large steel plate. This protects it from sparks 
and weld splatter and will act as a heat sink. 

Tack brackets in place so bracket will retain its correct orientation. 
MIG weld in place. Allow to air cool. Check alignment.

 Welding Tubes or Tube Header Joints 

TIG weld using aluminum wire designated Alcan MIG Electrode Wire, 
1.20-mm (3/16-in.) diameter, 4043 aluminum alloy or equivalent.

PAGE 4234
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 03A-04B: Turbocharger and Charge Air Cooler, FD-1060 and FD-1460 Diesel Engines

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Epoxy Repairs

 Surface Preparation 

Remove all paint, oil, grease, water and other foreign matter in area 
of the epoxy repair so epoxy will adhere to the bare aluminum.

 Epoxying Tubes or Headers 

Use only high-temperature epoxy. The recommended epoxy is a resin (CIBA 
GEIGY ARALDITE AV 138M) and a hardener (CIBA GEIGY HV 998) or equivalent. Mix 
and cure instructions on product label must be strictly adhered to.

PAGE 4235
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 03A-04B: Turbocharger and Charge Air Cooler, FD-1060 and FD-1460 Diesel Engines

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Cleaning After Weld or Epoxy Repairs

The cooler must be flushed after either a weld or an epoxy repair to 
remove all debris that may have dropped into the cooler during the repair.

The recommended procedure for cleaning is to power flush the cooler 
with water at a rate of 1.5 mm (5 in.)/sec. for three minutes. To assure that 
debris exits the cooler, orient the cooler so the tank containing the repair, 
or closest to the repair point, is at the bottom. The flushing water is to be 
introduced into the opposite tank at the top. When complete, invert the cooler 
and power flush in opposite direction.

If power flushing is not possible, flush cooler by hand. Lay cooler 
flat with inlet and outlet ports pointing up. Fill cooler to 40 percent of its 
volume with water, seal off both ports and agitate by hand so water flushes 
all internal surfaces at least ten times. Empty cooler and repeat flushing 
process until no more debris is found in the flushing water.

After flushing (either power or by hand) drain cooler of all water and 
allow to air dry. Leak test cooler to check all repairs prior to painting or 
installing cooler into vehicle.

================================================================================
PAGE 4236
================================================================================
1997 Cargo

Section 03A-04B: Turbocharger and Charge Air Cooler, FD-1060 and FD-1460 Diesel Engines

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Leak Testing Cooler After Repairs

 NOTE: To assure proper performance, repaired cooler must be leak-tested and 
pressure-checked prior to reinstalling it into vehicle.

Connect an air pressure gauge in one port of cooler and a stop/air 
supply in other port. Apply 345 kPa (50 psi) air pressure to cooler. Reduce 
pressure to 200 kPa (29 psi) and plug cooler to hold pressure. Let cooler 
stand a few minutes and note any loss of air pressure. Loss of air pressure 
should not exceed 10 kPa (1.5 psi) per minute. If leakage exceeds this limit, 
check cooler and make any necessary repairs. Leak test cooler again and 
continue until cooler will hold pressure as stated.

ADJUSTMENTS

Actuator Calibration

 CAUTION: The wastegate is set accurately at the factory. Adjustment is not 
necessary unless the wastegate actuator is removed. The turbocharger is a 
performance part and must not be tampered with after it is adjusted at the 
factory. Tampering with the wastegate components can reduce durability by 
increasing cylinder pressure and thermal loading due to incorrect inlet and 
exhaust manifold pressure, with a potential for poor fuel economy and failure 
to meet regulatory emissions laws. 

Before checking actuator calibration procedure, perform turbocharger 
wastegate functional test. Refer to Component Tests in this section.

Remove retaining clip and disconnect actuator rod from wastegate lever.

Adjust pressure regulator to 172 kPa (25 psi).

[FIGURE: A17637A.gif]

Pull wastegate lever toward actuator to fully close valve.

 CAUTION: Do not pull or push actuator rod to force alignment with clevis pin. 

Hole in actuator rod clevis should align with lever pin. If rod cannot 
be installed on lever, loosen clevis lock nut and turn clevis until hole 
aligns with pin.

[FIGURE: A17696A.gif]

Install retaining clip and tighten clevis lock nut.

Disconnect air supply at actuator.

Install hose on actuator and secure with clamp.

Section 03A-05: Drive Belts, Accessory, FD-1060 Diesel Engine

1997 Cargo Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Drive Belt, Accessory 

Ford FD-1060 diesel engine is equipped with a poly-V accessory drive 
belt. The drive belt type is selected for each engine based on performance 
requirements. To ensure maximum life, replacement belt must be of the same 
type as originally installed. The belt must be properly adjusted at all times. 
A loose belt will result in slippage, which can cause a noise complaint or 
improper accessory operation (generator will not charge, etc.). An overly 
tight belt will place severe loads on accessory bearings. 

The poly-V drive belt tension is maintained by an automatic belt 
tensioner. Regular inspection is required to check belt condition to ensure 
that excessive belt stretch does not occur. 

[FIGURE: Q4052A.gif]

Fan and Clutch, Engine Operated

The fan and clutch assembly is used to cool the engine. The fan is
